 مِثْلُ الشَّيْخِ جاكير أَوْ أَبِي الْوَفَاءِ أَوْ نُورِ الدِّينِ الشَّهِيدِ أَوْ غَيْرِهِمْ أَمْ لَا؟ وَكَذَلِكَ هَلْ تَجُوزُ النُّذُورُ لِقُبُورِ أَحَدٍ مِنْ آلِ بَيْتِ النُّبُوَّةِ وَمُدْرِكِهِ وَالْأَئِمَّةِ الْأَرْبَعَةِ وَمَشَايِخِ الْعِرَاقِ وَالْعَجَمِ وَمِصْرَ وَالْحِجَازِ وَالْيَمَنِ وَالْهِنْدِ وَالْمَغْرِبِ وَجَمِيعِ الْأَرْضِ وَجَبَلِ قَانٍ وَغَيْرِهَا أَمْ لَا؟ .
translated_text:
And is it permissible to seek out graves as places for supplication, to kiss them, or to light lanterns and lamps beside them? Do these acts performed by the living bring any benefit or harm to the dead?

And what of supplication at the “Prophet’s Footprint” in Dār al-Hadīth al-Ashrafiyyah in Damascus and elsewhere; at the footprint of Moses, the cradle of Jesus, the Station of Abraham, and the head of al-Husayn; at sites associated with Suhayb al-Rūmī, Bilāl al-Habashī, and Uways al-Qaranī; and at similar places throughout the lands, villages, coasts, mountains, shrines, mosques, and congregational mosques?

Likewise, what of their claim that supplication is answered at the tower of Bāb Kaysān, between Bāb al-Saghīr and Bāb al-Sharqī, when one turns one’s back to it and faces the qiblah; and what of supplication just inside Bāb al-Farrādīn? Has anything been established concerning supplications being answered at these places, or not?

Is it permissible to seek help from someone other than Allah Most High by saying, “O rank of Muhammad!” or “O Lady Nafīsah!” or “O my master Ahmad!”; or, when someone stumbles, encounters difficulty, or jumps from one place to another, to say, “O Ali!” or “O Shaykh so-and-so!”—or not?

Is it permissible to make vows to prophets or shaykhs, such as Shaykh Jākīr, Abū al-Wafā’, Nūr al-Dīn the Martyr, or others—or not? Likewise, is it permissible to make vows to the graves of any members of the Prophet’s household, Mudrikah, the four imams, or the shaykhs of Iraq, Persia, Egypt, the Hijaz, Yemen, India, the Maghreb, and throughout the earth, or to Mount Qān and other places—or not?

translated_text:
He replied:

All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds.

As for the claim that supplications are answered at the graves of the four aforementioned shaykhs—may Allah be pleased with them—it is of the same kind as someone else’s statement, “So-and-so’s grave is the tried-and-tested antidote,” and similar claims that supplications are answered at the graves of particular individuals.

Many people make such statements about certain graves. The grave in question may be known to belong to a righteous man from among the Companions, the Prophet’s household, or other righteous people. Alternatively, its attribution to that person may be false or unverified, as is the case with most alleged graves of prophets. The attribution may also be correct, yet the man himself may not have been righteous. All these cases occur in connection with people who make such claims, or who say that supplications are answered at a particular grave and that their own supplications were answered there, when in fact it is either the grave of someone known for sinfulness and religious innovation or the grave of a disbeliever. We have seen someone who supplicated and was then astonished when the truth about the graves was disclosed to him. We have witnessed various instances of this.

The fundamental point is this: the claim that supplications are answered at the graves of prophets and righteous people has no basis in the Book of Allah or the Sunnah of His Messenger. Nor was it stated by any of the Companions, those who followed them in righteousness, or any of the Muslim imams renowned for their leadership in religion, such as Mālik, al-Thawrī, al-Awzā'ī, al-Layth ibn Sa'd, Abū Hanīfah, al-Shāfi'ī, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and Ishāq

translated_text:
ibn Rāhawayh and Abū 'Ubaydah, nor by their shaykhs who served as exemplars, such as al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyād, Ibrāhīm ibn Adham, Abū Sulaymān al-Dārānī, and others like them.

None of the Companions, the Successors, or the early imams and shaykhs said that supplications are answered at the graves of prophets and righteous people, whether as a general claim or concerning particular graves. Nor did any of them say that supplicating at the graves of prophets and righteous people is better than supplicating elsewhere, or that prayer in such a place is better than prayer elsewhere. None of them deliberately sought out these graves for supplication or prayer.

Indeed, the best of all creation and their master is the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace. There is no grave on earth unanimously acknowledged to be that of a prophet except his; people have differed concerning the grave of Abraham, Allah’s intimate friend, and those of other prophets. The imams agree that, when visiting him, one should greet him and his two Companions with peace, in accordance with the report in the Sunan collections from Abū Hurayrah—may Allah be pleased with him—that the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“No man greets me with peace without Allah restoring my soul to me so that I may return his greeting.”

This is a good hadith. Ibn Abī Shaybah and al-Dāraqutnī also narrated from him:

“Whoever greets me with peace at my grave, I hear him; and whoever invokes blessings upon me from afar, it is conveyed to me.”

Its chain of transmission contains some weakness, but it has established corroborating reports. The compilers of the Sunan collections have narrated through several routes that blessings and greetings of peace invoked upon him from afar are conveyed to him. Thus, the Sunan collections report that he—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“Invoke blessings upon me frequently on Friday and on the night preceding Friday,

translated_text:
for your invocations of blessings are presented to me.”

They asked, “How will our invocations of blessings be presented to you when you have crumbled away?”—that is, decayed.

He replied, “Allah Most High has forbidden the earth to consume the flesh of the prophets.”

Al-Nasā’ī and others also narrated that he—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“Allah has assigned angels to my grave who convey to me the greetings of peace from my community.”

Despite this, none of them said that supplications are answered at his grave, or that it is recommended to make a point of supplicating while facing his grave. Rather, they explicitly stated the opposite, and all agreed that one should not supplicate while facing the grave. They differed, however, concerning greeting him with peace.

The majority, including Mālik, Ahmad, and others, said that one should greet him with peace while facing the grave. This is also what al-Shāfi‘ī’s followers stated, and I believe it is reported from him as well. Abū Hanīfah and his followers, however, said that one should greet him with peace while facing the qiblah.

“I do not consider it appropriate for someone to stand at the grave of the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—and supplicate. Rather, he should greet him with peace and move on.”

He also said in al-Mabsūt:

“There is no harm in someone returning from a journey or setting out on one standing at the grave of the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—invoking blessings upon him, and supplicating for him and for Abū Bakr and ‘Umar.”

I say:

The numerous hadiths reported concerning visiting his grave are all weak—indeed, fabricated. Neither the leading hadith scholars nor the compilers of the recognized Sunan collections, such as those of Abū Dāwūd and al-Nasā’ī, transmitted anything on this subject. However, the expression “visiting graves” occurs in other hadiths, such as his words—may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“I had forbidden you to visit graves. Now visit them, for they remind you of the Hereafter.”

He—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—used to teach his Companions that, when visiting graves, each of them should say:

“Peace be upon you, inhabitants of these dwellings, believers and Muslims. We shall, if Allah wills, join you. May Allah have mercy on those among us and you who have gone before and those who come later. We ask Allah for well-being for ourselves and for you.”

Yet, in the customary usage of many later generations, the expression “visiting graves” has come to encompass both innovated visits and visits prescribed by the religion. Most of them use it only in the innovated sense, not the prescribed one. This is why using the expression without qualification was considered objectionable.

As for visiting graves in the prescribed manner, it is akin to the funeral prayer over the deceased: its purpose is to supplicate for the deceased, just as that is the purpose of the funeral prayer. Thus Allah said concerning the hypocrites:

“Never pray over any of them who dies, nor stand at his grave.”

Standing at a believer’s grave after burial is akin to praying over him before burial: its purpose is to supplicate for him. This is the practice established by the Sunnah and recommended by the early generations when visiting the graves of prophets and righteous people.

As for “innovated visits,” they belong to the category of polytheism and the means leading to it, as exemplified by what the Jews and Christians did at the graves of prophets and righteous people. He—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said in hadiths widely transmitted in the collections of authentic hadith, the Sunan collections, and the Musnad collections:

“May Allah curse the Jews and Christians, who took the graves of their prophets as places of worship.”

He was warning against what they had done. He also said:

“Those before you used to take graves as places of worship. Take heed: do not take graves as places of worship, for I forbid you to do so.”

He also said:

“Among the worst of people are those who are alive when the Hour overtakes them, and those who take graves as places of worship.”

He also said:

“Allah has cursed women who visit graves and those who establish places of worship over them and place lamps upon them.”

Since he cursed those who take the graves of prophets and righteous people as places of worship, deliberately choosing these graves for supplication cannot be recommended. Wherever supplication is recommended, prayer is also recommended, since supplication following prayer is more likely to be answered. There is no place in Islamic law where prayer is prohibited yet supplication is recommended. translated_text:
by fear that the grave may lead people astray, not merely by its impurity, as some people suppose. For this reason, the early generations instructed that graves be levelled and that the traces of those liable to lead people astray be effaced. Thus, when Daniel’s grave was discovered in Tustar, ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb ordered that its traces be effaced. Abū Mūsā had written to him, mentioning that Daniel’s grave had been discovered and that people used to seek rain through him. ‘Umar wrote back, instructing him to dig thirteen graves during the day, then bury him in one of them at night and efface its traces, so that people would not be led astray through him.

What we have mentioned from Mālik and other leading scholars was well known among the early generations. Abū Ya‘lā al-Mawsilī narrated in his Musnad, and the hadith master Abū ‘Abd Allāh al-Maqdisī included in his selected collection, a report from ‘Alī ibn al-Husayn ibn ‘Alī ibn Abī Tālib, known as Zayn al-‘Ābidīn. He saw a man coming to an opening beside the Prophet’s grave—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—entering it and supplicating there. He forbade him from doing so, saying:

“Shall I not relate to you a hadith that I heard from my father, from my grandfather, from the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace? He said: ‘Do not make my grave a place of recurring observance, nor make your houses graves, for your greetings of peace reach me wherever you may be.’”

This hadith also appears in Sunan Abī Dāwūd, on the authority of Abū Hurayrah, who said: “The Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

‘Do not make your houses graves, nor make my grave a place of recurring observance. Send blessings upon me, for your blessings reach me wherever you may be.’”

translated_text:
al-Husayn ibn ‘Alī ibn Abī Tālib at the grave. He called to me while eating supper in Fātimah’s house, saying, ‘Come to supper.’ I replied, ‘I do not want any.’ He asked, ‘Why were you at the grave?’ I replied, ‘I greeted the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace.’

He said, ‘When you enter the mosque, offer your greeting of peace.’ Then he said, ‘The Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said: “Do not make my house a place of recurring observance, nor make your houses graves. May Allah curse the Jews: they took the graves of their prophets as places of worship. Send blessings upon me, for your blessings reach me wherever you may be. You and those in al-Andalus are alike.”’”

This principle has been discussed at length elsewhere. If this is what is prescribed concerning the grave of the foremost of Adam’s descendants, the best of creation and the most honoured of them before Allah, then what can be said concerning anyone else’s grave?

It has been transmitted through numerous independent reports from the Companions that whenever hardships befell them—as in times of drought and when seeking rain, or during battle and when seeking victory—they would supplicate to Allah and seek His aid in mosques and houses. They did not deliberately seek to supplicate at the grave of the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—or at any other graves of prophets and righteous people.

Indeed, it is established in the Sahīh that ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb said:

“O Allah, when drought afflicted us, we used to seek a means of approach to You through our Prophet, and You would grant us rain. Now we seek a means of approach to You through our Prophet’s uncle, so grant us rain.” They would then be granted rain.

Thus, they sought a means of approach to Allah through al-‘Abbās, just as they had done through the Prophet—that is, through his supplication and intercession. translated_text:
the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—nor did they adjure Allah by any of His creatures. Rather, they sought a means of approach to Him through the means He prescribed: righteous deeds and the supplications of believers. Thus, a servant seeks a means of approach to Allah through faith in His Prophet, love and allegiance to him, and sending blessings and peace upon him. Just as they sought a means of approach through his supplication and intercession during his lifetime, so too will people seek a means of approach through his supplication and intercession in the Hereafter.

One may also seek a means of approach through the supplications of the righteous, as the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“Are you granted victory and provision except through the weak among you—through their supplications, prayers and seeking forgiveness?”

It is self-evident that if supplicating at graves were better than supplicating elsewhere, more beloved to Allah and more readily answered, the early generations would have known this better than later generations and would have hastened to it. They knew best what Allah loves and is pleased with, and were foremost in obeying Him and seeking His pleasure. The Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—would also have explained this and encouraged it. For he commanded everything good and forbade everything evil. He left nothing that brings one closer to Paradise without telling his community about it, nor anything that distances one from the Fire without warning his community against it. He left his community upon a clear path, whose night is as bright as its day; none turns away from it after him except one who is doomed.

How could that be, when he forbade this kind of practice and cut it off at its root through his curse and his prohibition against taking graves as places of worship? He thus forbade praying to Allah while facing graves, even if the person praying neither worships the dead nor invokes them—just as prayer was forbidden at sunrise and sunset, because these are

the times when the polytheists prostrate to the sun—even though the person praying prostrates only to Allah—as a safeguard against what leads to such wrongdoing. How much more so when the harm actually occurs, with a person invoking the deceased and supplicating through him, just as it occurs when someone prostrates to the sun at sunrise or sunset!

Idol worship originally arose from the veneration of graves, as Allah Most High says:

“And they said, ‘Never abandon your gods; never abandon Wadd, Suwā‘, Yaghūth, Ya‘ūq, or Nasr.’”

The early generations, including Ibn ‘Abbās and others, said: These were righteous men among the people of Noah. When they died, people devoted themselves to their graves, then made images of them, and then worshipped them.

Furthermore, it is well known that among those buried in the Bāb al-Saghīr cemetery are Companions, their Successors, and the generation after them who are superior to these four shaykhs. Why, then, should these four be singled out for supplication at their graves rather than those who are superior to them? Moreover, each of these shaykhs and others like them has people who love him and honour him through supplication, rather than another shaykh. Has Allah commanded that supplication be offered at the grave of one rather than another, as the polytheists do with them? These people resemble those who

“took their rabbis and monks as lords besides Allah, and the Messiah, son of Mary, though they were commanded only to worship one God. There is no deity except Him. Exalted is He above whatever they associate with Him.”

Section

As for the statement attributed to some shaykhs:

“If a calamity or something you fear befalls you, turn to me, and your distress will be relieved, whether I am alive or dead.”

Such words and others like them are either a lie on the part of the transmitter or an error on the part of the speaker. This is a report of unknown authenticity attributed to someone who is not infallible. Whoever abandons an authenticated report from an infallible speaker and follows an unauthenticated report from someone who is not infallible has indeed strayed far astray. It is well known that neither Allah nor His messengers commanded anything of this kind. Rather, Allah Most High said:

“So when you have finished, strive diligently, and to your Lord direct your longing.”

He did not say: “Direct your longing to the prophets and angels.” And He Most High said:

“Say, ‘Call upon those whom you claim besides Him. They have no power to remove harm from you or transfer it.’ Those whom they invoke themselves seek a means of drawing near to their Lord, competing to be nearest; they hope for His mercy and fear His punishment. Indeed, your Lord’s punishment is to be feared.”

A group of the early generations said: Some people used to invoke Ezra, the Messiah, and the angels, so Allah revealed this verse.

The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, never said to any of his Companions:

“Be mindful of Allah, and He will protect you. Be mindful of Allah, and you will find Him before you. Know Allah in times of ease, and He will know you in times of hardship. When you ask, ask Allah; when you seek help, seek help from Allah.”

As for the report circulated by some ordinary people that he said:

“When you ask Allah, ask Him by virtue of my standing, for my standing with Allah is great.”

This is a false, fabricated hadith. No scholar has transmitted it, nor does it appear in any of the Muslims’ authoritative religious books. If a deceased person possesses any virtue, the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, has the greatest claim to every virtue, followed by his Companions. And if the living can benefit through the dead, his Companions would have been the people most entitled to benefit through him, both during his life and after his death.

It is thus clear that this is a form of misguidance. Even if one of the shaykhs did say this, it was an error on his part. Allah will forgive him if he exercised independent scholarly judgment and erred. He is not a prophet whose words must be followed, nor is he infallible in what he commands and forbids. Allah Most High has said:

“If you disagree over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger, if you believe in Allah and the Last Day.”

Seeking nearness through such an act constitutes associating partners with the Lord of all worlds. There is no doubt that Shaykh ‘Abd al-Qādir neither said this nor commanded it. Whoever attributes such a statement to him has lied about him. Such innovations are introduced only by people given to excess and associating partners with Allah: innovators who resemble the Christians, such as the Rāfidah who go to extremes concerning the imams, and those who resemble them in going to extremes concerning the shaykhs.

It is established in the Sahīh that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Do not sit on graves or pray facing them.”

If he forbade facing a grave when praying to Allah, how could it be permissible to turn toward it and supplicate to someone other than Allah, even from a distant dwelling? Is this not the same kind of conduct as that of the Christians toward Jesus, his mother, their religious scholars, and their monks, taking them as lords and gods whom they invoke, whose aid they seek in pursuing their needs, whom they ask, and through whom they make requests?

Some people deliberately choose to pray and supplicate at what is said to be the grave of a prophet, one of the Companions, or a member of the Prophet’s family, or at similar sites. Others press their bodies, or some part of their bodies, against a grave or against an adjacent piece of wood or other object. This includes someone who deliberately chooses to pray and supplicate on the southeastern side of the Great Mosque of Damascus, at the place said to be the grave of Hūd—although the scholars hold that it is the grave of Mu‘āwiyah ibn Abī Sufyān—or beside the wooden representation beneath which the head of John son of Zechariah is said to lie, and similar practices. As for his question:

“Is supplication especially likely to be accepted or answered swiftly at a particular time or place—at the grave of a prophet or a friend of Allah?”

There is no doubt that supplication is more readily answered at some times and in some circumstances than others. The depths of the night are the time when supplication is most readily answered, as established in the two Sahīh collections from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, who said:

“Our Lord descends to the lowest heaven when the last third of the night remains—in another narration, half the night—and says: ‘Who will call upon Me, that I may answer him? Who will ask Me, that I may give him? Who will seek My forgiveness, that I may forgive him?’—until dawn breaks.”

Another hadith states:

“The Lord is closest to His servant in the latter part of the night.”

Supplication is answered when rain falls, when battle is joined, at the adhān and iqāmah, at the close of prayers, and while prostrating. Likewise, the supplications of a fasting person, a traveller, and someone who has been wronged are answered, as are other supplications of this kind. All of this is attested by

the well-known hadiths in the Sahīh and Sunan collections. The same applies to supplication at the sacred pilgrimage sites, such as ʿArafah, Muzdalifah, Minā, al-Multazam and other sacred sites in Mecca, and to supplication in mosques generally. The greater a mosque’s merit—as with the three mosques—the greater the merit of prayer and supplication within it.

As for supplicating at a place because it contains the grave of a prophet or a friend of Allah, none of the early generations of the Muslim community or its imams ever said that supplication there is better than elsewhere. Rather, this is something introduced by some of those who pray towards the qiblah, in imitation of Christians and other polytheists. Its origin lies in the religion of the polytheists, not in the religion of Allah’s sincere servants. The same applies to taking graves as places of worship: none of the early generations of the Muslim community or its imams considered this recommended. Rather, some of those who pray towards the qiblah introduced it in imitation of those Jews and Christians whom the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, cursed.

Or is it permissible, when petitioning Allah, to adjure Him by the right of so-and-so, the sanctity of so-and-so, or the standing of those brought near to Him

translated_text:
by those creatures nearest to Him, or to adjure Him by their deeds and actions?”

The answer is:

This question involves several distinct issues.

The supplications transmitted in the Sunnah include asking Allah by His names and attributes and seeking refuge in His speech. Among the supplications recorded in the Sunan collections are his words:

“O Allah, I ask You by the fact that all praise belongs to You. You are Allah, Originator of the heavens and the earth. O Possessor of Majesty and Honour, O Ever-Living, O Sustainer of all!”

And his words:

“O Allah, I ask You by the fact that You are Allah, the One, the Eternal Refuge, who neither begets nor is born, and to whom none is equal.”

Another example is the supplication recorded in the Musnad:

“O Allah, I ask You by every name belonging to You with which You have named Yourself, which You have revealed in Your Book, which You have taught to any of Your creation, or which You have kept to Yourself in the knowledge of the unseen with You.”

As for the supplications recited by some ordinary people and written out by amulet sellers among the Turuqiyya, which contain such words as:

“I ask You by Ihtiyāt Qāf—which is Yūfi al-Mukhāf—and by Mount Sinai, the Throne, the Footstool, Zamzam, the Station of Abraham, and the Sacred City,”

neither these nor similar supplications have been transmitted from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, from the Companions, or from the imams of the Muslims. No one may swear by these things under any circumstances. Rather, it is authentically established that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever wishes to swear an oath must swear by Allah or remain silent.”

He also said:

“Whoever swears by anything other than Allah has committed shirk.”

Thus, no one may swear by created things at all. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, also said:

translated_text:
“Among Allah’s servants are those who, if they adjure Allah, He will fulfil their oath.”

He said this when Anas ibn al-Nadr said: “Will al-Rubayyiʿ’s front tooth be broken? No, by Him who sent you with the truth, al-Rubayyiʿ’s front tooth will not be broken!”

Likewise, al-Barā’ ibn Mālik said: “I adjure You, my Lord, to do such and such.” Both were among those whose oaths Allah would fulfil.

A servant asks his Lord through the means that bring about what he seeks: righteous deeds for which Allah has promised reward, and the supplications of His believing servants whom He has promised to answer. Thus, the Companions would seek a means of approach to Allah Most High through His Prophet, then through his uncle and other righteous men among them. They did so through his supplication and intercession, as recorded in the Sahīh: ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb—may Allah be pleased with him—sought rain through al-ʿAbbās, saying:

“O Allah, we used to seek a means of approach to You through our Prophet, and You would grant us rain. Now we seek a means of approach to You through our Prophet’s uncle, so grant us rain.”

They would then be granted rain. After the Prophet’s death, they sought a means of approach through al-ʿAbbās, just as they had done through the Prophet; this was through his supplication and intercession.

Another example is the report transmitted by the compilers of the Sunan and graded authentic by al-Tirmidhī:

“A man said to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: ‘Supplicate to Allah to restore my sight.’ He instructed him to perform ablution, pray two units of prayer, and say: ‘O Allah, I ask You and turn to You through Your Prophet Muhammad, the Prophet of mercy. O Muhammad, O Messenger of Allah, I turn through you to my Lord concerning this need of mine, that He may fulfil it. O Allah, accept his intercession on my behalf.’”

This man made his request of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, who instructed him to ask Allah to accept the Prophet’s intercession on his behalf. His turning to Allah through His Prophet was like the other Companions’ seeking a means of approach to Allah through him, for

translated_text:
this turning to Allah and seeking a means of approach is through his supplication and intercession.

As for someone saying:

“I ask You, or adjure You, by the right of Your angels, or by the right of Your prophets, or by Your prophet so-and-so, or by Your messenger so-and-so, or by the Sacred House, or by Zamzam and the Station, or by Mount Sinai and the Frequented House,”

or similar expressions, this kind of supplication has not been transmitted from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, his Companions, or those who followed them in righteousness. Indeed, a number of scholars, including Abū Hanīfah and his companions—such as Abū Yūsuf—and other scholars, explicitly stated that such supplication is impermissible. For the person has adjured Allah by a created being, and an oath by anything other than Allah is not valid, even if he asks Him through it on the grounds that it is a cause and a means of having his need fulfilled.

But when someone asks Allah through righteous deeds and through the supplication of His Prophet and His righteous servants, righteous deeds are a cause of reward, and supplication is a cause of receiving an answer. Asking Him through these is therefore asking through something that is a cause of attaining what is sought. This is the meaning of what is reported in the supplication said when going out to prayer:

“O Allah, I ask You by the right that those who ask You have upon You, and by the right of this walk of mine.”

Likewise, the people in the cave supplicated to Allah through their righteous deeds. Seeking a means of approach to Allah through the prophets therefore means doing so through faith in them and obedience to them—such as invoking blessings and peace upon them, loving them, and being loyal to them—or through their supplication and intercession.

As for their very persons, there is nothing in them that entails the fulfilment of what the servant seeks, even though they possess great standing and an exalted rank with Allah because of His honouring them, His kindness to them, and His bounty toward them. Nor is there

As for the saying that some of the common people attribute to him:

Section

As for the questioner’s words:

“Is it permissible to venerate a place containing khalūq (perfume) and saffron because the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was seen there?”

The answer is: Rather, venerating such places and turning them into mosques and places of visitation for that reason is among the practices of the People of the Book, whom we have been forbidden to imitate in these matters.

It is established that, while travelling, ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb saw some people hastening towards a place. He asked, “What is this?” They replied, “A place where the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prayed.”

He said, “And what if it is a place where the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prayed? Do you intend to turn the sites associated with your prophets into mosques? Whoever is there when the prayer falls due should pray; otherwise, he should continue on his way.”

ʿUmar said this in the presence of the Companions. It is well known that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would pray during his journeys

translated_text:
in various places. Believers would also see him in dreams in various places, yet the early generations did not turn any of these into a mosque or a place of visitation. Were this door opened, many—or most—Muslim homes would become mosques and places of visitation, for people continue to see the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in dreams, coming to their homes. Some see him many times. Perfuming these places with saffron is a disapproved innovation.

As for the further claims that liars invent—for example, when a footprint is seen somewhere and people say, “This is his footprint,” and similar claims—all of this is false. The stone footprints that people transport, claiming that they mark where he placed his foot, are a fabricated lie. Were they genuine, it would have been prescribed for Muslims to make such a place a mosque and a place of visitation. Yet Allah has not commanded that the standing-place of any prophet be made a place of prayer except the standing-place of Abraham, saying:

“And take the standing-place of Abraham as a place of prayer.”

Likewise, He has not commanded the touching and kissing of any stone except the Black Stone, nor prayer towards any house except the Sacred House. By the agreement of the Muslims, it is impermissible to extend this by analogy to anything else. Rather, that would be like instituting a pilgrimage for people to somewhere other than the Ancient House, or imposing a month of fasting other than the month of Ramadan, and similar things.

Thus, by the agreement of the Muslims, it is not prescribed to touch or kiss the Rock in Jerusalem. Nor does prayer or supplication beside it have any special merit over other parts of the mosque. وَأَمَّا الْأَشْجَارُ وَالْأَحْجَارُ وَالْعُيُونُ وَنَحْوُهَا مِمَّا يَنْذِرُ لَهَا بَعْضُ الْعَامَّةِ
translated_text:
are better than prayer and supplication beside it. When Umar ibn al-Khattāb conquered the city, he said to Kaʿb al-Ahbār, “Where do you think I should build the Muslims’ prayer hall?”

He replied, “Build it behind the Rock.”

Umar said, “Judaism has influenced you, son of a Jewish woman! Rather, I shall build it in front of the Rock, for the foremost parts of mosques belong to us.” He then built this prayer hall, which ordinary people call “al-Aqsā.” He neither rubbed the Rock nor kissed it nor prayed beside it. How could he have done so, when it is established in the Sahīh that, upon kissing the Black Stone, he said, “By Allah, I know that you are a stone that can neither harm nor benefit. Had I not seen the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, kissing you, I would not have kissed you.” When Abdullah ibn Umar came to al-Aqsā Mosque, he would pray there without going to the Rock. The same was true of others among the early generations.

Likewise, kissing or rubbing the burial chamber of our Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, the burial chamber of Abraham, the Close Friend of Allah, or other burial places containing a prophet or a righteous man is not recommended, by agreement of the imams. Rather, it is forbidden. Prostrating to any of these is disbelief, as is addressing the deceased in terms with which the Lord is addressed, such as saying, “Forgive me my sins,” or “Grant me victory over my enemy,” and the like.

He ordered that tree to be cut down, and it was cut down. The scholars of religion have agreed that if someone vows to perform an act of worship at any such place, this is not a vow that must be fulfilled, nor is there any special merit in worshipping there.

Allah through prayer, supplication, remembrance, recitation, and similar acts, except the mosques of the Muslims and the sacred sites of Hajj.

As for shrines over graves, whether or not they have been made into mosques; sites associated with particular prophets or righteous people; grottoes, caves, and other such places—these include “the Mount,” where Allah spoke to Moses; “the Cave of Hirāʾ,” where the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to worship before revelation came to him; “the cave” mentioned by Allah in His words, “one of two, when they were in the cave”; the cave on Mount Qāsiyūn in Damascus known as “the Cave of Blood”; and the two sites on its eastern and western sides, one called “the Station of Abraham” and the other “the Station of Jesus.” These and similar places and shrines throughout the east and west are not places to which travel for the purpose of visiting is prescribed. If someone vows to travel to them, he is not obliged to fulfil his vow, by agreement of the leading scholars of the Muslims.

Indeed, it is established in the two Sahīh collections, through the reports of Abū Hurayrah and Abū Saʿīd—and it is also narrated from others—that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Journeys are not to be undertaken except to three mosques: the Sacred Mosque, al-Aqsā Mosque, and this mosque of mine.”

When the Companions of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, conquered these lands—Greater Syria, Iraq, Egypt, Khurāsān, the Maghreb, and elsewhere—they did not seek out these places or visit them, nor did they deliberately seek to pray or supplicate there. Rather, they were

holding firmly to the law of their Prophet, maintaining the mosques concerning which Allah said:

“Who is more unjust than those who prevent Allah’s name from being mentioned in His mosques?”

And He said:

“Allah’s mosques are maintained only by those who believe in Allah and the Last Day, establish prayer, give zakāh, and fear none but Allah.”

And He, the Exalted, said:

“Say, ‘My Lord has commanded justice.’ And direct your faces to Him at every place of worship.”

And He, the Exalted, said:

“The mosques belong to Allah, so do not invoke anyone alongside Allah.”

There are other texts of this kind.

In the two Sahīh collections, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is reported to have said:

“A man’s prayer in the mosque surpasses his prayer at home or in the marketplace by twenty-five degrees. That is because, when a man performs ablution thoroughly and then comes to the mosque, prompted by nothing but prayer there, one of his two steps raises him a degree and the other removes a sin. When he sits awaiting prayer, he is counted as being in prayer for as long as he awaits it. When he has finished praying, the angels continue to pray for him as long as he remains in his place of prayer, saying, ‘O Allah, forgive him. O Allah, have mercy on him.’”

The later scholars differed concerning someone who travels to visit a prophet’s grave or other such shrines. Those among them who critically examined the matter held that this is a journey undertaken in disobedience to Allah, during which he is not to shorten his prayers, just as he is not to shorten them on any journey undertaken in disobedience to Allah. This was stated by Ibn ʿAqīl and others. Abū ʿAbd Allāh ibn Battah likewise stated that this is among the innovations introduced into Islam.

Indeed, deliberately seeking out these places to pray and supplicate there has no basis in Islamic law. Nor has it been transmitted from the earliest forerunners—may Allah be pleased

with them and grant them His pleasure—that they deliberately sought out these places for supplication and prayer. Rather, they went only to Allah’s mosques. Indeed, they did not even seek out mosques built contrary to Islamic law, such as the mosque built to cause harm, concerning which Allah said:

“And those who established a mosque to cause harm, promote disbelief, divide the believers, and provide an outpost for those who had previously fought against Allah and His Messenger—they will surely swear, ‘We intended nothing but good.’ But Allah bears witness that they are certainly liars.”

“Never stand in prayer there. A mosque founded on piety from the first day is more worthy of your standing in prayer there. In it are men who love to purify themselves, and Allah loves those who purify themselves.”

Furthermore, prayer is not permissible in mosques built over the graves of prophets and righteous people, and building them is forbidden, as several leading scholars have explicitly stated. This is because it is widely reported from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in the Sahīh, Sunan, and Musnad collections that he said:

“Those before you used to take graves as places of worship. Beware! Do not take graves as places of worship, for I forbid you to do so.”

During his final illness, he said:

“May Allah’s curse be upon the Jews and Christians: they took the graves of their prophets as places of worship.”

He was warning against what they had done. ʿĀ’ishah said, “Were it not for that, his grave would have been left exposed.” But he disliked the prospect of its being made a place of worship.

The chamber of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was outside his mosque. When al-Walīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik was ruler, he wrote to ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz

The chamber thus became part of the mosque. They built its enclosure in a pointed shape, out of alignment with the qiblah, so that no one would pray towards it.

Likewise, when the Muslims conquered the land, the “grave of Abraham, the Friend of Allah” was surrounded by the Solomonic wall. No one entered it or prayed beside it. Rather, the Muslims prayed in a mosque in the village of Hebron. This remained the case during the time of the Rightly Guided Caliphs and their successors, until that wall was breached and then fitted with a doorway.

It is said that the Christians were the ones who breached it and made it a church. Then, when the Muslims took the land from them, it was made into a mosque. For this reason, the righteous Muslim scholars would not pray in that place.

This is so even when the grave is genuine. How much more so when most graves attributed to the prophets are falsely identified? One example is the grave said to be the “grave of Noah”: this is undoubtedly a false attribution, put forward by ignorant people only relatively recently. The same applies to other such graves.

the Muslims would reside there to guard the frontier in Allah’s cause. The same was true of other places of this kind, such as Mount Lebanon, Alexandria, ‘Abbādān and similar places in Iraq, and Qazwīn and other towns that were frontier strongholds. The righteous would travel to these places to guard the frontier in Allah’s cause. It is established in Sahīh Muslim, on the authority of Salmān al-Fārisī, that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Guarding the frontier for a day and a night in Allah’s cause is better than fasting and praying at night for a month. Whoever dies while guarding the frontier dies as one striving in Allah’s cause. The reward for his deeds continues to accrue to him, his provision from Paradise continues to reach him, and he is kept safe from the one who puts him to trial.”

In Sunan Abī Dāwūd and elsewhere, ‘Uthmān reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Guarding the frontier for one day in Allah’s cause is better than a thousand days spent in any other place.”

Abū Hurayrah said: “I would rather spend one night guarding the frontier in Allah’s cause than spend the Night of Decree in prayer beside the Black Stone.”

For this reason, the scholars said that guarding the frontier strongholds is better than residing near the Two Noble Sanctuaries, because guarding the frontier is a form of jihad, whereas residing near the sanctuaries is a form of Hajj. By the consensus of the Muslims, jihad as a category is superior to Hajj as a category. As Allah Most High says:

“Do you consider providing water to pilgrims and maintaining the Sacred Mosque equal to the deeds of one who believes in Allah and the Last Day and strives in Allah’s cause? They are not equal in Allah’s sight, and Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.”

“Those who believe, emigrate, and strive in Allah’s cause with their wealth

and their lives are greater in rank in Allah’s sight, and it is they who will triumph.”

“Their Lord gives them glad tidings of mercy from Him, His good pleasure, and gardens where lasting bliss awaits them.”

“They will remain there forever. Indeed, with Allah is a tremendous reward.”

This, then, is the basis for holding these places in esteem. Some of them were subsequently inhabited by disbelievers and people of religious innovation and wickedness. Others fell into ruin, and places other than these became frontier strongholds. The rulings applying to places change as the circumstances of their inhabitants change. A place may be an abode of unbelief when its inhabitants are disbelievers, then become an abode of Islam when they embrace Islam. Thus Mecca—may Allah ennoble it—was initially an abode of unbelief and war. Allah said of it:

“How many a town was mightier than your town which drove you out!”

Then, when the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, conquered it, it became an abode of Islam, although in itself it is the Mother of Towns and the land most beloved to Allah. Likewise, the Holy Land was inhabited by the mighty people whom Allah Most High mentioned. As He Most High said:

“And when Moses said to his people, ‘O my people, remember Allah’s favor upon you when He raised prophets among you, made you kings, and gave you what He had not given anyone else in all the worlds.’”

“‘O my people, enter the Holy Land which Allah has assigned to you, and do not turn back, lest you become losers.’”

“They said, ‘O Moses, there are mighty people in it. We will never enter it until they leave. If they leave, then we will enter.’”

And the verses that follow. Allah Most High also said, when He saved Moses and his people from drowning:

“I will show you the abode of the defiantly disobedient.”

This is a principle that must be understood. A town may be praised or condemned at a particular time because of the condition of its inhabitants. Their condition may then change, and the judgment concerning them changes accordingly. For praise and blame, reward and punishment, depend solely on faith and righteous deeds, or their opposites: unbelief, wickedness, and disobedience.

Allah Most High said:

“O mankind, fear your Lord, who created you from a single soul, created from it its mate, and spread from the two of them many men and women. And fear Allah, in whose name you appeal to one another, and honor the ties of kinship.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“An Arab has no superiority over a non-Arab, nor a non-Arab over an Arab; neither a white person over a black person, nor a black person over a white person, except through piety. All people are children of Adam, and Adam was created from dust.”

The answer to all the other matters mentioned has now become clear: deliberately choosing to pray and supplicate at what is said to be a prophet’s footprint, a trace left by a prophet, or the grave of a prophet, a Companion, a shaykh, or a member of the Prophet’s household—or at towers or caves—is among the reprehensible innovations introduced into Islam. The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not prescribe this. Neither the foremost early Muslims nor those who followed them in righteousness practised it, nor did any of the leading Muslim scholars consider it recommended. Rather, it is among the causes of associating partners with Allah and the avenues leading to falsehood. This subject is discussed at length elsewhere, outside this response.

Section

As for someone saying when he stumbles, “O rank of Muhammad!” or “O Lady Nafīsah!” or “O my master, Shaykh so-and-so!” or similar expressions involving appeals to him for rescue and requests addressed to him, this is forbidden and is of the nature of associating partners with Allah. A deceased person, whether a prophet or anyone else, must not be invoked, petitioned, or called upon for rescue, whether at his grave or far from it. Rather, this is of the same nature as the religion of the Christians who:

“Have taken their rabbis and monks as lords besides Allah, and also the Messiah, son of Mary, although they were commanded to worship only one God. There is no deity except Him. Exalted is He above whatever they associate with Him.”

It is also of the same nature as the practice of those concerning whom He said:

“Say, ‘Call upon those whom you claim to be gods besides Him. They have no power to relieve your suffering or shift it elsewhere.’”

“Those whom they invoke themselves seek a means of drawing near to their Lord, striving to be the nearest. They hope for His mercy and fear His punishment. Indeed, your Lord’s punishment is something to beware of.”

The Most High has also said:

“It is not for any human being whom Allah has given the Scripture, wisdom, and prophethood to then tell people, ‘Be my worshippers rather than Allah’s.’ Rather, ‘Be devoted to the Lord through your teaching of the Scripture and your study of it.’

“Nor would he command you to take the angels and prophets as lords. Would he command you to disbelieve after you have submitted to Allah?”

This has been discussed at length elsewhere.

Section

Likewise, vows made to graves or to any of their occupants—such as vows to Abraham, the intimate friend of Allah, to shaykh so-and-so, to a member of the Prophet’s household, or to anyone else—are vows involving disobedience. By agreement of the leading scholars of the religion, fulfilling them is not obligatory; indeed, fulfilling them is not even permissible. For it is established in the Sahīh collection that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever vows to obey Allah, let him obey Him; and whoever vows to disobey Allah, let him not disobey Him.”

It is also reported from him in the Sunan collections that he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah has cursed women who visit graves and those who establish mosques and lamps over them.”

Thus, the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, cursed those who build mosques over graves and light lamps there:

such as lanterns, candles, and the like. If someone who does this is cursed, then whoever places gold and silver lanterns and candlesticks there, beside the graves, is all the more deserving of the curse.

Anyone who vows to provide oil, candles, gold, silver, a covering, or anything else to be placed at the grave of a prophet, a Companion, a relative of the Prophet, or a shaykh has made a vow involving disobedience, which it is not permissible to fulfil. Must he offer the expiation for a broken oath? The scholars have two opinions on this. If he gives what he vowed as charity to deserving members of the Prophet’s household, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, or to other righteous poor people, that would be better for him in Allah’s sight and more beneficial to him. This is a righteous deed for which Allah will reward him, for Allah rewards those who give charity and does not let the reward of those who do good go to waste.

One who gives charity does so seeking Allah’s Countenance, seeking his reward not from created beings but from Allah Most High. As the Most High says:

“But the most righteous will be kept away from it—he who gives his wealth to purify himself, not repaying a favour owed to anyone, but only seeking the Countenance of his Lord, the Most High. And he will surely be pleased.”

The Most High also says:

“And the example of those who spend their wealth seeking Allah’s pleasure and out of firm conviction within themselves is that of a garden on high ground”—to the end of the verse.

And He says of His righteous servants:

“We feed you only for the sake of Allah. We desire neither reward nor thanks from you.”

For this reason, no one should ask in the name of anyone other than Allah, as when someone says, “In honour of Abū Bakr and ʿAlī, or shaykh so-and-so, or shaykh so-and-so.” Rather, one should give only to someone who asks

for Allah’s sake. No one may ask for the sake of anyone other than Allah, for sincere devotion to Allah alone is obligatory in every physical and financial act of worship, such as prayer, charity, fasting, and Hajj. Bowing and prostration are proper only for Allah; fasting is only for Allah; Hajj is only to the House of Allah; and supplication is only to Allah. The Most High says:

“Fight them until there is no more persecution and all worship is devoted to Allah.”

The Most High also says:

“Ask those of Our messengers whom We sent before you: Did We appoint any gods besides the Most Merciful to be worshipped?”

And the Most High says:

“The revelation of the Book is from Allah, the Almighty, the All-Wise.”

“Indeed, We have sent down the Book to you in truth, so worship Allah, devoting your religion sincerely to Him.”

This is the foundation of Islam: that we worship none but Allah and worship Him only as He has prescribed, not through religious innovations. As the Most High says:

“So whoever hopes to meet his Lord, let him do righteous deeds and associate no one in the worship of his Lord.”

The Most High also says:

“To test you as to which of you is best in deeds.”

Al-Fudayl ibn ‘Iyād said: “That means the most sincere and the most correct.” They asked, “O Abū ‘Alī, what do you mean by the most sincere and the most correct?”

He replied: “If a deed is sincere but not correct, it will not be accepted. If it is correct but not sincere, it will not be accepted until it is both sincere and correct. Sincerity means that it is done for Allah, and correctness means that it accords with the Sunnah and the Book.”

All of this is because Allah’s Messenger conveyed His religion on His behalf. Nothing is forbidden except what Allah has forbidden, and religion consists only of what Allah has prescribed. Allah Most High condemned the polytheists because they prescribed

in religion what Allah had not authorized, declaring forbidden things that Allah had not forbidden, such as livestock designated as bahīrah, sā’ibah, wasīlah, and hām. They also instituted religious practices that Allah had not authorized, such as calling upon and worshipping others besides Him, and the monasticism that the Christians invented.

Islam is the religion of all the messengers, from the first to the last; all of them were sent with Islam. As Noah, peace be upon him, said:

“My people, if my presence among you and my reminding you of Allah’s signs have become too much for you, then in Allah I have put my trust. So settle on your plan together with your gods, leaving no uncertainty about it; then carry it out against me and give me no respite.”

“But if you turn away, I have asked you for no reward. My reward is with Allah alone, and I have been commanded to be among the Muslims.”

The Most High says:

“Who would turn away from the faith of Abraham except one who makes a fool of himself? We certainly chose him in this world, and in the Hereafter he will surely be among the righteous.”

“When his Lord said to him, ‘Submit,’ he replied, ‘I have submitted to the Lord of all worlds.’”

“Abraham enjoined this upon his sons, as did Jacob: ‘My sons, Allah has chosen this religion for you, so do not die except as Muslims.’”

The Most High says:

“Moses said, ‘My people, if you believe in Allah, then put your trust in Him, if you are Muslims.’”

The Most High says:

“And when I inspired the disciples to believe in Me and My messenger, they said, ‘We believe, so bear witness that we are Muslims.’”

It is established in the two Sahīh collections that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“We prophets all have one religion.”

Thus, the religion of all the messengers is one and the same: Islam, which is to worship Allah alone, with no partner, in accordance with what He has commanded and prescribed

as He says:

“He has ordained for you the religion He enjoined upon Noah, and that which We have revealed to you, and what We enjoined upon Abraham, Moses, and Jesus: uphold the religion and do not be divided within it. What you call the polytheists to is intolerable to them.”

What varies within this religion is the law and the prescribed way, as He says:

“For each of you We have appointed a law and a way.”

Likewise, the law prescribed for a single messenger may vary. In the early days of Islam, Allah commanded Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, to pray facing Jerusalem. Then, in the second year after the Hijrah, He commanded him to pray facing the Kaaba, the Sacred House. This, in its own time, was part of the religion of Islam. Likewise, the law of the Torah, in its time, was part of the religion of Islam, and the law of the Gospel, in its time, was part of the religion of Islam.

Whoever believed in the Torah but then rejected the Gospel departed from the religion of Islam and became a disbeliever. Likewise, whoever believed in the two earlier scriptures but rejected the Quran was a disbeliever outside the religion of Islam. For the religion of Islam entails belief in all the scriptures and all the messengers, as the Most High says:

“Say, ‘We believe in Allah and what has been revealed to us, and what was revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and the Tribes, and what was given to Moses and Jesus, and what was given to the prophets by their Lord. We make no distinction between any of them, and to Him we submit.’” (The verse.)

translated_text:
What do the esteemed scholars, the leading authorities in religion, say about the following?

A person faces a need relating to this world or the Hereafter, then goes to the grave of a prophet or another righteous person and supplicates there for relief from his distress. Is this Sunnah or an innovation? Is it prescribed in Islam or not? If it is not prescribed, their needs may nevertheless sometimes be fulfilled. Does that make it permissible for them to do this? What accounts for their needs being fulfilled? Please give us a ruling.

Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah have mercy on him—replied:

All praise is due to Allah, Lord of all worlds. This is not Sunnah; rather, it is an innovation. Neither the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, nor any of his Companions, nor any of the leading authorities whom Muslims follow in their religion ever did this. Nor was it commanded or recommended by the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, any of his Companions, or the leading authorities in religion.

Indeed, this is not known to have been practised by any person of knowledge and religion among the favoured generations praised by the Messenger of Allah—the Companions, the Successors, and their successors—whether in the Hijāz, Yemen, Syria, Iraq, Egypt, the Maghreb, or Khurāsān. It was only introduced later.

translated_text:
It is well known that anything neither prescribed nor recommended by the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, or by any of these authorities whom Muslims follow in their religion, is a reprehensible innovation. No one would call such a thing a good innovation. For a good innovation—according to those who divide innovations into good and bad—must be recommended by a scholar whose example is followed, and there must be evidence from Islamic law establishing that it is recommended.

Likewise, those who maintain that every innovation in the religious sense is blameworthy, citing the Prophet’s words, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in the authentic hadith:

“Every innovation is misguidance,”

explain that when ʿUmar said of the Tarāwīh prayers:

“What an excellent innovation this is!”

he called it an innovation only in the linguistic sense. According to them, an innovation in the religious sense is something for which no evidence from Islamic law establishes that it is recommended.

The two positions ultimately amount to the same thing, for they agree that whatever Islamic law has not made recommended or obligatory is neither obligatory nor recommended. Thus, anyone who adopts an act as worship and religion when it is neither obligatory nor recommended in Islamic law is misguided, by the agreement of the Muslims.

Going to graves in order to supplicate there, hoping that one’s supplication will be answered, falls into this category. It is not prescribed in Islamic law, whether as an obligation or a recommendation. It is therefore neither a religious practice nor something good, neither an act of obedience to Allah nor something He loves and is pleased with, neither a righteous deed nor a means of drawing near to Him. Whoever regards it as any of these things is misguided, by the agreement of the Muslims.

For this reason, when hardships befell the Companions of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and they wished to supplicate to Allah for relief from distress or to seek His mercy, they did not go to any graves, whether those of prophets or anyone else. Indeed, they did not even go to the Prophet’s grave, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, intending to supplicate there. Rather, it is established in Sahīh al-Bukhārī, on the authority of Anas, that whenever they suffered drought, Umar ibn al-Khattāb would seek rain through al-Abbās ibn Abd al-Muttalib, saying:

“O Allah, we used to seek to draw near to You through our Prophet, and You would grant us rain. Now we seek to draw near to You through our Prophet’s uncle, so grant us rain.”

And they would be granted rain.

Sahīh al-Bukhārī also relates that Abd Allāh ibn Dīnār said: “I heard Ibn Umar reciting these lines of Abū Tālib:

‘A fair-faced man, by whose countenance rain is sought from the clouds—
A refuge for orphans, a protector of widows.’”

It also relates, through Sālim ibn Abd Allāh ibn Umar, that his father said:

“At times I would recall the poet’s words while looking at the face of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, as he sought rain, while it came down until a gutter gushed with water for him:

‘A fair-faced man, by whose countenance rain is sought from the clouds—
A refuge for orphans, a protector of widows.’”

These are the words of Abū Tālib.

from a dead person, or to seek to draw near to Allah through him, or to engage in similar practices that some people regard as acts of religion and devotion. This shows the believer that these are innovations which the Companions regarded not as approved practices, but as reprehensible ones.

Section

This would suffice even if no prohibition indicating that these practices are forbidden had been transmitted from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his Companions. How much more so when his mass-transmitted Sunnah indicates that they are forbidden.

For example, in the two Sahīh collections, Ā’ishah said:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said during the illness from which he never recovered: ‘May Allah curse the Jews and Christians; they took the graves of their prophets as places of worship.’ Were it not for that, his grave would have been left exposed; however, he feared—or it was feared—that it would be taken as a place of worship.”

This is part of al-Bukhārī’s wording. Also in the two Sahīh collections, Ā’ishah said:

“During the illness of the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, some of his wives mentioned a church they had seen in Abyssinia called Māriyah. They spoke of its beauty and the images within it. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, raised his head and said: ‘When a righteous man among those people died, they would build a place of worship over his grave and then make those images within it. Those are the worst of creation in Allah’s sight.’”

This meaning is widely reported from him through several chains in the Sahīh, Sunan, and Musnad collections.

In Sahīh Muslim, Jundub reports that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said five days before his death:

“Those before you used to take graves—or he said, the graves of their prophets—as places of worship. Beware! Do not take graves as places of worship, for I forbid you to do so.”

The same report includes:

“If I were to take anyone on earth as an intimate friend, I would take Abū Bakr as an intimate friend. But your companion is Allah’s intimate friend.”

This meaning is reported through several chains in the two Sahīh collections. The report also includes:

“Let every small doorway opening into the mosque be sealed, except Abū Bakr’s doorway.”

He clarified these two matters, both of which have been mass-transmitted from him, and brought them together five days before his death: mentioning the excellence of Abū Bakr al-Siddīq and forbidding the taking of graves as places of worship. Together, they cut off the very source of the polytheism through which religion was corrupted and the religion of the polytheists came to prevail.

For Allah said in His Book concerning the people of Noah:

“And they said, ‘Never abandon your gods; never abandon Wadd, Suwāʿ, Yaghūth, Yaʿūq, or Nasr.’ And they have already led many astray.”

Al-Bukhārī narrated in his Sahīh, through his chain of transmission, that Ibn ʿAbbās said:

“The idols that had existed among the people of Noah came to be worshipped among the Arabs. Wadd belonged to Kalb at Dūmat al-Jandal; Suwāʿ belonged to Hudhayl; Yaghūth belonged to Murād, then to Banū Ghutayf at al-Jarf near Sabaʾ; Yaʿūq belonged to Hamdān; and Nasr belonged to Himyar, to the clan of Dhī

 ثُمَّ مِنْهُمْ مَنْ ذَكَرَ أَنَّهُمْ كَانُوا يَعْكُفُونَ عَلَى قُبُورِهِمْ ثُمَّ صَوَّرُوا تَمَاثِيلَهُمْ وَمِنْهُمْ مَنْ ذَكَرَ أَنَّهُمْ كَانُوا يَصْحَبُونَ تَمَاثِيلَهُمْ مَعَهُمْ فِي السَّفَرِ يَدْعُونَ عِنْدَهَا وَلَا يَعْبُدُونَهَا ثُمَّ بَعْدَ ذَلِكَ:
 عُبِدَتْ الْأَوْثَانُ.
 وَلِهَذَا:
 جَمَعَ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ بَيْنَ الْقُبُورِ وَالصُّوَرِ؛ فِي غَيْرِ حَدِيثٍ كَمَا فِي صَحِيحِ مُسْلِمٍ عَنْ 
{أَبِي الهياج الأسدي قَالَ: قَالَ لِي عَلِيُّ بْنُ أَبِي طَالِبٍ: أَلَا أَبْعَثُك عَلَى مَا بَعَثَنِي عَلَيْهِ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ؟ أَمَرَنِي أَنْ لَا أَدَعَ قَبْرًا مُشْرِفًا إلَّا سَوَّيْته وَلَا تِمْثَالًا إلَّا طَمَسْته}
 .
 فَأَمَرَهُ بِمَحْوِ الصُّوَرِ وَتَسْوِيَةِ الْقُبُورِ كَمَا قَالَ فِي الْحَدِيثِ الْآخَرِ الصَّحِيحِ:
 
{إنَّ أُولَئِكَ إذَا مَاتَ فِيهِمْ الرَّجُلُ الصَّالِحُ بَنَوْا عَلَى قَبْرِهِ مَسْجِدًا وَصَوَّرُوا فِيهِ تِلْكَ التَّصَاوِيرَ أُولَئِكَ شِرَارُ الْخُلُقِ عِنْدَ اللَّهِ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ}
 . وَالْأَحَادِيثُ عَنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ فِي النَّهْيِ عَنْ اتِّخَاذِ
translated_text:
al-Kalām. These were the names of righteous men from the people of Noah. When they died, Satan prompted their people: ‘Set up memorials at the places where they used to sit, and name them after them.’ They did so, but these were not worshipped until those people had died and knowledge had disappeared. Then they were worshipped.”

A number of the early generations related much the same meaning in works of Quran commentary, accounts of the prophets, and other works: these had been righteous people. Some related that people would keep vigil at their graves and later make images of them. Others related that they would take their images along when travelling and supplicate beside them, without worshipping them. Later, however, the idols came to be worshipped.

For this reason, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, mentioned graves and images together in several hadiths. For example, Sahīh Muslim records that Abū al-Hayyāj al-Asadī said:

“Alī ibn Abī Tālib said to me: ‘Shall I not send you on the same mission on which the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, sent me? He commanded me to leave no elevated grave without levelling it, and no image without obliterating it.’”

Thus, he commanded him to erase images and level graves, just as he said in another authentic hadith:

“When a righteous man among those people died, they would build a place of worship over his grave and make those images within it. Those people will be the worst of creation before Allah on the Day of Resurrection.”

The hadiths from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, forbidding the taking of

graves as places of worship and praying in graveyards are very numerous. For example, the two Sahīh collections and the Sunan collections report from Abū Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“May Allah destroy the Jews! They took the graves of their prophets as places of worship.”

Abdullāh ibn Masʿūd said: I heard the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, say:

“Among the worst of people are those who are still alive when the Hour overtakes them, and those who take graves as places of worship.”

This was narrated by Ahmad in al-Musnad and by Abū Hātim ibn Hibbān in his Sahīh.

Ibn ʿAbbās said:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, cursed women who visit graves and those who establish places of worship and lamps over them.”

This was narrated by Ahmad in al-Musnad, the compilers of the four Sunan collections, and Abū Hātim ibn Hibbān in his Sahīh.

He also narrated in his Sahīh that ʿĀʾishah said: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“May Allah curse those who took the graves of their prophets as places of worship.”

The two Sahīh collections report that Ibn ʿUmar said: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Offer some of your prayers in your homes, and do not turn them into graves.”

Sahīh Muslim reports from Abū Marthad al-Ghanawī that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Do not pray facing graves, and do not sit on them.”

Abdullāh ibn ʿAmr said:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, forbade praying in graveyards.”

Abū Hātim narrated this in his Sahīh. He also narrated from Anas:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, forbade praying among graves.”

Abū Saʿīd reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

 إنَّمَا هُوَ مَا فِي ذَلِكَ مِنْ التَّشَبُّهِ بِالْمُشْرِكِينَ وَأَنْ تَصِيرَ ذَرِيعَةً إلَى الشِّرْكِ؛ وَلِهَذَا نَهَى عَنْ اتِّخَاذِ قُبُورِ الْأَنْبِيَاءِ مَسَاجِدَ.
 وَقَالَ:
 
{إنَّ أُولَئِكَ إذَا مَاتَ فِيهِمْ الرَّجُلُ الصَّالِحُ بَنَوْا عَلَى قَبْرِهِ مَسْجِدًا وَصَوَّرُوا فِيهِ تِلْكَ التَّصَاوِيرَ}
 .
 وَقَالَ:
 
{إنَّ مَنْ كَانَ قَبْلَكُمْ كَانُوا يَتَّخِذُونَ الْقُبُورَ مَسَاجِدَ أَلَا فَلَا تَتَّخِذُوا الْقُبُورَ مَسَاجِدَ}
 وَنَهَى عَنْ الصَّلَاةِ إلَيْهَا.
translated_text:
“The whole earth is a place of prayer, except graveyards and bathhouses.”

This was narrated by Ahmad, the compilers of the four Sunan collections, and Ibn Hibbān in his Sahīh. Al-Tirmidhī said that its transmission contains inconsistency, because Sufyān al-Thawrī reported it with a disconnected chain. Other scholars, however, declared it authentic because other trustworthy narrators transmitted it with connected chains. Ibn Hazm also graded it authentic.

Sunan Abī Dāwūd reports that ʿAlī said:

“My beloved friend forbade me to pray in graveyards and forbade me to pray in the land of Babylon.”

The reports concerning this are very numerous.

Some scholars have supposed that praying in graveyards was forbidden because of ritual impurity, since their soil becomes mixed with the pus and flesh of the dead. These scholars may distinguish between new and old graveyards, and between cases where a barrier is present and those where it is not.

Yet this explanation is not mentioned in the hadith, nor does the hadith indicate it, either explicitly or by its apparent meaning. It is merely a reason they have conjectured. According to other scholars, the correct reason is what a number of earlier and later scholars—in the time of Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, Ahmad, and others—have explained: this practice involves imitating the polytheists and can become a means leading to associating partners with Allah. This is why he forbade taking the graves of prophets as places of worship. He said:

“When a righteous man among those people died, they would build a place of worship over his grave and make those images in it.”

He also said:

“Those who came before you used to take graves as places of worship. Beware! Do not take graves as places of worship.”

He also forbade praying facing them.

{اللَّهُمَّ لَا تَجْعَلْ قَبْرِي وَثَنًا يُعْبَدُ}

{لَا تَتَّخِذُوا قَبْرِي عِيدًا. وَصَلُّوا عَلَيَّ حَيْثُمَا كُنْتُمْ فَإِنَّ صَلَاتَكُمْ تَبْلُغُنِي}
 . وَمَا يَرْوِيهِ بَعْضُ النَّاسِ أَنَّهُ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ صَلَّى بِمَسْجِدِ الْخَلِيلِ أَوْ صَلَّى عِنْدَ قَبْرِ الْخَلِيلِ فَإِنَّ هَذَا الْحَدِيثَ غَيْرُ ثَابِتٍ عِنْدَ
translated_text:
And, supposing the prohibition were solely due to ritual impurity, it is well known that the graves of the prophets do not become foul-smelling. Indeed, the prophets’ bodies do not decay, and the soil of their graves is pure. Impurity in front of someone praying does not invalidate his prayer. Those who took graves as places of worship would spread clean coverings beside them, so they did not come into contact with impurity. Moreover, those who explain the prohibition in terms of impurity do not deny this other reason. Al-Shāfiʿī and others mentioned the prohibition against establishing mosques over graves and explained it as a precaution against imitating such practices.

Several scholars of the legal schools—including followers of Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, and Ahmad, as well as jurists of Kufa—expressly stated the prohibition against building mosques over graves. Several of them explicitly declared it unlawful. There can be no doubt about this in view of the curse pronounced by the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his emphatic prohibition of it.

Taking graves as places of worship encompasses two things: building a mosque over them, or praying beside them without any building. The latter is what he himself and his Companions feared would happen if they buried him in the open: they feared that people would pray beside him, thereby turning his grave into a place of worship.

Mālik’s Muwattaʾ reports that he said:

“O Allah, do not let my grave become an idol that is worshipped.”

This has been transmitted both with connected chains and with chains omitting the Companion. Sunan Abī Dāwūd reports that he said:

“Do not make my grave a place of recurring observance. Send blessings upon me wherever you may be, for your blessings reach me.”
