This is a broad subject. It is well known that if supplication beside the graves of prophets and righteous people were better than supplication elsewhere, then praying in those places and taking them as places of worship ought to be recommended, for prayer is accompanied by supplication. Hence no Muslim says that supplication in a place where prayer is prohibited—such as camel resting places, graveyards, or places contaminated by ritual impurity—is better than supplication elsewhere. Whoever says this has defied the Messenger and made the polytheism and means leading to it that he prohibited equal or preferable to the affirmation of Allah’s oneness and worship of Him alone that he commanded.

It was through this opening that the hypocrites introduced into Islam what they did. The man who invented the religion of the Rāfidah was a Jewish heretic who outwardly professed Islam while concealing unbelief, scheming to corrupt the Muslims’ religion—just as Paul schemed to corrupt the Christians’ religion. He worked to stir up discord among the Muslims until ʿUthmān was killed. Among the believers are some who respond to the hypocrites, as Allah Most High says:

“Had they gone forth among you, they would only have added to your disorder and hurried about in your midst, seeking to stir up discord among you; and among you are those who would listen to them.”

Then, when the Muslim community became divided, he introduced his claims concerning designation and infallibility in the imamate, and began openly disparaging Abū Bakr and ʿUmar. These claims found receptive hearts marked by ignorance and injustice, even though they were not unbelieving hearts. Thus emerged the innovation of Shiism, which is the key to the door of polytheism.

Then, when the heretics gained power, they ordered shrines to be built and mosques to be left unused, arguing that Friday and congregational prayers could only be performed behind the infallible imam. They transmitted lies concerning the lighting and veneration of shrines and supplication beside them, the like of which I have not encountered among the fabrications of the People of the Book that I have examined. Their leader, Ibn al-Nu'mān, even wrote a book entitled “The Rites of Pilgrimage to Shrines.” In it they fabricated lies about the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his household, thereby altering his religion and changing his faith.

They introduced polytheism, which contradicts the affirmation of Allah’s oneness, thus combining polytheism with lying, just as Allah has linked the two in several passages, including His words:

“And shun false speech, being true to Allah, associating no partners with Him.”

In an authentic report, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: “False testimony is equivalent to associating partners with Allah.” He said this twice, then recited this verse.

Allah Most High also says:

“Those who took the calf for worship will incur wrath from their Lord and humiliation in this worldly life. Thus do We recompense those who fabricate lies.”

And Allah Most High says:

“On the Day He calls them and says, ‘Where are those you claimed were My partners?’”

“And We will bring forth a witness from every community and say, ‘Produce your proof.’ Then they will know that the truth belongs to Allah, and whatever they used to fabricate will fail them.”

This right belongs to Allah, as is established in an authentic report that the Prophet said to Mu'ādh ibn Jabal:

“O Mu'ādh, do you know what Allah’s right over His servants is?”

He replied, “Allah and His Messenger know best.”

He said, “His right over His servants is that they worship Him and associate nothing with Him. O Mu'ādh, do you know what

the servants’ right over Allah is if they do so?”

He replied, “Allah and His Messenger know best.” He said, “Their right over Him is that He not punish them.”

Allah Most High says:

“And to ‘Ād We sent their brother Hūd. He said, ‘O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him. You are merely fabricating lies.’”

There are many such passages in the Quran in which He describes those who associate partners with Him as fabricators of lies. Hence He demands proof and authoritative evidence from them, as in His words:

“Whoever invokes another god alongside Allah, for which he has no proof, his reckoning rests only with his Lord.”

And His words:

“Say, ‘Have you considered those you invoke besides Allah? Show me what they have created of the earth. Or do they have a share in the heavens? Bring me a scripture preceding this, or some remnant of knowledge, if you are truthful.’”

He also says:

“So devote yourself to the religion, inclining to truth—the natural disposition Allah has instilled in mankind. There is no altering Allah’s creation. That is the upright religion, but most people do not know.

“Turn to Him in repentance, fear Him, establish prayer, and do not be among those who associate partners with Him—those who divided their religion and became sects, each faction rejoicing in what it has.

“When adversity touches people, they call upon their Lord, turning to Him in repentance. Then, when He lets them taste mercy from Him, a group of them associate partners with their Lord, showing ingratitude for what We have given them. So enjoy yourselves; soon you will know.

“Or have We sent down to them any authority that speaks in support of what they associate with Him?”

Allah Most High says, “Do not be among those who associate partners with Him—those who divided their religion and became sects,” because affirming Allah’s oneness is the religion of Allah with which He sent the messengers of earlier and later times. As Allah Most High says:

“We sent no messenger before you without revealing to him that

And He says:

“We certainly sent a messenger to every nation, saying, ‘Worship Allah and shun false gods.’”

It is established in the authentic hadith collection that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah is pleased with three things for you: that you worship Him without associating anything with Him; that you all hold firmly to the rope of Allah and do not become divided; and that you offer sincere counsel to those whom Allah has placed in authority over you.”

Thus, those who take graves as places of worship, owing to the association of partners with Allah found among them, have divided their religion and become sects. You find each group venerating the person they follow or their prophet, saying, “Supplication at his grave is answered.” Their hearts are attached to his grave rather than to the graves of other prophets and righteous people, even if another is superior to him. Likewise, each worshipper of celestial bodies and idols has taken his own desire as his god: he worships whatever he takes as a god, even if something else is superior to it.

They then call this “visitation,” a term sanctioned by Islamic law that they have misapplied. It is well known that the “prescribed visitation” which the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, instituted for his community entails greeting the deceased with peace and supplicating for him, much like offering the funeral prayer over him. The person offering the funeral prayer intends to supplicate for the deceased; Allah Most High shows the deceased mercy through his supplication and rewards the worshipper himself for his prayer. Likewise, when someone visits graves in the prescribed manner, greeting their occupants with peace and supplicating for them, they receive mercy through his supplication

It is permissible to visit the grave of a disbeliever to take a lesson, but not to seek forgiveness for him. Thus, in the two authentic hadith collections, Abū Hurayrah said:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, visited his mother’s grave and wept, causing those around him to weep. It is also authentically established from him, in a hadith narrated by Anas, that he said:

“I had forbidden you to visit graves; now visit them.”

At most, such reports are attributed to al-Dāraqutnī’s collection, which he intended to contain singular reports concerning the Sunnah. Indeed, Mālik and others disapproved of saying, “I visited the grave of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.” Mālik was the most knowledgeable authority on this subject, for the people of Medina knew more about it than the inhabitants of other cities, and Mālik was their imam. Had there been a sunnah transmitted from the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, containing the expression “visiting his grave,” it would not have escaped the scholars of his city and those living near his grave—may my father and mother be his ransom.

Accordingly, the established practice among the Companions and the imams of the Muslims was that, when a person offered salutations to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his two Companions, he would then supplicate to Allah facing the direction of prayer, not the chamber. The account related about Mālik and al-Mansūr to the contrary is false and has no basis. I know of no disagreement among the imams that the Sunnah is to face the direction of prayer when supplicating, rather than the Prophet’s grave. the grave. Abū Hanīfah said that one should offer salutations to him while facing the direction of prayer, with one’s back to the grave. ‘Abdullāh ibn ‘Umar would say, “Peace be upon you, O Messenger of Allah. Peace be upon you, O Abū Bakr. Peace be upon you, O my father,” and then leave.

If, even in the mosque of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, the imams instructed people to face the direction of prayer when supplicating—as reported from the Companions—and disapproved of facing the grave, what, then, of anyone else’s grave? This makes clear to you that deliberately seeking out graves to supplicate there is not part of the religion of the Muslims. Any author of works on pilgrimage rites or other subjects who states something contrary to this has neither evidence to support it nor a transmitted statement from a recognized imam. It is merely something that people have taken from one another, based on hadiths they thought authentic but which are false, or on innovated customs they supposed to be sunnah, without any basis in Islamic law.

During the most virtuous generations, there were no “shrines” built over graves. These only appeared and became widespread under the rule of Banū Buwayh. When the Qarmatians emerged in the lands of the East and West, there were unbelieving heretics in those lands whose aim was to alter the religion of Islam. The extent to which Banū Buwayh agreed with them in some of this, and embraced the innovations of the Jahmiyyah, Mu‘tazilah and Rāfidah, is well known to scholars. They therefore built spurious shrines, “such as the shrine of ‘Alī”—may Allah be pleased with him—and others like it. Fabricators composed hadiths about visiting shrines, praying and supplicating at them, and similar practices. Thus, these heretics and the people of innovation who followed them came to venerate shrines and demean mosques.

and this is contrary to the religion of the Muslims. They use Shiism as a cover. The previously cited, mass-transmitted hadiths from the Prophet concerning the honor due to al-Siddīq and the prohibition against taking graves as places of worship refute these two innovations, which are the root of associating partners with Allah and altering Islam.

Further evidence of this is that Allah did not mention “shrines” or command prayer in them; rather, His commands concern mosques. He, Exalted is He, said:

“Who is more unjust than one who prevents Allah’s name from being mentioned in His mosques and strives to destroy them?”

He did not say, “Allah’s shrines.” Indeed, “the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, commanded ‘Alī not to leave any raised grave without leveling it, or any image without effacing it.” He also prohibited taking graves as places of worship and cursed those who did so. This is therefore a command to demolish shrines, not to cultivate them, whether through physical construction or devotional activity.

He, Exalted is He, said:

“Do not have sexual relations with them while you are in devotional retreat in the mosques.”

He did not say, “in the shrines.” He, Exalted is He, also said:

“Say, ‘My Lord has commanded justice. Direct your faces to Him at every mosque.’”

He did not say, “at every shrine.”

He, Exalted is He, said:

“It is not for the polytheists to maintain Allah’s mosques.”

He did not say, “Allah’s shrines,” for those who maintain shrines are polytheists or resemble the polytheists. The passage continues to His words:

“Only those who believe in Allah and the Last Day, establish prayer, give zakah, and fear none but Allah maintain Allah’s mosques.”

He did not say, “maintain Allah’s shrines.” Rather, those who maintain shrines fear others besides Allah: they fear the dead, but do not fear

Allah; for they worship Him in a manner for which He has sent down no authority and which neither the Book nor the Sunnah has prescribed. As Allah’s close friend, peace be upon him, said when debating the polytheists, after they disputed with him and sought to frighten him with their gods:

“How should I fear what you associate with Allah, while you do not fear that you have associated with Allah that for which He has sent down no authority to you? Which of the two parties has more right to security, if you know?”

He, Exalted is He, said:

“Those who believe and do not mix their faith with injustice—it is they who will have security, and they are rightly guided.”

In the two Sahīh collections, Ibn Mas‘ūd reported:

“When this verse was revealed—‘Those who believe and do not mix their faith with injustice’—the Companions of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, found it distressing. They said, ‘O Messenger of Allah, which of us has not wronged himself?’ The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, replied, ‘It refers only to associating partners with Allah. Have you not heard the words of the righteous servant: “Indeed, associating partners with Allah is a tremendous injustice”?’”

He, Exalted is He, said:

“That was Our argument which We gave Abraham against his people. We raise in degrees whom We will.”

Zayd ibn Aslam and others said: “Through knowledge.”

He, Exalted is He, said:

“The mosques belong to Allah, so do not invoke anyone alongside Allah.”

He did not say, “The shrines belong to Allah.” Rather, those devoted to shrines invoke others alongside Allah. Thus, since building mosques over graves—known as “shrines”—and venerating them are not part of the religion of the Muslims, but rather of the religion of the polytheists, this has not been preserved. Allah has guaranteed us that He will preserve the Reminder He sent down, as He said:

“Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder, and indeed, We will preserve it.”

Thus, what Allah sent His Messenger with of the Book

and wisdom is preserved. Matters relating to shrines, however, have not been preserved. Indeed, most graves over which mosques have been built are either of doubtful authenticity or certainly falsely attributed. Examples include the grave at Karak said to contain Noah; the one outside Damascus said to be the grave of Ubayy ibn Ka‘b; the one on the other side said to be the grave of Uways al-Qaranī; the graves there thought to belong to ‘Ā’ishah, Umm Salamah—the wife of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace—or Umm Habībah; the grave within Najaf attributed to ‘Alī; the shrine in Cairo said to stand over al-Husayn; the shrine in Aleppo; and other such shrines. All these attributions are false, by the agreement of the scholars.

As for the grave in Homs said to be “the grave of Khālid ibn al-Walīd,” the one in Dārayyā said to be the grave of Abū Muslim al-Khawlānī, and similar graves, their attributions are doubtful. We may know in general that someone died in a particular region, without establishing that a particular spot is the location of his grave. Examples include the grave attributed to Bilāl and others outside Damascus, the grave attributed to Fātimah in Medina, and similar cases.

Most people who accept these attributions have learned of them through a dream, an unreliable report, or some other means. The identity of some of those buried in these graves may indeed be certain, but none of these innovated rulings follows from that.

For this reason, the early generations would close off this avenue. When the Muslims conquered Tustar, they found there a bier bearing a body still intact, which they said was “Daniel”

وَوَجَدُوا عِنْدَهُ كِتَابًا فِيهِ ذِكْرُ الْحَوَادِثِ وَكَانَ أَهْلُ تِلْكَ النَّاحِيَةِ يَسْتَسْقُونَ بِهِ. فَكَتَبَ فِي ذَلِكَ أَبُو مُوسَى الْأَشْعَرِيُّ إلَى عُمَرَ. فَكَتَبَ إلَيْهِ عُمَرُ أَنْ يُحْفَرَ بِالنَّهَارِ ثَلَاثَةَ عَشَرَ قَبْرًا ثُمَّ يُدْفَنَ بِاللَّيْلِ فِي وَاحِدٍ مِنْهَا وَيُعْفَى قَبْرُهُ؛ لِئَلَّا يَفْتَتِنَ النَّاسُ بِهِ.
 وَهَذَا كَمَا نَقَلُوا عَنْ عُمَرَ أَنَّهُ بَلَغَهُ:
 أَنَّ أَقْوَامًا يَزُورُونَ الشَّجَرَةَ الَّتِي بُويِعَ تَحْتَهَا بَيْعَةَ الرِّضْوَانِ وَيُصَلُّونَ هُنَاكَ فَأَمَرَ بِقَطْعِ الشَّجَرَةِ.
 وَقَدْ ثَبَتَ عَنْهُ أَنَّهُ كَانَ فِي سَفَرٍ فَرَأَى قَوْمًا يَنْتَابُونَ بُقْعَةً يُصَلُّونَ فِيهَا فَقَالَ:
 مَا هَذَا؟
 فَقَالُوا:
 هَذَا مَكَانٌ صَلَّى فِيهِ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ.
 فَقَالَ:
 وَمَكَانٌ صَلَّى بِهِ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ أَتُرِيدُونَ أَنْ تَتَّخِذُوا آثَارَ أَنْبِيَائِكُمْ مَسَاجِدَ إنَّمَا هَلَكَ بَنُو إسْرَائِيلَ بِهَذَا. مَنْ أَدْرَكَتْهُ فِيهِ الصَّلَاةُ فَلْيُصَلِّ وَإِلَّا فَلْيَمْضِ. وَاعْلَمْ أَنَّهُ لَيْسَ مَعَ أَحَدٍ مِنْ هَؤُلَاءِ مَا يُعَارِضُ بِهِ ذَلِكَ؛
 إلَّا حِكَايَةٌ عَنْ بَعْضِهِمْ أَنَّهُ قَالَ:
 إذَا كَانَتْ لَكُمْ إلَى اللَّهِ حَاجَةٌ؛
 فَادْعُوهُ عِنْدَ قَبْرِي أَوْ قَالَ:
 قَبْرُ فُلَانٍ هُوَ التِّرْيَاقُ الْمُجَرَّبُ وَأَمْثَالُ ذَلِكَ مِنْ هَذِهِ الْحِكَايَاتِ الَّتِي قَدْ تَكُونُ صِدْقًا وَقَدْ تَكُونُ كَذِبًا وَبِتَقْدِيرِ أَنْ يَكُونَ صِدْقًا: فَإِنَّ قَائِلَهَا غَيْرُ مَعْصُومٍ. وَمَا يُعَارِضُ النَّقْلَ الثَّابِتَ عَنْ الْمَعْصُومِ بِنَقْلِ غَيْرِ ثَابِتٍ عَنْ غَيْرِ مَعْصُومٍ إلَّا مَنْ يَكُونُ مِنْ الضَّالِّينَ إخْوَانِ الشَّيَاطِينِ. وَهَذَا مِنْ أَسْبَابِ الشِّرْكِ وَتَغْيِيرِ الدِّينِ.
translated_text:
and they found beside him a book recording events. The people of that region used to seek rain through him. Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī wrote to ʿUmar about this. ʿUmar wrote back instructing him to have thirteen graves dug during the day, then to bury him in one of them at night and erase all traces of his grave, lest people be led astray by him.

This resembles what has been reported about ʿUmar: when he learned that some people were visiting the tree beneath which the Pledge of Divine Pleasure had been given and praying there, he ordered the tree to be cut down.

It is authentically reported that, while travelling, he saw people frequenting a spot to pray there. He asked, “What is this?”

They replied, “This is a place where the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prayed.”

He said, “So it is a place where the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prayed! Do you wish to turn the sites associated with your prophets into mosques? This was precisely what brought about the destruction of the Children of Israel. Whoever happens to be there when prayer falls due should pray; otherwise, he should continue on his way.”

Know that none of these people has anything with which to counter this except an anecdote reporting that one of them said, “If you have a need to ask of Allah, call upon Him at my grave,” or, “The grave of so-and-so is the tried-and-tested antidote,” and similar anecdotes that may be true or false. Even supposing such an account is true, the person who made the statement is not infallible. Only those who are astray—the brothers of devils—would counter an established report from the infallible Prophet with an unsubstantiated report from someone who is not infallible. This is among the causes of associating partners with Allah and altering the religion.

original_text:
وَأَمَّا قَوْلُ الْقَائِلِ:
 إنَّ الْحَوَائِجَ تُقْضَى لَهُمْ بَعْضَ الْأَوْقَاتِ فَهَلْ يُسَوِّغُ ذَلِكَ لَهُمْ قَصْدَهَا؟
 فَيُقَالُ:
 لَيْسَ ذَلِكَ مُسَوِّغُ قَصْدِهَا لِوُجُوهِ: أَحَدُهَا: أَنَّ الْمُشْرِكِينَ وَأَهْلَ الْكِتَابِ يُقْضَى كَثِيرٌ مِنْ حَوَائِجِهِمْ بِالدُّعَاءِ عِنْدَ الْأَصْنَامِ وَعِنْدَ تَمَاثِيلِ الْقِدِّيسِينَ وَالْأَمَاكِنِ الَّتِي يُعَظِّمُونَهَا؛ وَتَعْظِيمُهَا حَرَامٌ فِي زَمَنِ الْإِسْلَامِ.
 فَهَلْ يَقُولُ مُسْلِمٌ:
 إنَّ مِثْلَ ذَلِكَ سَوَّغَ لَهُمْ هَذَا الْفِعْلَ الْمُحَرَّمَ بِإِجْمَاعِ الْمُسْلِمِينَ وَمَا تَجِدُ عِنْدَ أَهْلِ الْأَهْوَاءِ وَالْبِدَعِ مِنْ الْأَسْبَابِ - الَّتِي بِهَا ابْتَدَعُوا مَا ابْتَدَعُوهُ -
 إلَّا تَجِدُ عِنْدَ الْمُشْرِكِينَ وَأَهْلِ الْكِتَابِ مِنْ جِنْسِ تِلْكَ الْأَسْبَابِ مَا أَوْقَعَهُمْ فِي كُفْرِهِمْ وَأَشَدُّ وَمَنْ تَدَبَّرَ هَذَا:
 وَجَدَهُ فِي عَامَّةِ الْأُمُورِ فَإِنَّ الْبِدَعَ مُشْتَقَّةٌ مِنْ الْكُفْرِ وَكَمَالُ الْإِيمَانِ: هُوَ فِعْلُ مَا أَمَرَ اللَّهُ بِهِ وَرَسُولُهُ وَتَرْكُ مَا نَهَى اللَّهُ عَنْهُ وَرَسُولُهُ فَإِذَا تَرَكَ بَعْضَ الْمَأْمُورِ وَعَوَّضَ عَنْهُ بِبَعْضِ الْمَحْظُورِ كَانَ فِي ذَلِكَ مِنْ نَقْصِ الْإِيمَانِ بِقَدْرِ ذَلِكَ. وَالْبِدْعَةُ لَا تَكُونُ حَقًّا مَحْضًا؛ إذْ لَوْ كَانَتْ كَذَلِكَ لَكَانَتْ مَشْرُوعَةً وَلَا تَكُونُ مَصْلَحَتُهَا رَاجِحَةً عَلَى مَفْسَدَتِهَا؛ إذْ لَوْ كَانَتْ كَذَلِكَ لَكَانَتْ مَشْرُوعَةً وَلَا تَكُونُ بَاطِلًا مَحْضًا لَا حَقَّ فِيهِ؛ إذْ لَوْ كَانَتْ كَذَلِكَ لَمَا اشْتَبَهَتْ عَلَى أَحَدٍ وَإِنَّمَا يَكُونُ فِيهَا بَعْضُ الْحَقِّ وَبَعْضُ الْبَاطِلِ. وَكَذَلِكَ دِينُ الْمُشْرِكِينَ وَأَهْلِ الْكِتَابِ فَإِنَّهُ لَا يَكُونُ كُلَّ مَا يُخْبِرُونَ بِهِ كَذِبًا وَكُلُّ مَا يَأْمُرُونَ بِهِ فَسَادًا؛ بَلْ لَا بُدَّ أَنْ يَكُونَ فِي خَبَرِهِمْ صِدْقٌ
translated_text:
As for someone saying, “Their needs are sometimes fulfilled; does that justify their seeking out these graves?” the answer is that this does not justify seeking them out, for several reasons.

First, many needs of the polytheists and the People of the Book are fulfilled through supplication at idols, statues of saints, and places they venerate. Such veneration is forbidden in the era of Islam. Would any Muslim say that this justifies their engaging in conduct forbidden by the consensus of the Muslims?

Whatever factors lead the followers of whims and religious innovations to introduce their innovations, factors of the same kind—and worse—are found among the polytheists and the People of the Book, leading them into their disbelief. Whoever reflects on this will find it true of most matters, for religious innovations are derived from disbelief. Complete faith consists in doing what Allah and His Messenger have commanded and refraining from what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden. If a person neglects some of what is commanded and replaces it with something forbidden, his faith is diminished accordingly.

An innovation cannot be pure truth, for if it were, it would be religiously sanctioned. Nor can its benefit outweigh its harm, for if it did, it would be religiously sanctioned. Nor is it pure falsehood containing no truth, for if it were, no one would mistake it for truth. Rather, it contains some truth and some falsehood.

The same applies to the religion of the polytheists and the People of the Book: not everything they report is false, nor is everything they enjoin corrupt. Rather, there must be some truth in what they report

 وَالثَّالِثُ:
 الْإِخْبَارُ بِمَا يُقْضَى عِنْدَهُ مِنْ الْحَاجَاتِ فَمَا أَكْثَرَ مَا يَحْتَالُ الْمُعَظِّمُونَ لِلْقَبْرِ بِحِيَلِ يُلَبِّسُونَ عَلَى النَّاسِ أَنَّهُ حَصَلَ بِهِ خَرْقُ عَادَةٍ أَوْ قَضَاءُ حَاجَةٍ وَمَا أَكْثَرَ مَنْ يُخْبِرُ بِمَا لَا حَقِيقَةَ لَهُ وَقَدْ رَأَيْنَا مِنْ ذَلِكَ أُمُورًا كَثِيرَةً جِدًّا.
 الرَّابِعُ:

translated_text:
and some measure of benefit in what they enjoin. Yet they are disbelievers because of the truth they have abandoned and the falsehood they have embraced.

The second reason:

Lying is exceedingly common in this matter. Lying is associated with polytheism, as the Quran indicates in several places, while truthfulness is associated with sincere devotion to Allah. Believers are people of truthfulness and sincere devotion, whereas disbelievers are people of lying and polytheism. Since these shrines contain the polytheism that they do, lying accompanies them in various forms.

One is the claim that a particular place is the grave of some venerated person or the burial place of his head. There is much falsehood in such claims.

Second, reports about him in which falsehood abounds.

Third, reports of needs fulfilled at his grave. How often those who venerate a grave resort to tricks, misleading people into believing that an extraordinary event has occurred or a need has been fulfilled through it! How many people report things that have no basis in reality! We have witnessed a great many such things.

Fourth, reports about the lineage of those connected to him. Many people claim a connection to the deceased in that grave, whether through descent or otherwise. I have even seen someone who claims

that he is a descendant of Ibrāhīm ibn Adham, falsely claiming this so that he might become the custodian of his grave. As for lies about the Prophet’s family, they are too numerous to describe.

The Banū ʿUbayd—known as al-Qaddāh—claimed to be Fatimids, built Cairo, and remained kings for some two hundred years, claiming descent from ʿAlī. They gained control over half the Muslim realm, at times even taking control of Baghdad. They were as Abū Hāmid al-Ghazālī described them:

“Outwardly, their doctrine is Rāfidī Shiism; inwardly, it is pure disbelief.”

Judge Abū Bakr ibn al-Tayyib wrote his book entitled “Uncovering the Secrets and Tearing Away the Veils” to expose their true character. Numerous other Muslim scholars did likewise, including Judge Abū Yaʿlā and Abū ʿAbd Allāh Muhammad ibn ʿAbd al-Karīm al-Shahrastānī.

All scholars know that they were not descendants of Fātimah. Rather, they were descended from Magians; it has also been said that they descended from a Jew. They were among those furthest removed from the Messenger of Allah—may Allah’s blessings and peace be upon him—in their adherence to his Sunnah and religion. Their inward religion combines the religions of the Magians and the Sabians, while what they outwardly profess of the Muslims’ religion is Rāfidī Shiism. Thus, the best of their religious adherents are the Rāfidīs: their ignorant followers and common people, and everyone who joins them thinking himself a Muslim and believing Islam to be true.

Their elite, however—their kings and scholars—know that they stand outside all these religions: those of the Muslims, Jews, and Christians. And those closest

The third consideration:

If a Muslim’s need is fulfilled after he has offered a supplication at a grave, how does he know that the grave had any influence on the fulfillment of that need? The same applies to the vows they make at graves or elsewhere when their needs are fulfilled.

It is established in the two Sahihs that the Prophet—may Allah’s blessings and peace be upon him—forbade making vows and said:

“It brings no good; it merely extracts something from the miser.”

Another wording states:

“A vow brings the son of Adam nothing that was not already decreed for him. Rather, the vow brings him to the decree I have ordained.”

This authentic hadith establishes that a vow does not bring about the outcome upon which it is made conditional, whether securing a benefit or averting harm—even though the vow is a recompense for the fulfillment of that need and is conditional upon it, and despite the many people whose needs are fulfilled after they have made vows conditional upon their fulfillment. Graves are therefore even less likely to be a cause of such fulfillment.

Furthermore, that need must have been fulfilled either without his supplication or through his supplication. If the former is the case, there is nothing further to discuss; but if

The fourth consideration:

Even supposing that graves have some influence in this regard—whether through the graves themselves, as the would-be philosophers and those who follow their approach maintain, claiming that the departed soul connects with the supplicant’s soul, thereby strengthening him, as Ibn Sīnā, Abū Hāmid, and others like them allege concerning visits to graves, or through some other cause—the response is:

Not every means by which a person obtains what he needs is prescribed by Islamic law, or even permissible. A means is prescribed only when its benefit outweighs its harm. If its harm predominates, however, it is not prescribed; rather, it is forbidden, even if it yields some benefit.

This includes the prohibition of sorcery, despite its effects and its fulfillment of certain needs, and the practices it encompasses, such as worshipping the heavenly bodies, invoking them, and summoning the jinn. The same applies to soothsaying, divination by arrows, and the various practices forbidden by Islamic law, even though they sometimes involve some disclosure of hidden matters or produce certain effects. This provides a general indication of the means by which their needs are fulfilled. As for

a detailed account of this, it would require extensive discussion, as would an explanation of the kinds of sorcery, the reason for its effects, and the sīmiyā (a form of sorcery) it involves, along with the kinds of associating partners with Allah and what prompted the polytheists to worship idols.

Any rational person knows that no nation has ever unanimously adopted a practice without a reason. Abraham, Allah’s intimate friend, peace be upon him, says:

“And keep me and my sons away from worshipping idols.”

“My Lord, indeed they have led many people astray.”

Anyone who imagines that idol-worshippers believed their idols created the world, sent down rain, caused plants to grow, created animals, or anything of that kind is ignorant of their beliefs. Rather, their purpose in turning to their idols was of the same kind as that of those who associate partners with Allah through graves when they turn to the graves they venerate, or that of Christians when they turn to the graves of saints: they take them as intercessors, intermediaries, and means of approach. Indeed, reliable reports have established for us that some of those who worship at graves do more there than many idol-worshippers do. It is enough for a Muslim to know that Allah has forbidden nothing unless its harm is either unmixed or predominant.

As for anything whose benefit is unmixed or outweighs its harm, Allah has prescribed it. For the messengers were sent to secure and perfect benefits, and to eliminate and reduce harms. Just as associating partners with Allah is linked with falsehood, it is also linked with sorcery, as in His words, Exalted is He:

“Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Scripture? They believe in sorcery and false gods, and say of those who disbelieve, ‘These are better guided than the believers as to the way.’”

فَأَجَابَ:
لَيْسَ الدُّعَاءُ عِنْدَ الْقُبُورِ بِأَفْضَلَ مِنْ الدُّعَاءِ فِي الْمَسَاجِدِ وَغَيْرِهَا مِنْ الْأَمَاكِنِ وَلَا قَالَ أَحَدٌ مِنْ السَّلَفِ وَالْأَئِمَّةِ:
 إنَّهُ مُسْتَحَبٌّ أَنْ يَقْصِدَ الْقُبُورَ لِأَجْلِ الدُّعَاءِ عِنْدَهَا؛ لَا قُبُورَ الْأَنْبِيَاءِ وَلَا غَيْرِهِمْ؛ بَلْ قَدْ ثَبَتَ فِي صَحِيحِ الْبُخَارِيِّ أَنَّ عُمَرَ بْنَ الْخَطَّابِ اسْتَسْقَى بِالْعَبَّاسِ - عَمِّ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ -
 وَقَالَ:
 اللَّهُمَّ إنَّا كُنَّا نَسْتَسْقِي إلَيْك بِنَبِيِّنَا فَتَسْقِيَنَا وَإِنَّا نَتَوَسَّلُ إلَيْك بِعَمِّ نَبِيِّنَا فَاسْقِنَا فَيُسْقَوْنَ. فَاسْتَسْقَوْا بِالْعَبَّاسِ كَمَا كَانُوا يَسْتَسْقُونَ بِالنَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ لِأَنَّهُ عَمُّ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ. وَمَا كَانُوا يَسْتَسْقُونَ عِنْدَ قَبْرِهِ وَلَا يَدْعُونَ عِنْدَهُ؛
 بَلْ قَدْ ثَبَتَ عَنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ فِي الصِّحَاحِ أَنَّهُ قَالَ:
 
{لَعَنَ اللَّهُ الْيَهُودَ وَالنَّصَارَى اتَّخَذُوا قُبُورَ أَنْبِيَائِهِمْ مَسَاجِدَ}
 يُحَذِّرُ مَا فَعَلُوا وَقَالَ قَبْلَ أَنْ
translated_text:
He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

“Is supplication at graves, such as those of the righteous and the friends of Allah, permissible or not? Is it more likely to be answered there than at the graves of others? And which places are best for supplication?”

He replied:

Supplication at graves is no better than supplication in mosques or elsewhere. None of the early generations or the imams said that it is recommended to go to graves specifically to supplicate there, whether the graves of prophets or anyone else. Rather, it is established in Sahīh al-Bukhārī that ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb sought rain through al-ʿAbbās—the uncle of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him—and said:

“O Allah, we used to seek rain from You through our Prophet, and You would grant us rain. Now we seek a means of drawing near to You through our Prophet’s uncle, so grant us rain.”

And they would be granted rain. Thus, they sought rain through al-ʿAbbās just as they had sought it through the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, because he was the Prophet’s uncle. They did not seek rain at his grave or supplicate there. Indeed, it is established in the authentic hadith collections that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“May Allah curse the Jews and Christians: they took the graves of their prophets as places of worship.”

He was warning against what they had done. He also said, before he

died—five days beforehand:

“Those before you used to take graves as places of worship. Beware! Do not take graves as places of worship, for I forbid you to do so.”

The Sunan collections also report that he, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“May Allah curse women who visit graves and those who set up places of worship and lamps over them.”

Since he forbade taking graves as places of worship and lighting lamps over them, it is clear that he did not designate them as places for worshipping Allah and supplicating. Rather, he prescribed that those who visit graves should greet the deceased and supplicate for them, just as he prescribed offering the funeral prayer over them before burial and supplicating for them. Thus, the purpose of what he, peace and blessings be upon him, prescribed is to supplicate for the deceased, not to invoke them. And Allah knows best.

original_text:
وَقَالَ الشَّيْخُ مُحَمَّدُ بْنُ عَبْدِ الْهَادِي:
 
(*)
بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمَنِ الرَّحِيمِ
الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ رَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ،
 أَمَّا بَعْدُ فَهَذِهِ فُتْيَا أَفْتَى بِهَا الشِّيحُ الْإِمَامُ تَقِيُّ الدِّينِ أَبُو الْعَبَّاسِ أَحْمَد ابْنُ تَيْمِيَّة رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ ثُمَّ بَعْدَ مُدَّةٍ نَحْوَ سَبْعَ عَشْرَةَ سَنَةً أَنْكَرَهَا بَعْضُ النَّاسِ وَشَنَّعَ بِهَا جَمَاعَةٌ عِنْدَ بَعْضِ وُلَاةِ الْأُمُورِ وَذُكِرَتْ بِعِبَارَاتِ شَنِيعَةٍ:
 فَفَهِمَ مِنْهَا جَمَاعَةٌ غَيْرَ مَا هِيَ عَلَيْهِ وَانْضَمَّ إلَى الْإِنْكَارِ وَالشَّنَاعَةِ وَتَغَيُّرِ الْأَلْفَاظِ أُمُورٌ أَوْجَبَ ذَلِكَ كُلُّهُ مُكَاتَبَةَ السُّلْطَانِ - سُلْطَانِ الْإِسْلَامِ بِمِصْرِ - أَيَّدَهُ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى فَجَمَعَ قُضَاةَ بَلَدِهِ ثُمَّ اقْتَضَى الرَّأْيُ حَبْسَهُ فَحُبِسَ بِقَلْعَةِ دِمَشْقَ الْمَحْرُوسَةِ بِكِتَابِ وَرَدَ سَابِعَ شَعْبَانَ الْمُبَارَكِ سَنَةَ سِتٍّ وَعِشْرِينَ وَسَبْعِمِائَةٍ. وَفِي ذَلِكَ كُلِّهِ لَمْ يَحْضُرْ الشَّيْخُ الْمَذْكُورُ بِمَجْلِسِ حُكْمٍ وَلَا وَقَفَ عَلَى خَطِّهِ الَّذِي أَنْكَرَ وَلَا ادَّعَى عَلَيْهِ بِشَيْءِ. فَكَتَبَ بَعْضُ الْغُرَبَاءِ مِنْ بَلَدِهِ هَذِهِ الْفُتْيَا وَأَوْقَفَ عَلَيْهَا بَعْضَ عُلَمَاءِ بَغْدَادَ فَكَتَبُوا عَلَيْهَا بَعْدَ تَأَمُّلِهَا وَقِرَاءَةِ أَلْفَاظِهَا.

وهنا تنبيهات:
الأول: أن فتوى الشيخ رحمه الله وما نقله ابن عبد الهادي بعدها من فتاوى المؤيدين له من العلماء مذكورة بلفظها في (العقود الدرية من مناقب شيخ الإسلام أحمد بن تيمية) لابن عبد الهادي: ٣٤٦ - ٣٧٦.

الثالث: أن هناك فروقاً يسيرة إلى ثمانية فروق تقريبا بين الفتوى التي نقلها ابن عبد الهادي رحمه الله - والمنشورة في هذا الموضع -، والفتوى التي ذكرها الشيخ رحمه الله في الإخنائية ومختصرها، وأهم الفروق هي:
١ - ٢٧/ ١٨٥: (وقد احتج أبو محمد المقدسى على جواز السفر لزيارة القبور بأنه صلى الله عليه وسلم كان يزور مسجد قباء [وأنه كان يزور القبور])، وما بين المعقوفتين موجود في الإخنائية ص ٤٤، وفي مختصرها الموجود في الفتاوى: ٢٧/ ٢١٩، وهو ساقط من هذا الموضع.
٢٧/ ١٨٨ - : (وأما إذا نذر الرجل أن يسافر إليها لغرض مباح، فهذا جائز)، في الإخنائية ص ٤٥، ومختصرها (٢٧/ ٢٢١): (وأما إذا قدر أن الرجل سافر إليها. . .) وهو الأظهر.
٣ - ٢٧/ ١٨٩: (وفي سنن سعيد بن منصور: أن عبد الله بن حسن بن الحسين بن على بن أبي طالب، رأى رجلاً يختلف إلى قبر النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم [ويدعو عنده]، فقال: يا هذا، إن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم قال: " لا تتخذوا قبرى عيدًا، وصلوا على، فإن صلاتكم حيثما كنتم تبلغنى ". فما أنت ورجل بالأندلس منه إلا سواء).
وما بين المعقوفتين ساقط من الإخنائية ص ٤٦، ومختصرها (٢٧/ ٢٢٢)، وهو الموافق لرواية الحديث.
٤ - ٢٧/ ١٩١: (وأول من وضع هذه الأحاديث في السفر لزيارة المشاهد التى على القبور، أهل البدع، من الرافضة ونحوهم، الذين يعطلون المساجد، ويعظمون المشاهد، [يَدَعُون بيوت الله التى أمر أن يذكر فيها اسمه، ويعبد وحده لا شريك له، ويعظمون المشاهد] التي يشرك فيها ويكذب، ويبتدع فيها دين لم ينزل الله به سلطانًا؛ فإن الكتاب والسنة إنما فيهما ذكر المساجد، دون المشاهد)
وما بين المعقوفتين سقط - بسبب انتقال نظر الناسخ من كلمة " يعظمون المشاهد " الأولى إلى الثانية - من الإخنائية ص ٤٨، ومختصرها (٢٧/ ٢٢٤)، والله تعالى أعلم.
translated_text:
Shaykh Muhammad ibn Abd al-Hādī also said:

(*)
In the name of Allah, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful.

All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds.

To proceed: This is a fatwa issued by the shaykh and imam, Taqī al-Dīn Abū al-Abbās Ahmad ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah be pleased with him. Then, some seventeen years later, certain people denounced it, and a group used it to vilify him before some of those in authority. It was presented in inflammatory terms, leading some people to misunderstand its actual meaning. Other matters compounded this denunciation, vilification, and alteration of its wording. All of this prompted correspondence with the Sultan—the Sultan of Islam in Egypt—may Allah Most High support him. He assembled the judges of his land, and it was subsequently decided to imprison the shaykh. He was therefore imprisoned in the citadel of Damascus, may Allah protect it, pursuant to a written order that arrived on the seventh of the blessed month of Shaʿbān, 726 AH.

Throughout all of this, the aforementioned shaykh had not appeared before a court, nor had he seen the written text of his that was denounced, nor had any formal claim been brought against him. Some men from his town who were away from home then copied out this fatwa and showed it to some of the scholars of Baghdad. After carefully considering it and reading its wording, they wrote their responses to it.
translated_footnote:
(*) Shaykh Nāsir ibn Hamad al-Fahd stated (pp. 211–213):
The following points should be noted:
First: The Shaykh’s fatwa—may Allah have mercy on him—and the supporting fatwas of other scholars subsequently quoted by Ibn 'Abd al-Hādī appear verbatim in Ibn 'Abd al-Hādī’s al-'Uqūd al-Durriyya min Manāqib Shaykh al-Islām Ahmad ibn Taymiyya, pp. 346–376.
Second: Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah have mercy on him—also reproduced the text of this fatwa in al-Radd 'alā al-Ikhnā'ī, pp. 40–49. This passage from al-Radd 'alā al-Ikhnā'ī also appears in its abridgment, published in al-Fatāwā, 27/214–228.
Third: There are a few minor differences—approximately eight—between the fatwa transmitted by Ibn 'Abd al-Hādī—may Allah have mercy on him—and published here, and the fatwa reproduced by the Shaykh—may Allah have mercy on him—in al-Ikhnā'iyya and its abridgment. The most significant differences are:
1 — 27/185: “Abū Muhammad al-Maqdisī argued that travelling to visit graves is permissible, citing the fact that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, used to visit the mosque of Qubā' [and that he used to visit graves].” The bracketed words appear in al-Ikhnā'iyya, p. 44, and its abridgment in al-Fatāwā, 27/219, but are missing here.
27/188 — “If a man vows to travel to them for a permissible purpose, this is permissible.” In al-Ikhnā'iyya, p. 45, and its abridgment, 27/221, the wording is: “If, however, it is supposed that a man travelled to them…” This is the more plausible reading.
3 — 27/189: “In the Sunan of Sa'īd ibn Mansūr, it is reported that 'Abd Allāh ibn Hasan ibn al-Husayn ibn 'Alī ibn Abī Tālib saw a man repeatedly visiting the Prophet’s grave [and supplicating there]. He said: ‘O man, the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said: “Do not make my grave a place of celebration. Send blessings upon me, for your blessings reach me wherever you may be.” Thus, you and a man in al-Andalus are on an equal footing in relation to him.’”
The bracketed words are absent from al-Ikhnā'iyya, p. 46, and its abridgment, 27/222. Their omission accords with the transmitted wording of the hadith.
4 — 27/191: “The first to fabricate these hadiths concerning travel to visit shrines erected over graves were the people of innovation, such as the Rāfida and others like them, who leave mosques unused and venerate shrines. [They abandon the houses of Allah, in which He has commanded that His name be mentioned and that He alone be worshipped, without partner, and venerate shrines] where partners are associated with Him, lies are told, and a religion is invented for which Allah has sent down no authority. For the Book and the Sunnah mention mosques, not shrines.”
The bracketed words were omitted from al-Ikhnā'iyya, p. 48, and its abridgment, 27/224, because the copyist’s eye skipped from the first occurrence of “venerate shrines” to the second. And Allah Most High knows best.

وَسُئِلَ بَعْضُ مَالِكِيَّةِ دِمَشْقَ عَنْهَا فَكَتَبُوا كَذَلِكَ. وَبَلَغَنَا أَنَّ بِمِصْرِ مَنْ وَقَفَ عَلَيْهَا فَوَافَقَ. وَنَبْدَأُ الْآنَ بِذِكْرِ السُّؤَالِ الَّذِي كَتَبَ عَلَيْهِ أَهْلُ بَغْدَادَ وَبِذِكْرِ الْفُتْيَا وَجَوَابِ الشَّيْخِ الْمَذْكُورِ عَلَيْهَا وَجَوَابِ الْفُقَهَاءِ بَعْدَهُ. وَهَذِهِ صُورَةُ السُّؤَالِ وَالْأَجْوِبَةِ.
 الْمَسْئُولُ مِنْ إنْعَامِ السَّادَةِ الْعُلَمَاءِ وَالْهُدَاةِ الْفُضَلَاءِ أَئِمَّةِ الدِّينِ وَهُدَاةِ الْمُسْلِمِينَ وَفَّقَهُمْ اللَّهُ لِمَرْضَاتِهِ وَأَدَامَ بِهِمْ الْهِدَايَةَ:
 أَنْ يَنْعَمُوا وَيَتَأَمَّلُوا الْفَتْوَى وَجَوَابَهَا الْمُتَّصِلَ بِهَذَا السُّؤَالِ الْمَنْسُوخِ عَقِبَهُ وَصُورَةُ ذَلِكَ: مَا يَقُولُ السَّادَةُ الْعُلَمَاءُ أَئِمَّةُ الدِّينِ نَفَعَ اللَّهُ بِهِمْ الْمُسْلِمِينَ: فِي رَجُلٍ نَوَى السَّفَرَ إلَى 
" زِيَارَةِ قُبُورِ الْأَنْبِيَاءِ وَالصَّالِحِينَ "
 مِثْلِ نَبِيِّنَا مُحَمَّدٍ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ وَغَيْرِهِ. فَهَلْ يَجُوزُ لَهُ فِي سَفَرِهِ أَنْ يَقْصُرَ الصَّلَاةَ؟ وَهَلْ هَذِهِ الزِّيَارَةُ شَرْعِيَّةٌ أَمْ لَا؟ ؟
 وَقَدْ رُوِيَ عَنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ أَنَّهُ قَالَ:
 
{مَنْ حَجَّ وَلَمْ يَزُرْنِي فَقَدْ جَفَانِي}
 
{وَمَنْ زَارَنِي بَعْدَ مَوْتِي كَمَنْ زَارَنِي فِي حَيَاتِي}
translated_text:
Some Mālikī scholars in Damascus were also asked about it, and they wrote similarly. We have heard that someone in Egypt examined it and concurred. We shall now present the question on which the scholars of Baghdad wrote, the request for a ruling and the aforementioned shaykh’s answer to it, followed by the jurists’ responses. Here is the text of the question and the answers.

Our esteemed scholars and virtuous guides, the imams of the religion and guides of the Muslims—may Allah grant them success in attaining His pleasure and perpetuate guidance through them—are kindly requested to examine the request for a ruling and its answer, attached to this inquiry and transcribed below. Its wording is as follows:

What do the esteemed scholars, the imams of the religion—may Allah benefit the Muslims through them—say concerning a man who intends to travel to “visit the graves of the prophets and the righteous,” such as our Prophet Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, and others? May he shorten his prayers during his journey? Is such a visit prescribed by Islamic law or not?

It has been reported that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Whoever performs Hajj but does not visit me has slighted me.”

“And whoever visits me after my death is like one who visited me during my lifetime.”

original_text:
وَقَدْ رُوِيَ عَنْهُ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ أَيْضًا أَنَّهُ قَالَ:
 
{لَا تُشَدُّ الرِّحَالُ إلَّا إلَى ثَلَاثَةِ مَسَاجِدَ: الْمَسْجِدِ الْحَرَامِ وَمَسْجِدِي هَذَا وَالْمَسْجِدِ الْأَقْصَى}
 . أَفْتُونَا مَأْجُورِينَ رَحِمَكُمْ اللَّهُ.
فَأَجَابَ:
الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ رَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ، أَمَّا مَنْ سَافَرَ لِمُجَرَّدِ زِيَارَةِ قُبُورِ الْأَنْبِيَاءِ وَالصَّالِحِينَ فَهَلْ يَجُوزُ لَهُ قَصْرُ الصَّلَاةِ؟

 وَالْقَوْلُ الثَّانِي:
 أَنَّهُ يُقْصَرُ وَهَذَا يَقُولُهُ مَنْ يُجَوِّزُ الْقَصْرَ فِي السَّفَرِ الْمُحَرَّمِ كَأَبِي حَنِيفَةَ. وَيَقُولُهُ بَعْضُ الْمُتَأَخِّرِينَ مِنْ أَصْحَابِ الشَّافِعِيِّ
translated_text:
And it has also been reported that he, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Do not undertake a journey except to three mosques: the Sacred Mosque, this mosque of mine, and al-Aqsā Mosque.”

Give us your ruling—may you be rewarded, and may Allah have mercy on you.

He replied:

Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds. As for someone who travels solely to visit the graves of the prophets and the righteous, may he shorten his prayers? There are two well-known opinions on this:

The first is that shortening the prayers during such a journey is not permissible, because it is a prohibited journey. This is the view of earlier scholars who do not permit shortening the prayers on a sinful journey, such as Abū ‘Abd Allāh ibn Batta, Abū al-Wafā’ ibn ‘Aqīl, and many groups of earlier scholars. The position of Mālik, al-Shāfi‘ī, and Ahmad is that prayers may not be shortened during a journey prohibited by Islamic law.

The second opinion is that he may shorten his prayers. This is held by those who permit shortening the prayers during a forbidden journey, such as Abū Hanīfa. It is also held by some later followers of al-Shāfi‘ī

and Ahmad who permit travelling to visit the graves of the prophets and the righteous, such as Abū Hāmid al-Ghazālī, Abū al-Hasan ibn ‘Abdūs al-Harrānī, and Abū Muhammad ibn Qudāma al-Maqdisī.

These scholars say that such travel is not forbidden, citing the general wording of the Prophet’s statement, peace and blessings be upon him:

“Visit the graves.”

Some who are unfamiliar with hadith may cite reports concerning visiting the Prophet’s grave, peace and blessings be upon him, such as his saying:

“Whoever visits me after my death, it is as though he visited me during my lifetime.”

This was narrated by al-Dāraqutnī and Ibn Mājah.

As for the saying mentioned by some people:

“Whoever performs Hajj but does not visit me has shunned me,”

none of the scholars has narrated it. It is like the saying:

“Whoever visits me and my father Abraham in the same year, I guarantee him Paradise from Allah.”

The scholars agree that no one has narrated this either, nor has anyone cited it as evidence. Rather, some of them cite the report narrated by al-Dāraqutnī and similar reports.

Abū Muhammad al-Maqdisī argued that travelling to visit graves is permissible on the grounds that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, used to visit the mosque of Qubā’. He answered the hadith, “Do not undertake a journey,” by interpreting it as meaning that such travel is not recommended.

As for the former group, they cite as evidence the Prophet’s saying, peace and blessings be upon him, recorded in the two Sahīh collections:

“No journey should be undertaken except to three mosques: the Sacred Mosque, this mosque of mine, and al-Aqsā Mosque.”

The imams agree that this hadith is authentic and is to be acted upon. If a man vows to undertake a journey to pray or observe a devotional retreat at a mosque or shrine other than these three mosques, or to travel there, he is not obliged to fulfil that vow, by agreement of the imams. If he vows to travel to the Sacred Mosque for Hajj or ‘umrah, he is obliged to do so, by agreement of the scholars.

If he vows to visit the Prophet’s Mosque, peace and blessings be upon him, or al-Aqsā Mosque for prayer or a devotional retreat, he must fulfil this vow according to Mālik, al-Shāfi‘ī in one of his two opinions, and Ahmad. According to Abū Hanīfah, however, he is not obliged to do so, because in his view a vow becomes binding only when the act belongs to a category already made obligatory by Islamic law.

The majority, however, hold that a vow to perform any act of obedience must be fulfilled, as established in Sahīh al-Bukhārī, on the authority of ‘Ā’ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Whoever vows to obey Allah, let him obey Him; and whoever vows to disobey Allah, let him not disobey Him.”

Travelling to these two mosques is an act of obedience; therefore, a vow to do so must be fulfilled.

{لَا تُشَدُّ الرِّحَالُ}

 يُجَابُ عَنْهُ بِوَجْهَيْنِ:
translated_text:
As for travelling to a place other than the three mosques, no scholar has held that someone who vows to make such a journey is obliged to do so. Indeed, the scholars explicitly stated that one should not travel to the Mosque of Qubā’, since it is not one of the three mosques—even though visiting it is recommended for those in Medina, because this does not involve undertaking a journey. As stated in the authentic hadith:

“Whoever purifies himself at home, then comes to the Mosque of Qubā’ intending only to pray there, will receive the reward of an ‘umrah.”

They also argued that travelling to visit the graves of the prophets and the righteous is an innovation that none of the Companions or Successors practised, that the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, never commanded, and that none of the imams of the Muslims deemed recommended. Whoever believes this to be an act of worship and undertakes it therefore contravenes the Sunnah and the consensus of the imams. This is among the innovations contrary to the Sunnah and scholarly consensus that Abū ‘Abd Allāh ibn Battah mentioned in al-Ibānah al-Sughrā.

This makes clear the invalidity of Abū Muhammad al-Maqdisī’s argument: the Prophet’s visits to the Mosque of Qubā’, peace and blessings be upon him, did not involve undertaking a journey, and al-Maqdisī concedes their point that a vow to travel there does not make that journey obligatory.

His statement that the hadith whose purport is “No journey should be undertaken” is to be understood as denying that such travel is recommended can be answered in two ways:

First: this is an admission on his part that such travel is not a righteous deed, a means of drawing near to Allah, an act of obedience, or a good deed. Thus, whoever believes that travelling to visit the graves of the prophets and the righteous is a means of drawing near to Allah, an act of worship, and an act of obedience has contradicted scholarly consensus. If he travels in the belief that doing so is an act of obedience, this is forbidden by the consensus of the Muslims. The prohibition therefore arises from treating it as a means of drawing near to Allah, and it is well known that no one travels to these graves except for that purpose. If, however, a man vows to travel to them for a permissible purpose, that is permissible and does not fall into this category.

Second: this hadith entails a prohibition, and a prohibition entails that the act is forbidden. As for the hadiths they cite concerning visiting the Prophet’s grave, peace and blessings be upon him, they are all weak according to the consensus of hadith scholars; indeed, they are fabricated. None of the compilers of the authoritative Sunan collections narrated any of them, nor did any of the imams cite any of them as evidence. Rather, Mālik—the imam of the people of the Prophet’s city, who are the most knowledgeable about the ruling on this matter—disapproved of a man saying, “I visited his grave, peace and blessings be upon him.” Had this expression been familiar among them, sanctioned by the religion, or transmitted from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, the scholar of Medina would not have disapproved of it.

They buried him, peace and blessings be upon him, in the chamber of Ā’ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, contrary to their usual practice of burial in open ground, so that no one would pray at his grave and make it a place of worship, thereby turning his grave into an idol.

While the Prophet’s chamber remained separate from the mosque—until the time of al-Walīd ibn Abd al-Malik—none of the Companions or Successors would enter it to pray there, rub against the grave, or supplicate there. Rather, they would do all of this only in the mosque. When the early generations of Companions and Successors greeted the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and wished to supplicate, they would supplicate facing the direction of prayer, not the grave.

As for standing to greet him, may Allah’s blessings and peace be upon him, Abū Hanīfah said:

“One should face the direction of prayer in this case too, not the grave.”

Most of the imams, however, said:

“Rather, one should face the grave specifically when offering the greeting.”

None of the imams said that one should face the grave when supplicating. The only report to that effect is a fabricated account attributed to Mālik, whose own position is contrary to it.

The imams also agreed that one should neither rub against the grave of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, nor kiss it. All of this serves to safeguard monotheism.

One of the roots of associating partners with Allah is taking graves as places of worship. Thus, a number of the early generations commented on Allah’s words:

“They said, ‘Never abandon your gods, and never abandon Wadd, Suwā‘, Yaghūth, Ya‘ūq, or Nasr.’”

They said:

“These were righteous men among Noah’s people. When they died, people gathered devotedly at their graves, then fashioned statues in their likeness. After a long time had passed, they worshipped them.”

Al-Bukhārī reported the substance of this account from Ibn ‘Abbās in his Sahīh. Muhammad ibn Jarīr al-Tabarī and others also related it in their Quran commentaries from several of the early generations. Wathīmah and others related it through several chains of transmission in their accounts of the prophets. I have discussed the foundations of these matters at length elsewhere.

The first to fabricate these hadiths concerning travel to visit shrines erected over graves were adherents of religious innovation among the Rāfidah and others like them, who leave mosques unused and exalt shrines. They abandon the houses of Allah, in which He commanded that His name be remembered and that He alone be worshipped, without any partner. Instead, they exalt shrines where partners are associated with Him, truth is denied, and a religion is invented for which Allah has sent down no authority. The Quran and Sunnah mention mosques, not shrines, as Allah Most High says:

When they obtained this answer in Damascus, they copied it and sent it to Egypt. The Shāfiʿī judge wrote upon it:

“I checked the answer to this question against the text in Ibn Taymiyyah’s handwriting and found it correct.”

Later in his statement, he said:

“The distortion lies in his declaring that visiting the grave of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and the graves of the other prophets—may Allah Most High be pleased with them all—is a sin conclusively established by consensus.”

These were his words.

Consider this misrepresentation of Shaykh al-Islām! His answer contains no prohibition against visiting the graves of the prophets and the righteous. He merely mentioned two opinions concerning undertaking travel solely to visit graves.

And visiting graves without undertaking a journey to them is one matter; undertaking a journey solely to visit them is another. The Shaykh does not prohibit visits that involve no such journey; rather, he considers them recommended and encourages them. His books and manuals of pilgrimage rites bear witness to this. In his fatwa, the Shaykh did not address such visits, declare them sinful, or report a consensus prohibiting them. Nothing is hidden from Allah, glorified and exalted be He.

When the aforementioned judge’s written statement reached Egypt, much controversy arose and the turmoil intensified. The judges there were summoned, and they gathered and deliberated. Some recommended imprisoning the Shaykh, and the Sultan ordered it. What has already been recounted then took place. Afterwards, other events befell those involved in this case, which cannot be related here.

The Shaykh’s answer to this question reached the scholars of Baghdad. They rose to his defence and wrote expressing their agreement with him. I have seen their statements in their own handwriting.

 مُحَمَّدٍ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَعَلَى آلِهِ وَصَحْبِهِ أَجْمَعِينَ. إنَّهُ حَيْثُ قَدْ مَنَّ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى عَلَى عِبَادِهِ وَتَفَضَّلَ بِرَحْمَتِهِ عَلَى بِلَادِهِ بِأَنْ وَسَّدَ أُمُورَ الْأُمَّةِ الْمُحَمَّدِيَّةِ وَأَسْنَدَ أَزِمَّةَ الْمِلَّةِ الْحَنِيفِيَّةِ إلَى مَنْ خَصَّصَهُ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى بِأَفْضَلِ الكمالات النَّفْسَانِيَّةِ وَخَصَّصَهُ بِأَكْمَلِ السَّعَادَاتِ الرُّوحَانِيَّةِ مُحْيِي سُنَنِ الْعَدْلِ وَمُبْدِي سُنَنِ الْفَضْلِ الْمُعْتَصِمِ بِحَبْلِ اللَّهِ الْمُتَوَكِّلِ عَلَى اللَّهِ الْمُكْتَفِي بِنِعَمِ اللَّهِ الْقَائِمِ بِأَوَامِرِ اللَّهِ الْمُسْتَظْهِرِ بِقُوَّةِ اللَّهِ الْمُسْتَضِيءِ بِنُورِ اللَّهِ أَعَزَّ اللَّهُ سُلْطَانَهُ وَأَعْلَى عَلَى سَائِرِ الْمُلُوكِ شَانَهُ وَلَا زَالَتْ رِقَابُ الْأُمَمِ خَاضِعَةً لِأَوَامِرِهِ وَأَعْنَاقُ الْعِبَادِ طَائِعَةً لِمَرَاسِمِهِ وَلَا زَالَ مُوَالِي دَوْلَتِهِ بِطَاعَتِهِ مَجْبُورًا وَمُعَادِي صَوْلَتِهِ بِخِزْيِهِ مَذْمُومًا مَدْحُورًا. فَالْمَرْجُوُّ مِنْ أَلْطَافِ الْحَضْرَةِ الْمُقَدَّسَةِ - زَادَهَا اللَّهُ تَعَالَى عُلُوًّا وَشَرَفًا - أَنْ يَكُونَ لِلْعُلَمَاءِ الَّذِينَ هُمْ وَرَثَةُ الْأَنْبِيَاءِ وَصَفْوَةُ الْأَصْفِيَاءِ
translated_text:
In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

The servant, ever in need of Allah Most High, declares, after praising Allah, whose blessings abound and whose favours are longstanding, and invoking blessings upon the noblest of the prophets and messengers, Muhammad—may Allah bless him and all his family and Companions:

Allah Most High has bestowed His favour upon His servants and graciously extended His mercy to His lands by entrusting the affairs of Muhammad’s community and the reins of the upright faith to one whom He has endowed with the finest qualities of soul and the fullest spiritual felicity: one who revives the ways of justice and manifests the ways of generosity; who holds fast to Allah’s rope, relies upon Allah, finds sufficiency in Allah’s blessings, upholds Allah’s commands, draws strength from Allah’s might, and seeks illumination through Allah’s light. May Allah strengthen his sovereignty and exalt his standing above all other kings. May the nations ever bow to his commands and the people submit to his decrees. May whoever supports his rule ever be strengthened through obedience to him, and whoever opposes his might be disgraced, condemned, and driven away.

It is therefore hoped, through the graciousness of the august court—may Allah Most High increase its eminence and honour—that the scholars, who are the heirs of the prophets and the choicest of the elect

وَعِمَادُ الدِّينِ وَمَدَارُ أَهْلِ الْيَقِينِ:
 حَظٌّ مِنْ الْعِنَايَةِ السُّلْطَانِيَّةِ وَافِرٌ وَنَصِيبٌ مِنْ الرَّحْمَةِ وَالشَّفَقَةِ فَإِنَّهَا مَنْقَبَةٌ لَا يُعَادِلُهَا فَضِيلَةٌ وَحَسَنَةٌ لَا يُحِيطُهَا سَيِّئَةٌ لِأَنَّهَا حَقِيقَةُ التَّعْظِيمِ لِأَمْرِ اللَّهِ تَعَالَى وَخُلَاصَةُ الشَّفَقَةِ عَلَى خَلْقِ اللَّهِ تَعَالَى. وَلَا رَيْبَ أَنَّ الْمَمْلُوكَ وَقَفَ عَلَى مَا سُئِلَ عَنْهُ الشَّيْخُ الْإِمَامُ الْعَلَّامَةُ وَحِيدُ دَهْرِهِ وَفَرِيدُ عَصْرِهِ تَقِيُّ الدِّينِ أَبُو الْعَبَّاسِ أَحْمَد ابْنُ تَيْمِيَّة وَمَا أَجَابَ بِهِ.
 فَوَجَدْته خُلَاصَةَ مَا قَالَهُ الْعُلَمَاءُ فِي هَذَا الْبَابِ حَسْبَ مَا اقْتَضَاهُ الْحَالُ:
 مِنْ نَقْلِهِ الصَّحِيحِ وَمَا أَدَّى إلَيْهِ الْبَحْثُ مِنْ الْإِلْزَامِ وَالِالْتِزَامِ لَا يُدَاخِلُهُ تَحَامُلٌ وَلَا يَعْتَرِيهِ تَجَاهُلٌ. وَلَيْسَ فِيهِ - وَالْعِيَاذُ بِاَللَّهِ - مَا يَقْتَضِي الْإِزْرَاءَ وَالتَّنْقِيصَ بِمَنْزِلَةِ الرَّسُولِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ.
 وَكَيْفَ يَجُوزُ لِلْعُلَمَاءِ أَنْ تَحْمِلَهُمْ الْعَصَبِيَّةُ:
 أَنْ يَتَفَوَّهُوا بِالْإِزْرَاءِ وَالتَّنْقِيصِ فِي حَقِّ الرَّسُولِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ؟
 وَهَلْ يَجُوزُ أَنْ يَتَصَوَّرَ مُتَصَوِّرٌ:
 أَنَّ زِيَارَةَ قَبْرِهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ تَزِيدُ فِي قَدْرِهِ وَهَلْ تَرْكُهَا مِمَّا يُنْقِصُ مِنْ تَعْظِيمِهِ؟ حَاشَا لِلرَّسُولِ مِنْ ذَلِكَ. نَعَمْ لَوْ ذَكَرَ ذَلِكَ ذَاكِرٌ ابْتِدَاءً وَكَانَ هُنَاكَ قَرَائِنُ تَدُلُّ عَلَى الْإِزْرَاءِ وَالتَّنْقِيصِ أَمْكَنَ حَمْلُهُ عَلَى ذَلِكَ. مَعَ أَنَّهُ كَانَ يَكُونُ كِنَايَةً لَا صَرِيحًا
translated_text:
and the pillars of the faith and the mainstay of those endowed with certainty—may receive an ample share of the sovereign’s care and a measure of mercy and compassion. For this is a distinction unmatched by any other virtue, and a good deed that no evil can overshadow: it embodies true reverence for Allah Most High’s command and the essence of compassion for His creation.

I, your humble servant, have indeed examined the question put to the shaykh, imam, and erudite scholar, unequalled in his day and peerless in his age, Taqī al-Dīn Abū al-'Abbās Ahmad ibn Taymiyyah, together with his answer. I found it to be a distillation of what the scholars have said on this subject, suited to the circumstances, drawing upon his accurate citations and the implications established and accepted in the course of the discussion. It is neither tainted by prejudice nor marred by a wilful disregard of the facts. Nor does it contain—Allah forbid—anything that would disparage or diminish the Messenger’s standing, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

How could scholars allow partisanship to lead them to utter words disparaging or belittling the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace? Could anyone conceivably imagine that visiting his grave, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, enhances his stature, or that refraining from visiting it diminishes the reverence due to him? The Messenger is far above such a notion!

Admittedly, if someone were to make such a statement unprompted, and there were indications of disparagement and belittlement, it could be construed in that sense—though even then it would be an implicit allusion, not an explicit statement.

فَكَيْفَ وَقَدْ قَالَهُ فِي مَعْرِضِ السُّؤَالِ وَطَرِيقِ الْبَحْثِ وَالْجَدَلِ؟ .

{لَا تُشَدُّ الرِّحَالُ}
 - إلَى آخِرِهِ " أَنَّهُ لَا يَجُوزُ شَدُّ الرِّحَالِ إلَى غَيْرِ مَا ذَكَرَ أَوْ وُجُوبُهُ أَوْ ندبيته. فَإِنْ فَعَلَهُ كَانَ مُخَالِفًا لِصَرِيحِ النَّهْيِ وَمُخَالَفَةُ النَّهْيِ مَعْصِيَةٌ - إمَّا كُفْرٌ أَوْ غَيْرُهُ - عَلَى قَدْرِ الْمَنْهِيِّ عَنْهُ وَوُجُوبِهِ وَتَحْرِيمِهِ وَصِفَةِ النَّهْيِ وَالزِّيَارَةُ أَخَصُّ مِنْ وَجْهٍ. فَالزِّيَارَةُ بِغَيْرِ شَدٍّ غَيْرُ مَنْهِيٍّ عَنْهَا وَمَعَ الشَّدِّ مَنْهِيٌّ عَنْهَا. وَبِالْجُمْلَةِ فَمَا ذَكَرَهُ الشَّيْخُ تَقِيُّ الدِّينِ عَلَى الْوَجْهِ الْمَذْكُورِ الْمَوْقُوفِ عَلَيْهِ لَمْ يَسْتَحِقَّ عَلَيْهِ عِقَابًا وَلَا يُوجِبْ عِتَابًا. وَالْمَرَاحِمُ السُّلْطَانِيَّةُ أَحْرَى بِالتَّوْسِعَةِ وَالنَّظَرِ بِعَيْنِ الرَّأْفَةِ وَالرَّحْمَةِ إلَيْهِ وَلِلْآرَاءِ الْمَلَكِيَّةِ عُلُوُّ الْمَزِيدِ. حَرَّرَهُ ابْنُ الْكُتُبِيِّ الشَّافِعِيُّ. حَامِدًا لِلَّهِ عَلَى نِعَمِهِ. اهـ
translated_text:
How, then, could it be construed that way when he said it in response to a question and in the course of inquiry and debate?

Moreover, what is understood from the scholars’ statements and the reflections of discerning people is that visitation is not, in itself, an act of worship or obedience. Thus, if someone swore to perform an act of worship or obedience, he would not fulfil his oath through such a visit. However, Judge Ibn Kajj—one of the later scholars of our school—held that a vow to undertake this visitation constitutes an act of devotion binding upon the person making it. He stands alone in this view: neither an explicit textual authority nor a sound analogy supports him.

The unqualified wording of the prophetic report—his saying, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, “Journeys are not to be undertaken,” and the remainder of the hadith—implies that undertaking journeys to places other than those he mentioned is not permissible—or that such journeys are not obligatory or recommended. Whoever does so contravenes the explicit prohibition. Contravening a prohibition is a sin—whether disbelief or something less—depending on the matter prohibited, its obligatory or forbidden status, and the nature of the prohibition. Visitation is more specific in one respect: visitation without undertaking a journey is not prohibited, whereas visitation involving such a journey is prohibited.

In short, what Shaykh Taqī al-Dīn stated, in the form described and examined, merits neither punishment nor reproach. The sovereign’s merciful benevolence is more fittingly expressed by granting him relief and regarding him with compassion and mercy. May the sovereign’s counsels rise ever higher.

Written by Ibn al-Kutubī al-Shāfi'ī, praising Allah for His blessings. End of quotation.

جَوَابٌ آخَرُ:
اللَّهُ الْمُوَفِّقُ.
مَا أَجَابَ بِهِ الشَّيْخُ الْأَجَلُّ الْأَوْحَدُ بَقِيَّةُ السَّلَفِ وَقُدْوَةُ الْخَلَفِ رَئِيسُ الْمُحَقِّقِينَ وَخُلَاصَةُ الْمُدَقِّقِينَ؛

 مِنْ الْخِلَافِ فِي هَذِهِ الْمَسْأَلَةِ: صَحِيحٌ مَنْقُولٌ فِي غَيْرِ مَا كِتَابٍ مِنْ كُتُبِ أَهْلِ الْعِلْمِ لَا اعْتِرَاضَ عَلَيْهِ فِي ذَلِكَ إذْ لَيْسَ فِي ذَلِكَ ثَلْبٌ لِرَسُولِ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ وَلَا غَضٌّ مِنْ قَدْرِهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ. وَقَدْ نَصَّ الشَّيْخُ أَبُو مُحَمَّدٍ الجُوَيْنِي فِي كُتُبِهِ عَلَى تَحْرِيمِ السَّفَرِ لِزِيَارَةِ الْقُبُورِ. وَهَذَا اخْتِيَارُ الْقَاضِي الْإِمَامِ عِيَاضِ بْنِ مُوسَى بْنِ عِيَاضٍ فِي إكْمَالِهِ. وَهُوَ مِنْ أَفْضَلِ الْمُتَأَخِّرِينَ مِنْ أَصْحَابِنَا.
 وَمِنْ الْمُدَوِّنَةِ:
 وَمَنْ قَالَ: عَلَيَّ الْمَشْيُ إلَى الْمَدِينَةِ أَوْ بَيْتِ الْمَقْدِسِ فَلَا يَأْتِيهِمَا أَصْلًا إلَّا أَنْ يُرِيدَ الصَّلَاةَ فِي مَسْجِدَيْهِمَا فَلْيَأْتِهِمَا. فَلَمْ يَجْعَلْ نَذْرَ زِيَارَةِ قَبْرِهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ طَاعَةً يَجِبُ الْوَفَاءُ بِهَا؛
 إذْ مِنْ أَصْلِنَا:
 أَنَّ مَنْ نَذَرَ طَاعَةً لَزِمَهُ الْوَفَاءُ بِهَا
translated_text:
Another Response

Allah is the One who grants success.

What the most eminent and peerless shaykh—a surviving exemplar of the early generations and a model for later generations, foremost among critical scholars and finest of meticulous investigators, Taqī al-Milla wa-l-Haqq wa-l-Dīn—stated in his response regarding the disagreement on this issue is correct and recorded in numerous scholarly works. There is no ground for objecting to him on this account, for it neither disparages the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, nor diminishes his standing, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

Shaykh Abū Muhammad al-Juwaynī explicitly stated in his books that travelling to visit graves is forbidden. This is also the position adopted by the judge and imam, ‘Iyād ibn Mūsā ibn ‘Iyād, in his Ikmāl. He is among the most distinguished later scholars of our school.

Al-Mudawwana states:

“Whoever says, ‘I undertake to walk to Medina or Jerusalem,’ is not to go to either place at all unless he intends to pray in their two mosques; in that case, he is to go.”

Thus, he did not regard a vow to visit the Prophet’s grave, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, as an act of obedience that must be fulfilled, since one of our fundamental principles is that whoever vows to perform an act of obedience is bound to fulfil it

translated_text:
, whether an act of the same kind is obligatory under the Sacred Law—as stipulated in Abū Hanīfa’s school—or not.

The judge Abū Ishāq Ismā‘īl ibn Ishāq said after discussing this issue:

“Were it not for prayer in those two mosques, he would not be obliged to go to them. Even if he had vowed a visit as an act of obedience, he would not be obliged to do so.”

Al-Qayrawānī mentioned this in his Taqrīb, as did Shaykh Ibn Sīrīn in his Tanbīh.

In al-Mabsūt, Mālik said concerning someone who vows to walk to one of the mosques to pray there:

“I disapprove of that for him, because the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: ‘Mounts are not to be ridden on a journey except to three mosques: the Sacred Mosque, the Mosque of Jerusalem, and this mosque of mine.’”

Muhammad ibn al-Mawwāz related in al-Mawwāziyya:

“Unless it is nearby, in which case he must fulfil his vow, since this does not constitute setting out on a journey.”

Shaykh Abū ‘Umar ibn ‘Abd al-Barr said in his book al-Tamhīd:

“It is forbidden for Muslims to take the graves of the prophets and the righteous as places of worship.”

Since this has been established, it is not permissible to accuse of disbelief someone who answers this question by stating that such travel is forbidden. Whoever declares him an unbeliever on this account without valid grounds is himself an unbeliever if he considers doing so lawful; otherwise, he is sinfully disobedient.

Imam Abū ‘Abd Allāh Muhammad ibn ‘Alī al-Māzarī said in his book al-Mu‘lim:

“Whoever declares anyone who prays facing the qiblah an unbeliever has himself disbelieved if he considers doing so lawful; otherwise, he is sinfully disobedient.”

When his case is brought before the judge, the judge must discipline him and impose a discretionary punishment sufficient to deter others like him. If the judge leaves him unpunished despite having the power to act, he is sinful. And Allah Most High knows best.

translated_text:
all—is clear beyond dispute and manifest beyond concealment. Indeed, it is clearer than the sun and moon, and more evident than daybreak to anyone with eyes to see.

The principal basis in this matter is the hadith whose authenticity is agreed upon. The disagreement among the scholars arises from the two possible meanings of its wording.

The Prophet’s words—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—

“Journeys are not undertaken”

admit two interpretations: a statement of negation or a prohibition.

If understood as a negation, they negate the merit and recommended status of undertaking journeys and riding mounts to places other than the three mosques. For, supposing that these acts do occur, their occurrence cannot be denied. The negation must therefore concern their merit and recommended status, not the acts themselves. This applies generally to every destination to which travelling and riding mounts are believed to be acts of devotion and merit: mosques, visits to the graves of the righteous, and similar purposes. Indeed, its scope is broader still.

This is established by the necessity of affirming, for what follows “except,” the predicate implicitly negated at the beginning of the sentence. Otherwise, the ruling would not differ between what precedes “except” and what follows it, whereas it does differ. In that case, denying merit and recommended status does not entail denying permissibility. This is the reasoning relied upon by those who consider such travel permissible: they understand this wording as a negation and, on that basis, allow the shortening of prayers.

If, however, the wording is understood as a prohibition, it means that he forbade riding mounts and undertaking journeys to places other than the three mosques. For the generally accepted principle among scholars of legal theory is that a prohibition entails that an act is either forbidden or reprehensible, according to what the evidence requires.

translated_text:
This, then, is the reasoning relied upon by those who hold that shortening the prayers during such a journey is impermissible, because the journey itself is prohibited.

Among those who declared it forbidden were Shaykh and Imam Abū Muhammad al-Juwaynī of the Shāfi‘ī school and Shaykh Abū al-Wafā’ Ibn ‘Aqīl of the Hanbalī school. This is also the position that al-Qādī ‘Iyād of the Mālikī school indicated he preferred. The hadiths recommending visits to graves are understood to concern visits that do not involve undertaking a journey or riding mounts, thereby reconciling the two sets of reports.

It might also be argued that no other hadith can stand in opposition to the hadith,

“Journeys are not undertaken,”

because it does not equal it in rank, the latter belonging to the highest category of authentic hadith. And Allah knows best.

I have been informed that the respondent has suffered harm and been subjected to pressure. This is something that bewilders the discerning, astonishes the intelligent, and fills them with troubling doubts. His answer to this question sets out the disagreement among the scholars; it does not entail any disparagement of the righteous or the prophets.

Acting according to the purport of his words—may Allah’s blessings and peace be upon him—in a hadith whose authentic attribution to him is agreed upon represents the utmost adherence to his commands and prohibitions. Can the critic’s conduct be explained by anything other than his mounting the emaciated steed of desire, which carries its rider to ruin? For anyone who draws upon his valuable insights and gathers his rare gems of learning surely deserves esteem and honour from those of sound understanding and sound judgment.

And, to all appearances, is not the one who joins forces against him aptly described by the familiar proverb:

“Barley is eaten, yet reviled.”

And by the poet’s words:

“His sons repaid Abū al-Ghaylān for his years
and kindly deeds as Sinimmār was repaid.”

And another poet’s words:

“Speech I relish, which those who describe it
say is weighed with care;
splendid speech, at times allusive—
the finest speech is that which hints.”

Allah Most High said:

“And do not let the hatred of a people prevent you from being just. Be just; that is nearer to righteousness. And fear Allah; indeed, Allah is Acquainted with what you do.”

And He, Most High, said:

“Cooperate in righteousness and piety, but do not cooperate in sin and aggression. And fear Allah; indeed, Allah is severe in punishment.”

And He, Most High, said:

“O you who believe, fear Allah and speak words of truth and justice.”

“He will set right your deeds for you and forgive you your sins. Whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger has indeed achieved a great triumph.”

And He, Most High, said:

“Allah will surely support those who support Him. Indeed, Allah is Powerful and Almighty.”

Were it not for fear of causing weariness, I would not have refrained from writing at greater length. We ask Allah, the Generous, to lead us and you along the path of guidance and to keep us and you away from the path of error. He has power over all things and is most worthy of answering our prayers. Allah is sufficient for us; He is the best disposer of affairs and the best helper. All praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds. May Allah’s blessings and peace be upon the master of the messengers, Muhammad the Prophet, his pure family, and his noble, chosen Companions.

This is the response of the shaykh, imam and eminent scholar Jamāl al-Dīn Yūsuf ibn ʿAbd al-Mahmūd ibn ʿAbd al-Salām ibn al-Battī al-Hanbalī, may Allah Most High have mercy on him.

translated_text:
Another Response
By a Mālikī Scholar of Syria

Praise be to Allah, who is sufficient for me.

Journeying to places other than the three mosques is not prescribed. As for someone who journeys to the Prophet’s Mosque to pray there and offer greetings of peace to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and to his two Companions, may Allah be pleased with them both, such a journey, as described, is prescribed by agreement of the scholars.

As for undertaking a journey to visit him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, without intending to pray: if a person mentions the scholarly disagreement concerning this journey—that some scholars have said it is prohibited, while others have said it is permissible; that, according to both views, it is neither an act of obedience nor a means of drawing near to Allah; and that, consequently, under these two views, treating it as an act of obedience and a means of drawing near to Allah is forbidden by consensus—and presents the evidence for each view or gives preference to one of them, he does not incur the same liability as someone who disparages the Prophet, since this involves neither disparagement nor disrespect toward the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

translated_text:
Mālik, may Allah have mercy on him, was asked by a man who had vowed to visit the Prophet’s grave, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. He replied:

“If he intended the Prophet’s Mosque, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, let him go there and pray in it. But if he intended the grave, he should not do so, because of the hadith: ‘Journeys are not to be undertaken except to three mosques.’”

Allah knows best.

Written by Abū ʿAmr ibn Abī al-Walīd al-Mālikī.
ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī al-Walīd al-Mālikī likewise affirms this.

The author, may Allah have mercy on him, said: “I transcribed all these responses from the handwriting of the muftis who issued them.”

He continued:

I also examined a letter that arrived with the responses from the scholars of Baghdad. Its text is as follows:

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Bestower of Mercy.

Praise be to Allah, who upholds the Islamic faith and strengthens the law brought by Muhammad through the enduring, blessed sultanic rule of al-Malik al-Nāsir. May Allah Most High clothe it in lasting might and adorn it with uninterrupted victory throughout the passing nights and days. Blessings and peace be upon the Prophet sent to all mankind; may Allah bless him and his righteous, noble family.
