translated_text:
O Allah, Your door has always been open to those who ask, and Your bounty has always been freely bestowed upon those who come seeking it. Whoever You have accustomed to asking You alone asks no one besides You; whoever You have granted gifts from Your bounty turns to no one else and seeks refuge only in Your protection. You are the Mighty Lord, the Generous, the Most Generous. Your servants are forbidden to seek any door other than Yours. You are He besides whom there is no god, and none is worthy of worship but You. Whoever is under Your protection is secure; exalted is Your praise, holy are Your names, and great is Your bounty. There is no god besides You.

Your established way with Your creation has always been to test Your friends and those You love, as a grace and kindness from You towards them, so that they may remember You more in every circumstance and thank You for Your blessings through every change of fortune. Yet most people do not know.

“These are the parables We set forth for people, but none will understand them except those of knowledge.”

O Allah, You are the Knower who is not known, and You are the Generous One who is never miserly. You know, O Knower of what is hidden and what is manifest, that our hearts have always sincerely offered earnest supplication, and our tongues have voiced it in private and in public: that You answer us by granting this blessed and auspicious sultanic rule of al-Nāsir still greater eminence, dignity and strength; and that You fulfil our hopes for it by making the word of faith supreme, strengthening the foundations that uphold religion, and thwarting the schemes of the heretics. For this is a rule untainted by partiality and injustice, and free from the excesses of pen and sword.

And what lies within the hearts of Muslims and fills the innermost souls of believers is:

original_text:
أَنَّ السُّلْطَانَ الْمَلِكَ النَّاصِرَ لِلدِّينِ مِمَّنْ قَالَ فِيهِ رَبُّ الْعَالَمِينَ وَإِلَهُ السَّمَوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِينَ:
 الَّذِي بِتَمْكِينِهِ فِي أَرْضِهِ حَصَلَ التَّمْكِينُ لِمُلُوكِ الْأَرْضِ وَعُظَمَاءِ السَّلَاطِينِ فِي كِتَابِهِ الْعَزِيزِ الَّذِي يُتْلَى فَمَنْ شَاءَ فَلْيَتَدَبَّرْ: 
{الَّذِينَ إنْ مَكَّنَّاهُمْ فِي الْأَرْضِ أَقَامُوا الصَّلَاةَ وَآتَوُا الزَّكَاةَ وَأَمَرُوا بِالْمَعْرُوفِ وَنَهَوْا عَنِ الْمُنْكَرِ}
 وَهُوَ مِمَّنْ مَكَّنَهُ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى فِي الْأَرْضِ تَمْكِينًا يَقِينًا لَا ظَنًّا وَهُوَ مِمَّنْ يُعْنَى بِقَوْلِهِ تَعَالَى 
{وَعَدَ اللَّهُ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا مِنْكُمْ وَعَمِلُوا الصَّالِحَاتِ لَيَسْتَخْلِفَنَّهُمْ فِي الْأَرْضِ كَمَا اسْتَخْلَفَ الَّذِينَ مِنْ قَبْلِهِمْ وَلَيُمَكِّنَنَّ لَهُمْ دِينَهُمُ الَّذِي ارْتَضَى لَهُمْ وَلَيُبَدِّلَنَّهُم مِنْ بَعْدِ خَوْفِهِمْ أَمْنًا يَعْبُدُونَنِي لَا يُشْرِكُونَ بِي شَيْئًا}
 .
 وَاَلَّذِي عَهِدَهُ الْمُسْلِمُونَ وَتَعَوَّدَهُ الْمُؤْمِنُونَ مِنْ الْمَرَاحِمِ الْكَرِيمَةِ وَالْعَوَاطِفِ الرَّحِيمَةِ:
 إكْرَامُ أَهْلِ الدِّينِ وَإِعْظَامُ عُلَمَاءِ الْمُسْلِمِينَ. وَاَلَّذِي حَمَلَ عَلَى رَفْعِ هَذِهِ الْأَدْعِيَةِ الصَّرِيحَةِ إلَى الْحَضْرَةِ الشَّرِيفَةِ - وَإِنْ كَانَتْ لَمْ تَزَلْ مَرْفُوعَةً إلَى اللَّهِ سُبْحَانَهُ بِالنِّيَّةِ الصَّحِيحَةِ - قَوْلُهُ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ 
{الدِّينُ النَّصِيحَةُ قِيلَ: لِمَنْ يَا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ؟
 قَالَ:
 لِلَّهِ وَلِرَسُولِهِ وَلِأَئِمَّةِ الْمُسْلِمِينَ وَعَامَّتِهِمْ}
 وَقَوْلُهُ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ 
{إنَّمَا الْأَعْمَالُ بِالنِّيَّاتِ}
 فَهَذَانِ الْحَدِيثَانِ مَشْهُورَانِ بِالصِّحَّةِ وَمُسْتَفِيضَانِ فِي الْأُمَّةِ.
translated_text:
that Sultan al-Malik al-Nāsir li-l-Dīn is among those of whom the Lord of all worlds, the God of the heavens and the earth—through whose granting of authority on His earth its kings and mighty sultans have gained their power—speaks in His mighty Book, which is recited. Let whoever wishes reflect:

“Those who, if We establish them in the land, establish prayer, give zakah, enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong.”

He is indeed among those whom Allah Most High has established in authority on earth: this is certain, not conjectural. He is among those meant by His words, Most High:

“Allah has promised those of you who believe and do righteous deeds that He will surely grant them succession in the land, as He granted it to those before them; that He will surely establish for them their religion, which He has approved for them; and that He will surely replace their fear with security. They worship Me, associating nothing with Me.”

Among the gracious acts of mercy and compassionate care that Muslims have known and believers have grown accustomed to are the honouring of religious people and the esteem shown to Muslim scholars. What prompted the presentation of these explicit supplications to your august presence—although they have always been raised to Allah, Glorified is He, with sincere intention—is the saying of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Religion is sincerity.” He was asked, “Towards whom, O Messenger of Allah?” He replied, “Towards Allah, His Messenger, the leaders of the Muslims and their common people.”

And his saying, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Actions are judged only by intentions.”

These two hadiths are well known to be authentic and are widely transmitted throughout the Muslim community.

original_text:
ثُمَّ إنَّ هَذَا الشَّيْخَ الْمُعَظَّمَ الْجَلِيلَ وَالْإِمَامَ الْمُكَرَّمَ النَّبِيلَ:
 أَوْحَدُ الدَّهْرِ وَفَرِيدُ الْعَصْرِ؛
 طِرَازُ الْمَمْلَكَةِ الْمَلَكِيَّةِ وَعَلَمُ الدَّوْلَةِ السُّلْطَانِيَّةِ لَوْ أَقْسَمَ مُقْسِمٌ بِاَللَّهِ الْعَظِيمِ الْقَدِيرِ:
 أَنَّ هَذَا الْإِمَامَ الْكَبِيرَ لَيْسَ لَهُ فِي عَصْرِهِ مُمَاثِلَ وَلَا نَظِيرٌ لَكَانَتْ يَمِينُهُ بَرَّةً غَنِيَّةً عَنْ التَّكْفِيرِ وَقَدْ خَلَتْ مِنْ وُجُودِ مِثْلِهِ السَّبْعُ الْأَقَالِيمُ إلَّا هَذَا الْإِقْلِيمَ يُوَافِقُ عَلَى ذَلِكَ كُلُّ مُنْصِفٍ جُبِلَ عَلَى الطَّبْعِ السَّلِيمِ.
 وَلَسْت بِالثَّنَاءِ عَلَيْهِ أُطْرِيهِ بَلْ لَوْ أَطْنَبَ مُطْنِبٌ فِي مَدْحِهِ وَالثَّنَاءِ عَلَيْهِ لَمَا أَتَى عَلَى بَعْضِ الْفَضَائِلِ الَّتِي هِيَ فِيهِ:
 أَحْمَد ابْن تَيْمِيَّة دُرَّةٌ يَتِيمَةٌ يُتَنَافَسُ فِيهَا تُشْتَرَى وَلَا تُبَاعُ لَيْسَ فِي خَزَائِنِ الْمُلُوكِ دُرَّةٌ تُمَاثِلُهَا وَتُؤَاخِيهَا انْقَطَعَتْ عَنْ وُجُودِ مِثْلِهِ الْأَطْمَاعُ.
 وَلَقَدْ أَصَمَّ الْأَسْمَاعَ وَأَوْهَى قُوَى الْمَتْبُوعِينَ وَالْأَتْبَاعِ:
 سَمَّاعُ رَفْعِ أَبِي الْعَبَّاسِ - أَحْمَد ابْنِ تَيْمِيَّة - إلَى الْقِلَاعِ. وَلَيْسَ يَقَعُ مِنْ مِثْلِهِ أَمْرٌ يُنْقَمُ مِنْهُ عَلَيْهِ إلَّا أَنَّهُ يَكُونُ أَمْرًا قَدْ لُبِّسَ عَلَيْهِ وَنُسِبَ إلَى مَا يُنْسَبُ مِثْلُهُ إلَيْهِ. وَالتَّطْوِيلُ عَلَى الْحَضْرَةِ الْعَالِيَةِ لَا يَلِيقُ إنْ يَكُنْ فِي الدُّنْيَا قُطْبٌ فَهُوَ الْقُطْبُ عَلَى التَّحْقِيقِ قَدْ نَصَّبَ اللَّهُ السُّلْطَانَ أَعْلَى اللَّهُ شَأْنَهُ فِي هَذَا الزَّمَانِ مَنْصِبَ يُوسُفَ الصِّدِّيقِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَى نَبِيِّنَا وَعَلَيْهِ لَمَّا صَرَفَ اللَّهُ وُجُوهَ أَهْلِ الْبِلَادِ إلَيْهِ حِينَ أَمْحَلَتْ الْبِلَادُ وَاحْتَاجَ أَهْلُهَا إلَى الْقُوتِ الْمُدَّخَرِ لَدَيْهِ. وَالْحَاجَةُ بِالنَّاسِ الْآنَ إلَى قُوتِ الْأَرْوَاحِ الْمُشَارِ فِي ذَلِكَ الزَّمَانِ إلَيْهَا لَا خَفَاءَ
translated_text:
Now this revered and illustrious shaykh, this honoured and noble imam, is unrivalled in his age and unique in his time, the ornament of the royal realm and the standard of the sultan’s state. Were anyone to swear by Allah, the Almighty, the All-Powerful, that this great imam has neither equal nor peer in his age, his oath would be true and require no expiation. The seven regions are devoid of his like, save this region. Every fair-minded person endowed with a sound disposition agrees with this.

I am not exaggerating in praising him. Indeed, however extensively someone might praise and commend him, he would not encompass even some of his virtues. Ahmad ibn Taymiyyah is a peerless pearl for which people vie, one to be bought but never sold. No pearl in the treasuries of kings matches or resembles it. All hope of finding his equal has vanished.

Hearing that Abū al-ʿAbbās—Ahmad ibn Taymiyyah—had been taken up to the citadels has deafened ears and sapped the strength of leaders and followers alike. Nothing deserving reproach could come from a man like him, unless it involved a matter that had been obscured for him and he had been accused of the sort of thing of which men like him are accused.

It would be unfitting to burden your august presence with a lengthy account. If there is a qutb (spiritual pole) in this world, he is unquestionably that pole. Allah has placed the Sultan—may Allah exalt his standing—in this age in the position occupied by Joseph the truthful—may Allah bless our Prophet and him—when Allah turned the people of the lands towards him after drought had afflicted their lands and they needed the food stored with him. As for people’s present need for the nourishment of souls referred to at that time, there is no doubt

original_text:
الزَّمَانِ إلَيْهَا لَا خَفَاءَ أَنَّهَا لِلْعُلُومِ الشَّرِيفَةِ وَالْمَعَانِي اللَّطِيفَةِ. وَقَدْ كَانَتْ فِي بِلَادِ الْمَمْلَكَةِ السُّلْطَانِيَّةِ - حَرَسَهَا اللَّهُ تَعَالَى - تُكَالُ إلَيْنَا جُزَافًا بِغَيْرِ أَثْمَانٍ مِنْحَةً عَظِيمَةً مِنْ اللَّهِ لِلسُّلْطَانِ وَنِعْمَةً جَسِيمَةً إذْ خَصَّ بِلَادَ مَمْلَكَتِهِ وَإِقْلِيمَ دَوْلَتِهِ بِمَا لَا يُوجَدُ فِي غَيْرِهَا مِنْ الْأَقَالِيمِ وَالْبُلْدَانِ وَكَانَ قَدْ وَفَدَ الْوَافِدُونَ مِنْ سَائِر الْأَمْصَارِ إلَى تِلْكَ الدِّيَارِ؛
 فَوَجَدُوا صَاحِبَ صُوَاعِ الْمَلِكِ قَدْ رُفِعَ إلَى الْقِلَاعِ وَمِثْلُ هَذِهِ الْمِيزَةِ لَا تُوجَدُ فِي غَيْرِ تِلْكَ الْبِلَادِ لِتُشْتَرَى أَوْ تُبَاعَ فَصَادَفَ ذَلِكَ جَدْبُ الْأَرْضِ وَنَوَاحِيهَا جَدْبًا أَعْطَبَ أَهَالِيهَا حَتَّى صَارُوا مِنْ شِدَّةِ حَاجَتِهِمْ إلَى الْأَقْوَاتِ كَالْأَمْوَاتِ وَاَلَّذِي عَرَضَ لِلْمَلِكِ بِالتَّضْيِيقِ عَلَى صَاحِبِ صُوَاعِهِ مَعَ شِدَّةِ الْحَاجَةِ إلَى غِذَاءِ الْأَرْوَاحِ لَعَلَّهُ لَمْ يَتَحَقَّقْ عِنْدَهُ أَنَّ هَذَا الْإِمَامَ مِنْ أَكَابِرِ الْأَوْلِيَاءِ وَأَعْيَانِ أَهْلِ الصَّلَاحِ وَهَذِهِ نَزْغَةٌ مِنْ نَزَغَاتِ الشَّيْطَانِ قَالَ اللَّهُ سُبْحَانَهُ:
 
{وَقُلْ لِعِبَادِي يَقُولُوا الَّتِي هِيَ أَحْسَنُ إنَّ الشَّيْطَانَ يَنْزَغُ بَيْنَهُمْ إنَّ الشَّيْطَانَ كَانَ لِلْإِنْسَانِ عَدُوًّا مُبِينًا}
 . وَأَمَّا إزْرَاءُ بَعْضِ الْعُلَمَاءِ عَلَيْهِ فِي فَتْوَاهُ وَجَوَابِهِ عَنْ مَسْأَلَةِ شَدِّ الرِّحَالِ إلَى الْقُبُورِ.
 فَقَدْ حَمَلَ جَوَابَ عُلَمَاءِ هَذِهِ الْبِلَادِ إلَى نُظَرَائِهِمْ مِنْ الْعُلَمَاءِ وَقُرَنَائِهِمْ مِنْ الْفُضَلَاءِ وَكُلُّهُمْ أَفْتَى:
 أَنَّ الصَّوَابَ فِي الَّذِي بِهِ أَجَابَ.
translated_text:
that this nourishment consists of noble learning and subtle meanings. Within the Sultan’s dominions—may Allah Most High protect them—it had been dispensed to us in abundance, without charge: a magnificent gift from Allah to the Sultan and an immense blessing, for He had distinguished his kingdom and the territory under his rule with something found in no other region or land. Visitors had come from every province to those lands,

only to find that the keeper of the king’s measuring cup had been taken up to the citadels. Such a bounty could not be found elsewhere to be bought or sold. This coincided with a drought throughout the land and its surrounding regions, a drought that devastated its inhabitants until their desperate need for sustenance left them as though dead. Whoever suggested to the king that he impose restrictions on the keeper of his measuring cup, despite the pressing need for nourishment of the soul, may not have realized that this imam is among the greatest friends of Allah and the foremost righteous men. This is one of Satan’s incitements. Allah, Glorified is He, says:

“And tell My servants to say that which is best. Indeed, Satan sows discord among them. Indeed, Satan is ever a clear enemy to mankind.”

As for certain scholars’ disparagement of his fatwa and his answer concerning undertaking journeys to graves, the response of the scholars of these lands was conveyed to their fellow scholars and learned peers. All of them ruled that the answer he had given was correct.

original_text:
وَالظَّاهِرُ بَيْنَ الْأَنَامِ أَنَّ إكْرَامَ هَذَا الْإِمَامِ وَمُعَامَلَتَهُ بِالتَّبْجِيلِ وَالِاحْتِرَامِ فِيهِ قِوَامُ الْمُلْكِ وَنِظَامُ الدَّوْلَةِ وَإِعْزَازُ الْمِلَّةِ؛ وَاسْتِجْلَابُ الدُّعَاءِ وَكَبْتُ الْأَعْدَاءِ وَإِذْلَالُ أَهْلِ الْبِدَعِ وَالْأَهْوَاءِ؛
 وَإِحْيَاءُ الْأُمَّةِ وَكَشْفُ الْغُمَّةِ وَوُفُورُ الْأَجْرِ وَعُلُوُّ الذِّكْرِ وَرَفْعُ الْبَأْسِ وَنَفْعُ النَّاسِ وَلِسَانُ حَالِ الْمُسْلِمِينَ تَالٍ قَوْلَ الْكَبِيرِ المتعال:
 
{فَلَمَّا دَخَلُوا عَلَيْهِ قَالُوا يَا أَيُّهَا الْعَزِيزُ مَسَّنَا وَأَهْلَنَا الضُّرُّ وَجِئْنَا بِبِضَاعَةٍ مُزْجَاةٍ فَأَوْفِ لَنَا الْكَيْلَ وَتَصَدَّقْ عَلَيْنَا إنَّ اللَّهَ يَجْزِي الْمُتَصَدِّقِينَ}
 .
 وَالْبِضَاعَةُ الْمُزْجَاةُ:
 هِيَ هَذِهِ الْأَوْرَاقُ الْمَرْقُومَةُ بِالْأَقْلَامِ وَالْمِيزَةُ الْمَطْلُوبَةُ: هِيَ الْإِفْرَاجُ عَنْ شَيْخِ الْإِسْلَامِ وَاَلَّذِي حَمَلَ عَلَى هَذَا الْإِقْدَامِ قَوْلُهُ عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ 
{الدِّينُ النَّصِيحَةُ}
 وَالسَّلَامُ. وَصَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَى سَيِّدِنَا مُحَمَّدٍ وَآلِهِ الطَّيِّبِينَ الْكِرَامِ وَسَلَّمَ تَسْلِيمًا. هَذَا آخِرُ هَذَا الْكِتَابِ.
قَالَ الْمُؤَلِّفُ:
 وَوَقَفْت عَلَى 
" كِتَابٍ آخَرَ "
 مِنْ بَغْدَادَ أَيْضًا.

It has been reported that the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

‘Whoever performs Hajj but does not visit me has slighted me.’

And:

‘Whoever visits me after my death, it is as though he visited me during my lifetime.’

It has also been reported that he said:

‘No journey should be undertaken except to three mosques: the Sacred Mosque, al-Aqsā Mosque, and this mosque of mine.’”

The wording of the answer:

Praise be to Allah. Regarding someone who travels solely to visit the graves of the prophets and the righteous, there are two well-known views on whether he may shorten his prayers.

The first is that shortening the prayers on such a journey is not permissible, because it is a prohibited journey. This is the view of the earlier scholars who do not permit shortening prayers on a sinful journey and who regard this journey as sinful, such as Abū ‘Abd Allāh ibn Battah, Abū al-Wafā’ ibn ‘Aqīl, and many groups of earlier scholars. The position of Mālik, al-Shāfi‘ī, and Ahmad is that prayers may not be shortened on a journey prohibited by Islamic law.

The second view is that prayers may be shortened on such a journey. This is held by those who permit shortening prayers on a prohibited journey, such as Abū Hanīfah. It is also held by some later followers of al-Shāfi‘ī and Ahmad who permit travelling to visit the graves of the prophets and the righteous, such as Abū Hāmid al-Ghazālī, Abū Muhammad al-Maqdisī, and Abū al-Hasan ibn ‘Abdūs

This, too, is baseless by scholarly consensus. Ahmad did not narrate it, nor has anyone cited it as evidence. Some of them merely cite al-Dāraqutnī’s hadith as evidence—the respondent subsequently added a marginal note to it.

However, although none of the scholars narrated this report in “books of jurisprudence and hadith,” whether as proof or as supporting evidence, and although some later scholars mentioned it, Abū Ahmad ibn ‘Adī did narrate it in his “Book of Weak Narrators” to demonstrate the weakness of its transmission. He cited it through al-Nu‘mān ibn Shibl al-Bāhilī al-Misrī, from Mālik, from Nāfi‘, from Ibn ‘Umar, who reported that the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“Whoever performs Hajj but does not visit me has slighted me.”

Ibn ‘Adī said: “No one other than this man narrated it from Mālik.” That is, it is known that this is not among Mālik’s hadiths, so it is clear that the flaw originated with this narrator.

—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—or to al-Masjid al-Aqsā for prayer or a devotional retreat, he is obliged to fulfil this vow according to Mālik, al-Shāfi‘ī in one of his two opinions, and Ahmad. According to Abū Hanīfah, however, he is not obliged to do so, because, in his view, a vow creates an obligation only when the act belongs to a category already made obligatory by Islamic law.

The majority, however, hold that a vow to perform any act of obedience must be fulfilled, as established in Sahīh al-Bukhārī, where ‘Ā’ishah reported that the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“Whoever vows to obey Allah, let him obey Him; and whoever vows to disobey Allah, let him not disobey Him.”

Travelling to these two mosques is an act of obedience; hence a vow to do so must be fulfilled. As for travelling to any place other than the three mosques, no scholar has held that such a journey becomes obligatory through a vow. Indeed, the scholars explicitly stated that one should not travel to the Mosque of Qubā’, because it is not one of the three, even though visiting the Mosque of Qubā’ is recommended for someone already in Medina. That does not involve undertaking a journey, as stated in the authentic hadith:

“Whoever purifies himself at home, then comes to the Mosque of Qubā’ intending only to pray there, it is equivalent to an ‘umrah.”

—In the margin: This hadith was narrated by the compilers of the Sunan collections, such as al-Nasā’ī, Ibn Mājah and al-Tirmidhī, who graded it good.

He said:

They also said: Moreover, travelling to visit the graves of the prophets and the righteous is an innovation that none of the Companions or their successors practised. The Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—did not command it, nor did any of the imams of the Muslims deem it recommended. Whoever regards this as an act of worship and performs it is acting contrary to the Sunnah and the consensus of the imams. This is among the innovations contrary to the Sunnah that Abū ‘Abd Allāh ibn Battah mentioned in al-Ibānah al-Sughrā.

translated_text:
This makes clear the weakness of Abū Muhammad al-Maqdisī’s argument, for the Prophet’s visits—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—to the Mosque of Qubā’ did not involve undertaking a journey, and travelling there does not become obligatory through a vow. His claim that the Prophet’s words—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—“No journeys are to be undertaken” should be understood as merely denying that such travel is recommended admits of two responses.

The first is that this amounts to an acknowledgement on his part that such travel is neither a righteous deed, nor a means of drawing near to Allah, nor an act of obedience, nor a good deed. Thus, anyone who believes that travelling to visit the graves of the prophets and the righteous is a means of drawing near to Allah, an act of worship and an act of obedience has contradicted the consensus. If he travels because he believes it to be an act of obedience, that is forbidden by the consensus of the Muslims. The prohibition thus arises on these grounds. It is well known that no one travels to these graves except for this purpose. If, however, we suppose that a man travels to them for a permissible purpose, that is permissible and does not fall within the matter under discussion.

The second response is that this hadith conveys a prohibition, and a prohibition entails unlawfulness. As for the hadiths mentioned by the questioner concerning visiting the Prophet’s grave—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—they are all weak by agreement of the hadith scholars; indeed, they are fabricated.

None of the compilers of the authoritative Sunan collections included any of them, nor did any of the imams cite any of them as evidence. Indeed, Mālik, the imam of the people of the Prophet’s city, who are the most knowledgeable concerning the ruling on this matter, disapproved of a man saying:

“I visited the grave of the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace.”

And had this wording been familiar to them, prescribed in religion, or transmitted from the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—the scholar of Medina would not have disapproved of it.

When Imām Ahmad, the most knowledgeable person of his time concerning the Sunnah, was asked about this, the only hadith he had on which he could rely was the report of Abū Hurayrah that the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“No man greets me with peace without Allah restoring my soul to me so that I may return his greeting.”

This was also the report on which Abū Dāwūd relied in his Sunan. Likewise, Mālik related in al-Muwatta’ that whenever ‘Abd Allāh ibn ‘Umar entered the mosque, he would say: “Peace be upon you, O Messenger of Allah. Peace be upon you, O Abū Bakr. Peace be upon you, my father.” Then he would leave.

In the Sunan of Abū Dāwūd, it is reported that the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“Do not make my grave a place of recurring gatherings. Send blessings upon me wherever you are, for your blessings reach me.”

In the Sunan of Sa‘īd ibn Mansūr, it is related that ‘Abd Allāh ibn al-Hasan ibn al-Husayn saw a man repeatedly visiting the grave of the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace. He said: “The Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

‘Do not make my grave a place of recurring gatherings. Send blessings upon me wherever you are, for your blessings reach me.’

In this regard, you and those in al-Andalus are equal.”

In the two Sahīh collections, it is reported that during his final illness the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“May Allah curse the Jews and Christians: they took the graves of their prophets as places of worship.”

In the days of the Companions and Successors, while the “Prophet’s chamber” remained separate from the mosque—until the time of al-Walīd ibn ‘Abd al-Malik—no one would enter it to pray there, rub the grave, or supplicate there. Rather, they did all of this only in the mosque. When the early generations among the Companions and Successors greeted the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—and wished to supplicate, they would face the qiblah, not the grave.

As for a Muslim standing at his grave, Abū Hanīfah said: “He should face the qiblah here too, not the grave.” Most of the imams, however, said: “Rather, he should face the grave only when greeting him with peace.” None of the imams said that one should face the grave when supplicating—that is, when supplicating for oneself—except in a fabricated account attributed to Mālik, whose school holds the contrary. The imams agreed that one should neither touch the Prophet’s grave—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—nor kiss it.

All of this is to safeguard monotheism, for turning graves into places of worship is among the origins of associating partners with Allah. Thus, concerning the words of Allah Most High:

Some of his followers held that, in these two matters, the same ruling applies to the other prophets as to him: some said this concerning swearing by them, and others concerning visiting their graves. Likewise, Abū Muhammad al-Juwaynī and those Shāfiʿī scholars who agreed with him held that the hadith entails a prohibition on travelling to places other than the three mosques.

Other followers of al-Shāfiʿī, Mālik, and Ahmad said that the hadith means that such travel has no particular merit, is not recommended, and does not become obligatory through a vow—not that it is impermissible. This is the view of Shaykh Abū Hāmid, Abū ʿAlī, Abū al-Maʿālī, al-Ghazālī, and others. It is also the view of Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr, Abū Muhammad al-Maqdisī, and those followers of Mālik and Ahmad who agreed with them.

These, then, are the two views found in Muslim scholarly works. The respondent mentioned both and knew of no recognized Muslim scholar who had stated in these works that travelling to visit the graves of the prophets and the righteous is recommended. Had he known of a third view on the matter, he would have reported it. But he knew of none, and to this day he knows of no one who has said this. Many scholars, however, have stated without qualification that visiting the Prophet’s grave, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is recommended, and some have reported a consensus on this. The respondent did not mention any disagreement over this in his answer, for it is well known, on the basis of explicit textual evidence and consensus, that travelling to the Prophet’s mosque, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is recommended. How, then, could he not intend to travel there? Anyone who knowingly acts of his own free choice must necessarily intend what he does. People of ignorance and misguidance, however, treat travelling to visit him like their customary journeys to visit the grave of someone they venerate. This is among the practices for which the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, cursed the People of the Book and which he forbade his community to follow. Whoever fails to distinguish between what is prescribed and what is forbidden in visiting graves does not understand the religion of Islam in this matter. The purpose here is to draw attention to the contents of this work, written by the objector against the aforementioned response, and to expose its ignorance and fabrications.

Among these is his statement concerning the response:

“What has become clear to me from the explicit wording of that discussion, its implications, its intended purpose and its thrust, is that he prohibits visiting the graves of the prophets and all other graves, and travelling to them, and claims that this is a forbidden act of disobedience whose prohibition is established by consensus.”

The reply is as follows:

Anyone who has read the response knows that it contains no prohibition on visiting graves—whether those of the prophets or anyone else—when no journey is involved. Nor does it claim a consensus on the prohibition of travelling; rather, it explicitly acknowledges the disagreement over that.

How, then, can he be reported as saying that visiting graves in itself, without qualification, is a forbidden act of disobedience whose prohibition is established by consensus? This is a blatant fabrication against the response. Moreover, the objector contradicts himself: after this, he reports that the respondent acknowledged the disagreement over the permissibility of travelling.

Then, at the end of his discussion, he says that the respondent claimed there was consensus on its prohibition, and that he contradicts himself in this. Yet it is the objector himself who contradicts himself in this account. As for the respondent,

translated_text:
he reported their views on the permissibility of travelling and their agreement that it is neither an act of devotion nor an act of obedience to Allah. Whoever believes it to be an act of devotion has therefore opposed the consensus. If he undertakes it believing it to be an act of obedience, it is forbidden by consensus. Its prohibition thus arises from treating it as an act of devotion. This is the wording of the response.

It is well known that whenever Muslims disagree over whether an action is forbidden or merely permissible—not an act of devotion—whoever treats it as an act of devotion has opposed the consensus. If he performs it to draw nearer to Allah, doing so is forbidden by consensus. Examples include seeking nearness to Allah by playing backgammon or chess, exchanging one dirham for two, having anal intercourse with women, listening to singing and musical instruments, and similar actions concerning which people hold two views: prohibition and permissibility. No one has said that these are acts of devotion. Thus, whoever makes such an action an act of worship through which he seeks nearness to Allah, just as he does through prescribed acts of worship, has committed something forbidden by consensus.

This resembles seeking nearness to Allah through amusements and musical instruments. The majority of Muslims hold that these are forbidden, while some have permitted them; no one has said that they are acts of devotion. Whoever says this therefore opposes the consensus. Only a heretic would say such a thing—as in the account Abū Abd al-Rahmān al-Sulamī related from Ibn al-Rāwandī, who said: “The jurists disagree over whether singing is forbidden or lawful, but I say that it is obligatory.” It is well known that this is not one of the positions held by Muslim scholars.

Those who seek nearness to Allah by listening to poems, taghbīr, and the like are mistaken according to the great majority of the imams, even though none of these people says that singing is an act of devotion

Through it, they stir feelings of love and eagerness to obey Allah, as well as sorrow, fear, and dread of disobedience. This is what some people describe as an act of devotion. Nevertheless, the majority hold that they would be mistaken if they treated it as an act of devotion, because it is an innovation that is neither obligatory nor recommended, and because its harms outweigh the benefits they imagine it brings. The same applies to wine and gambling: although they contain benefits for people, their sin is greater than their benefit. The Sharia enjoins what is wholly or predominantly beneficial, such as faith and jihad. Faith is wholly beneficial; jihad, although it involves the taking of lives, brings benefits that outweigh its harms.

The tribulation of disbelief causes greater harm than killing, as Allah Most High says:

“Persecution is more grievous than killing.”

He has forbidden what is wholly or predominantly harmful, just as He has forbidden shameful deeds, whether open or concealed, and “sin, unjust aggression, associating with Allah that for which He has sent down no authority, and saying about Allah what you do not know.” He never permits these things under any circumstances or in any religious dispensation.

The prohibition of blood, carrion, pork, wine, and similar things concerns matters whose harm predominates. The Sharia permits this category in cases of necessity, because the harm of losing one’s life is greater than the harm of consuming them. whether it quenches thirst. Those who prohibit it say that it only increases the drinker’s thirst and therefore does not sustain life. Those who permit it say that it may, on the contrary, provide enough hydration to sustain life. Whichever of these two premises accords with reality, the view based upon it is the more correct. A fuller discussion belongs elsewhere.

The point is that when scholars disagree over whether something is forbidden or permissible, anyone who regards it as an act of devotion contradicts their consensus. Likewise, when the Companions hold two positions on a matter, anyone who introduces a third contradicts their consensus.

For this reason, no Muslim has held that listening to singing is an act of devotion without qualification. Even if someone says that listening to words—subject to the conditions of a suitable place, opportunity, and companions, and consisting of encouragement to obey Allah and warnings against disobedience—is an act of devotion, he never says that everyone who listens to musical entertainment is thereby drawing closer to Allah. Yet someone similarly claims that travelling to the graves of prophets and righteous people is an act of devotion, and that anyone who vows to travel to visit their graves should fulfil that vow. Such a view is not known to have been held by any of the leading scholars of the Muslims.

Although they may state in general terms that travelling to visit the Prophet’s grave, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is an act of devotion, or say that it is an act of devotion established by consensus, this is true when their intended meaning is understood, as al-Qādī ‘Iyād, Ibn Battāl, and others have explained. They mean the prescribed journey to his mosque and the prescribed worship performed there, which is called visiting his grave. Mālik and others, however, dislike calling it a visit to his grave. translated_text:
in this sense is undoubtedly valid. But this is not a consensus in favour of what they expressly prohibited or declared not to be an act of devotion or obedience.

Mālik and others, such as al-Qādī Ismā‘īl and al-Qādī ‘Iyād, expressly stated that travelling to places other than the three mosques is prohibited: neither someone who has vowed to undertake it nor someone doing so voluntarily should do it. They also expressly stated that travelling to Medina or Jerusalem for a purpose other than praying in their two mosques falls within the prohibited journeys. A person may not undertake such a journey even if he has vowed to do so, whether he travels to visit any prophet, any of their graves, the graves of others, or a mosque other than the three. All of this, according to them, constitutes prohibited travel. How, then, could they call it an act of devotion?

However, consensus that it is forbidden to treat it as an act of devotion does not contradict disagreement over the act considered in itself. This consensus, reported from the early generations and the leading scholars, is not undermined by dissent from some later scholars, if any such dissent exists. If, however, any of the recognized righteous people of the early generations were found to have said that travelling solely to visit graves, or solely to visit the graves of prophets and righteous people, is recommended, this would undermine that consensus, and there would then be three positions on the matter. In that case, the scholar reporting the consensus would simply have been unaware of this view, as frequently happens to many scholars. Even so, this view must be referred back to the Quran and Sunnah for judgment. It is not permissible to compel people to follow it without proof, for doing so is contrary to the consensus of the Muslims.

Among these is his assumption that visiting the grave of the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is of the same kind as the customary visitation of other people’s graves. He therefore cites visits to al-Baqīʿ, to the martyrs of Uhud, and to his mother’s grave as evidence for it. Another is that he portrays anyone who prohibits travelling to visit his grave or other graves as openly declaring hostility to the prophets and displaying defiance towards them.

Yet it is well known that this is the position of most earlier scholars, including Mālik and most of his followers, Abū Muhammad al-Juwaynī and other followers of al-Shāfiʿī, and most of Ahmad’s earlier followers. His position thus entails that his own imam, Mālik, and other leading religious scholars openly declare hostility to the prophets and defy them.

Even if he had said this about matters in which they were mistaken, he would deserve severe punishment. How much more so when he says it about matters in which they followed the Messenger and his authentic Sunnah, prohibiting what he prohibited! He has thus portrayed someone who obeys Allah and His Messenger, and whose conduct Allah, His Messenger, and His prophets approve, as openly declaring hostility to them and defying them.  وَكَذَلِكَ إذَا تَبَيَّنَ أَنَّ هَذَا الْقَوْلَ لَيْسَ بِكُفْرِ بَلْ هُوَ مِمَّا اتَّفَقَ الْمُسْلِمُونَ عَلَى أَنَّهُ قَوْلٌ سَائِغٌ وَقَائِلُهُ مُجْتَهِدٌ مَأْجُورٌ عَلَى اجْتِهَادِهِ سَوَاءٌ أَصَابَ أَوْ أَخْطَأَ فَإِذَا أَصَرَّ عَلَى تَكْفِيرِ مَنْ تَبَيَّنَ بِالْكِتَابِ وَالسُّنَّةِ وَالْإِجْمَاعِ أَنَّهُ لَا يَكْفُرُ وَتَبَيَّنَ لَهُ أَنَّهُ يَكْفُرُ:
 فَأَصَرَّ عَلَى مُشَاقَّةِ الرَّسُولِ وَاتِّبَاعِ غَيْرِ سَبِيلِ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ فَإِنَّهُ يُسْتَتَابُ فَإِنْ تَابَ وَإِلَّا قُتِلَ كَمَنْ جَعَلَ اعْتِقَادَ أَنَّ الْمَسِيحَ عَبْدُ اللَّهِ مُعَادَاةً لِلْمَسِيحِ أَوْ اعْتَقَدَ أَنَّ مَنْ قَالَ: لَا تَحْلِفْ بِالْأَنْبِيَاءِ فَقَدْ عَادَاهُمْ وَكَفَرَ؛ فَإِنَّ مِثْلَ هَذَا يُسْتَتَابُ. وَمِنْهَا أَنَّ هَذِهِ الْمَسْأَلَةَ قَدْ نَصَّ عَلَيْهَا مَالِكٌ إمَامُهُ وَجُمْهُورُ أَصْحَابِهِ وَهُوَ فِي كُتُبِهِمْ الْكِبَارِ وَالصِّغَارِ وَهُوَ لَمْ يُعْرَفْ مِمَّا قَالُوا بَلْ يَكْفُرُ وَيُلْعَنُ وَيُشْتَمُ مَنْ قَالَ بِنَفْسِ الْقَوْلِ الَّذِي قَالُوهُ فَيَلْزَمُهُ تَكْفِيرُهُمْ وَسَبُّهُمْ وَاسْتِحْلَالُ دِمَائِهِمْ.
 وَمِنْهَا أَنَّهُ قَالَ:
 وَرَدَ فِي زِيَارَةِ قَبْرِهِ أَحَادِيثُ صَحِيحَةٌ وَغَيْرُهَا مِمَّا لَمْ يَبْلُغْ دَرَجَةَ الصَّحِيحِ؛ لَكِنَّهَا يَجُوزُ الِاسْتِدْلَالُ بِهَا عَلَى الْأَحْكَامِ
translated_text:
the Messenger and upheld by the earliest Muslims and the community’s imams, as attested by the Book and the Sunnah. If it becomes clear to him that this is what the Messenger brought, yet he persists in opposing the Messenger and following a path other than that of the believers, he must be called upon to repent; if he does not repent, he is to be put to death.

Likewise, if it becomes clear that this position does not constitute disbelief, but is one that Muslims agree is permissible to hold, and that its proponent exercises independent scholarly judgment and is rewarded for that effort, whether right or wrong—then, if he persists in declaring someone an unbeliever when the Book, the Sunnah, and scholarly consensus establish that this person is not an unbeliever, and it becomes clear to him that he is committing disbelief, yet he persists in opposing the Messenger and following a path other than that of the believers, he must be called upon to repent; if he does not repent, he is to be put to death. This is like someone who considers belief that the Messiah is Allah’s servant to be hostility towards the Messiah, or believes that anyone who says, “Do not swear by the prophets,” has thereby shown hostility towards them and become an unbeliever. Such a person must be called upon to repent.

Another point is that his own imam, Mālik, and the majority of Mālik’s followers explicitly addressed this issue. It appears in their books, both large and small, yet he is unfamiliar with what they said. Rather, he declares an unbeliever, curses, and insults anyone who holds the very position they held. His position thus entails declaring them unbelievers, reviling them, and deeming their blood lawful to shed.

Another point is his statement:

“Authentic hadiths have been transmitted concerning visiting his grave, along with others that do not reach the degree of authenticity, but which may nevertheless be cited as evidence for rulings

original_text:
الشَّرْعِيَّةِ. وَهَذَا كَلَامُ مَنْ لَا يَعْرِفُ مَا رُوِيَ فِي هَذَا الْبَابِ وَلَا مَا قَالَ فِيهِ عُلَمَاءُ الْمُسْلِمِينَ؛
 بَلْ هُوَ بِمَنْزِلَةِ الرافضي الَّذِي يَقُولُ:
 قَدْ رُوِيَ فِي النَّصِّ عَلَى عَلِيٍّ أَنَّهُ الْإِمَامُ بَعْدَ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ أَحَادِيثُ صَحِيحَةٌ وَأُخَرُ دُونَهَا.
 وَمَعْلُومٌ أَنَّ الْأَحَادِيثَ الَّتِي فِيهَا ذِكْرُ زِيَارَةِ قَبْرِهِ لَمْ يُخَرِّجْ شَيْئًا مِنْهَا أَهْلُ الصَّحِيحِ وَلَا السُّنَنِ الْمُعْتَمَدِ عَلَيْهَا:
 كَسُنَنِ أَبِي دَاوُد وَالتِّرْمِذِيِّ؛
 وَلَا الْمَسَانِيدِ الَّتِي هِيَ مِنْ هَذَا الْجِنْسِ:
 كَمُسْنَدِ أَحْمَد. وَلَا اسْتَدَلَّ بِشَيْءِ مِنْهَا إمَامٌ؛ وَهُوَ مَعَ ذَلِكَ لَمْ يَذْكُرْ مِنْهَا حَدِيثًا وَاحِدًا فَضْلًا عَنْ أَنْ يَعْزُوَهُ إلَى كِتَابٍ.
 وَقَوْلُهُ:
 إنَّ مَا لَمْ يَبْلُغْ دَرَجَةَ الصَّحِيحِ مِنْهَا يَجُوزُ الِاسْتِدْلَالُ بِهَا. إنَّمَا يَكُونُ إذَا كَانَتْ حَسَنَةً عِنْدَ مَنْ قَسَّمَ الْحَدِيثَ إلَى ثَلَاثَةِ أَنْوَاعٍ وَهَذَا مَوْقُوفٌ عَلَى الْعِلْمِ بِحُسْنِهَا وَأَئِمَّةُ الْحَدِيثِ لَمْ يَحْكُمُوا بِذَلِكَ وَهُوَ وَأَمْثَالُهُ لَا يَعْرِفُونَ ذَلِكَ.
 فَالْقَوْلُ بِذَلِكَ مِنْ أَعْظَمِ الْقَوْلِ بِلَا عِلْمٍ فِي الدِّينِ وَالْجُرْأَةِ عَلَى سُنَّةِ رَسُولِ رَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ:
 بِأَنْ يُدْخِلَ فِيهَا مَا لَيْسَ مِنْهَا بِالْجَهْلِ وَالضَّلَالِ. فَكَيْفَ إذَا كَانَ جَمِيعُ مَا رُوِيَ فِي هَذَا الْبَابِ مِمَّا ضَعَّفَهُ أَهْلُ الْمَعْرِفَةِ بِالْحَدِيثِ؛ بَلْ حَكَمُوا بِأَنَّهُ كَذِبٌ مَوْضُوعٌ كَمَا قَدْ بُسِطَ الْكَلَامُ عَلَى مَا رُوِيَ فِي هَذَا الْبَابِ فِي غَيْرِ هَذَا الْكِتَابِ.
وَمِنْهَا أَنَّهُ لَمْ يُفَرِّقْ بَيْنَ 
" الزِّيَارَةِ الشَّرْعِيَّةِ "
 الَّتِي كَانَ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ يَفْعَلُهَا وَمَقْصُودُهَا الدُّعَاءُ لِلْمَيِّتِ؛ كَالصَّلَاةِ عَلَى جِنَازَتِهِ
translated_text:
of Islamic law.” This is the statement of someone who knows neither what has been narrated on this subject nor what Muslim scholars have said about it. Rather, he is like a Rāfidī (rejectionist Shiite) who says:

“Authentic hadiths have been narrated explicitly designating Alī as the imam after the Messenger of Allah, along with others of a lesser grade.”

It is well known that none of the hadiths mentioning visitation to his grave were included by the compilers of the authentic hadith collections, the authoritative Sunan collections—such as those of Abū Dāwūd and al-Tirmidhī—or comparable Musnad collections, such as the Musnad of Ahmad. Nor has any imam cited any of them as evidence. Moreover, he has not mentioned even a single such hadith, let alone identified the book in which it appears.

As for his statement that those reports which do not reach the degree of authenticity may nevertheless be cited as evidence, this would apply only if they were graded good according to those who divide hadith into three categories. This depends on knowing that they merit that grade. Yet the leading hadith scholars have not judged them to be so, and neither he nor others like him possess such knowledge.

Such an assertion is among the gravest instances of speaking about religion without knowledge and presumptuously tampering with the Sunnah of the Messenger of the Lord of all worlds: introducing into it, through ignorance and misguidance, what does not belong to it. How much worse, then, when everything narrated on this subject has been judged weak by those knowledgeable in hadith—indeed, they have judged it to be fabricated falsehood—as has been discussed at length elsewhere than in this book.

Another point is that he has failed to distinguish between the “religiously prescribed visitation” which the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to perform, and whose purpose is to supplicate for the deceased, as in the funeral prayer for him

original_text:
وَبَيْنَ مَا ابْتَدَعَهُ الضَّالُّونَ مِنْ الْإِشْرَاكِ بِالْمَيِّتِ وَالْحَجِّ إلَى قَبْرِهِ وَدُعَائِهِ مِنْ دُونِ اللَّهِ وَمَقْصُودُهُ بِزِيَارَتِهِ وَالسَّفَرِ إلَيْهِ أَنَّهُ يَدْعُوهُ مِنْ دُونِ اللَّهِ؛ لَا أَنَّهُ يَدْعُو لَهُ. وَهَذِهِ الزِّيَارَةُ لَمْ يَفْعَلْهَا الرَّسُولُ وَلَا أَذِنَ فِيهَا قَطُّ؛ فَكَيْفَ بِالسَّفَرِ إلَيْهَا وَهُوَ مِنْ جِنْسِ الْحَجِّ إلَى الطَّوَاغِيتِ.
وَمِنْهَا أَنَّهُ جَعَلَ زِيَارَةَ الْمَيِّتِ كَزِيَارَتِهِ حَيًّا وَاسْتَدَلَّ بِحَدِيثِ 
{الَّذِي زَارَ أَخًا لَهُ فِي الْحَيَاةِ}
 عَلَى أَنَّهُ يُسْتَحَبُّ زِيَارَةُ الْمَيِّتِ وَهَذِهِ التَّسْوِيَةُ وَالْقِيَاسُ مَا عُرِفَتْ عَنْ أَحَدٍ مِنْ عُلَمَاءِ الْمُسْلِمِينَ؛
 فَإِنَّهُ مِنْ الْمَعْلُومِ أَنَّ الصَّحَابَةَ الَّذِينَ سَافَرُوا إلَى الرَّسُولِ فَسَاعَدُوهُ وَسَمِعُوا كَلَامَهُ وَخَاطَبُوهُ وَسَأَلُوهُ فَأَجَابَهُمْ وَعَلَّمَهُمْ وَأَدَّبَهُمْ وَحَمَّلَهُمْ رَسَائِلَ إلَى قَوْمِهِمْ وَأَمَرَهُمْ بِالتَّبْلِيغِ عَنْهُ:
 لَا يَكُونُ مِثْلَهُمْ أَحَدٌ بِالْأَعْمَالِ الْفَاضِلَةِ: كَالْجِهَادِ وَالْحَجِّ.
 فَكَيْفَ يَكُونُ بِمُجَرَّدِ رُؤْيَةِ ظَاهِرِ حُجْرَتِهِ مِثْلَهُمْ أَوْ تُقَاسُ هَذِهِ الزِّيَارَةُ بِهَذِهِ الزِّيَارَةِ فَقَدْ ثَبَتَ بِالسُّنَّةِ وَاتِّفَاقِ الْأُمَّةِ أَنَّ كُلَّ مَا يُفْعَلُ مِنْ الْأَعْمَالِ الصَّالِحَةِ فِي الْمَسْجِدِ عِنْدَ حُجْرَتِهِ مِنْ صَلَاةٍ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَامٍ وَثَنَاءٍ وَإِكْرَامٍ وَذِكْرِ مَحَاسِنَ وَفَضَائِلَ:
 مُمْكِنٌ فِعْلُهُ فِي سَائِرِ الْأَمَاكِنِ وَيَكُونُ لِصَاحِبِهِ مِنْ الْأَجْرِ مَا يَسْتَحِقُّهُ كَمَا قَالَ: 
{لَا تَتَّخِذُوا بَيْتِي عِيدًا وَصَلُّوا عَلَيَّ فَإِنَّ صَلَاتَكُمْ تَبْلُغُنِي حَيْثُ كُنْتُمْ}
 . وَلَوْ كَانَ لِلْأَعْمَالِ عِنْدَ الْقَبْرِ فَضِيلَةٌ لَفَتَحَ لِلْمُسْلِمِينَ بَابَ الْحُجْرَةِ؛ فَلَمَّا مُنِعُوا مِنْ الْوُصُولِ إلَى الْقَبْرِ
translated_text:
and what the misguided have innovated: associating the deceased with Allah in worship, making pilgrimage to his grave, and invoking him besides Allah. Such a person’s purpose in visiting the deceased and journeying to him is to invoke him besides Allah, not to supplicate for him. The Messenger never practiced this kind of visitation, nor did he ever permit it. How much worse, then, is journeying for this purpose, which is akin to making pilgrimage to false objects of worship!

Another point is that he equated visiting the deceased with visiting him during his lifetime, citing the hadith about “the man who visited a brother of his while the latter was alive” as evidence that visiting the deceased is recommended. No such equation or analogy is known to have been made by any Muslim scholar.

It is well known that no one, through virtuous deeds such as jihad and Hajj, can equal the Companions who journeyed to the Messenger, supported him, heard his words, spoke with him, and asked him questions which he answered; whom he taught and instructed in proper conduct; and whom he entrusted with messages for their people and commanded to convey his teachings. How, then, could someone equal them merely by seeing the exterior of his chamber? Or how could this visitation be compared with theirs?

The Sunnah and the consensus of the Muslim community establish that all the righteous deeds performed in the mosque beside his chamber—sending blessings and peace upon him, praising and honoring him, and recounting his admirable qualities and virtues—can be performed anywhere else, with those performing them receiving the reward they deserve. As he said:

“Do not make my house a place of recurring gatherings, and send blessings upon me, for your blessings reach me wherever you may be.”

Had deeds performed at the grave possessed any special merit, he would have opened the door of the chamber to the Muslims. Since, then, they were prevented from reaching the grave

original_text:
وَأُمِرُوا بِالْعِبَادَةِ فِي الْمَسْجِدِ:
 عُلِمَ أَنَّ فَضِيلَةَ الْعَمَلِ فِيهِ لِكَوْنِهِ فِي مَسْجِدِهِ كَمَا أَنَّ صَلَاةً فِي مَسْجِدِهِ بِأَلْفِ صَلَاةٍ فِيمَا سِوَاهُ وَلَمْ يَأْمُرْ قَطُّ بِأَنْ يُقْصَدَ بِعَمَلِ صَالِحٍ أَنْ يُفْعَلَ عِنْدَ قَبْرِهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ. وَمِنْهَا افْتِرَاؤُهُ عَلَى الْمُجِيبِ فِي مَوَاضِعَ مُتَعَدِّدَةٍ افْتِرَاءً ظَاهِرًا وَسَبَبُ افْتِرَائِهِ عَلَيْهِ أَنَّهُ ذَكَرَ قَوْلَ عُلَمَاءِ الْمُسْلِمِينَ وَرَجَّحَ مَا قَالَهُ مَالِكٌ وَغَيْرُهُ مِنْ السَّلَفِ لِكَوْنِ سُنَّةِ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ الصَّحِيحَةِ الصَّرِيحَةِ تُوَافِقُهُمْ وَهَذَا يَسْتَلْزِمُ مُعَادَاةَ اللَّهِ وَرَسُولِهِ؛ إذْ كُلُّ مَنْ عَادَى سُنَّتَهُ وَشَرِيعَتَهُ وَدِينَهُ فَقَدْ عَادَاهُ وَمَنْ عَادَى شَخْصًا لِأَجْلِ ذَلِكَ فَإِنَّمَا عَادَى الرَّسُولَ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ فِي الْحَقِيقَةِ وَإِنْ لَمْ يَقْصِدْ ذَلِكَ. فَكَيْفَ يَجُوزُ الْكَذِبُ وَالِافْتِرَاءُ مَرَّةً بَعْدَ مَرَّةٍ وَهُوَ كَذِبٌ ظَاهِرٌ. وَلَوْ كَانَ الْمُجِيبُ مُخْطِئًا لَمَا جَازَ ذَلِكَ؛ فَإِنَّ الْكَذِبَ وَالِافْتِرَاءَ حَرَامٌ مُطْلَقًا. وَاَللَّهُ أَوْجَبَ الصِّدْقَ وَالْعَدْلَ لِكُلِّ أَحَدٍ عَلَى كُلِّ أَحَدٍ فِي كُلِّ حَالٍ.

 قَوْلُهُ هَذَا الْمُتَضَمِّنُ عَدَاوَةَ الرَّسُولِ وَعَدَاوَةَ مَا جَاءَ بِهِ وَعَدَاوَةَ مَنْ اتَّبَعَهُ وَإِنْ لَمْ يَكُنْ عَالِمًا بِمَا تَضَمَّنَهُ قَوْلُهُ. فَقَوْلُهُ مَعَ عَدَمِ الْعِلْمِ مِنْ جِنْسِ أَقْوَالِ الْمُحَادِّينَ لِلَّهِ وَلِرَسُولِهِ الْمُوَالِينَ لِأَهْلِ
translated_text:
and were commanded to worship in the mosque, it is clear that the special merit of deeds performed there derives from their being performed in his mosque, just as one prayer in his mosque is worth a thousand prayers elsewhere. He—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—never commanded that any righteous deed be deliberately performed at his grave.

Another point is his blatant fabrications against the respondent in numerous passages. His reason for fabricating these allegations is that the respondent cited the views of Muslim scholars and favored the position of Mālik and others among the early generations, because the authentic, explicit Sunnah of Allah’s Messenger—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—supports their position. Such conduct entails enmity toward Allah and His Messenger, for whoever opposes his Sunnah, his law, and his religion has opposed him. Whoever bears enmity toward someone on that account is, in reality, bearing enmity toward the Messenger—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—even if he does not intend this. How, then, can repeated lies and fabrications be permissible when their falsehood is plain? Even if the respondent were mistaken, this would not be permissible, for lying and fabrication are forbidden without exception. Allah has required everyone to be truthful and just toward everyone else, in every circumstance.

How much worse, then, when the views cited by the respondent are those of people who follow the Messenger—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—while the objector disparages them and their statements, insults those who believe in the Messenger, obey him, and follow him, and declares them unbelievers for the very things that constitute following the Messenger and believing in him! This statement of his entails enmity toward the Messenger, toward what he brought, and toward those who follow him, even if he is unaware of what his statement entails. falsehood and polytheism who resemble Christians and their like, even though they do not realize that their statements entail this, owing to their limited knowledge, poor understanding, and lack of the qualifications needed for independent scholarly judgment, reasoning from scriptural evidence, and knowledge of what the leading religious scholars have said. Indeed, on a momentous issue such as this, they make statements whose speaker is in greater need of being called to repent, disciplined, taught, and helped to understand than of being refuted or engaged in debate. Similarly, among the ignorant adherents of religious innovations—the Rāfidah, the Kharijites, and others—are those who hasten to declare unbelievers those among the early generations who followed the Messenger, owing to their limited knowledge and poor understanding of what the Messenger brought. Thus, they adopt religious innovations out of ignorance and declare those who disagree with them unbelievers.

Those who adhere to the Sunnah and possess knowledge and faith, however, recognize the truth, follow the Messenger’s Sunnah, show mercy to people, treat them justly, and excuse those who strive to discover the truth but are unable to ascertain it. They condemn only those whom Allah and His Messenger condemn: those who neglect to seek the truth, thereby abandoning a duty, and those who transgress by following their desires without knowledge, thereby committing what is forbidden. Thus, they condemn anyone who neglects a duty or commits what is forbidden, but they do not punish him until the proof has been established against him, as the Most High says:

“We never punish until We have sent a messenger.”

This is especially so in matters over which scholars have differed and concerning which knowledge is obscure to most people. And anyone who does not speak in the manner of the people of

knowledge, but instead speaks recklessly without knowledge, is unfit for debate except in the manner in which one debates ignorant laypeople who follow religious innovations and resemble the polytheists and Christians. They regard anyone who speaks the truth about a created being as reviling and insulting him, while they themselves revile, insult, and offend Allah. They do not fear reviling and insulting the Creator and associating partners with Him as they fear speaking the truth about a created being. As Abraham, Allah’s intimate friend, said to them:

“How could I fear what you associate with Him, while you do not fear associating with Allah that for which He has sent down no authority to you? Which of the two parties has more right to security, if you know?”

“Those who believe and do not taint their faith with wrongdoing—it is they who will have security, and they are rightly guided.”

Likewise, the Most High says of the polytheists:

“When the disbelievers see you, they only ridicule you, saying, ‘Is this the one who speaks against your gods?’ Yet they themselves disbelieve in the mention of the Most Merciful.”

They are not as angered by false statements about the Most Merciful as they are by truthful statements about their gods.

The Most High also says:

“O People of the Scripture, do not go to extremes in your religion, and say nothing about Allah except the truth. The Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, was only a messenger of Allah, His word which He conveyed to Mary, and a spirit from Him. So believe in Allah and His messengers, and do not say, ‘Three.’ Desist—it is better for you. Allah is only One God. Exalted is He above having a son! To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on earth. And Allah is sufficient as a Guardian.”

“The Messiah would never disdain to be a servant of Allah, nor would the angels brought near to Him.”

translated_text:
when they came to the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace), said, ‘O Muhammad, have you not mentioned our companion?’ He asked, ‘Who is your companion?’ They replied, ‘Jesus.’ He said, ‘What should I say of him? He is Allah’s servant.’ They said, ‘Rather, he is Allah.’ He replied, ‘It is no disgrace for him to be a servant of Allah.’ They said, ‘Yes, it is.’ So Allah revealed this verse.”

In both Sahīh collections, the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) is reported to have said:

“No one is more patient than Allah with the offensive things he hears: they ascribe to Him a child and a partner, yet He grants them well-being and provides for them.”

It is also reported in both Sahīh collections that he said:

“Allah says: ‘The son of Adam insults Me, though he has no right to do so, and the son of Adam calls Me a liar, though he has no right to do so. His insult against Me is his claim that I have taken a child, whereas I am the One, the Self-Sufficient, who neither begets nor was begotten, and none is equal to Me. His calling Me a liar is his statement, “He will not bring me back as He first created me,” although creating him the first time is no easier for Me than bringing him back.’”

Mu‘ādh ibn Jabal used to say of the Christians: “Do not show them mercy, for they have insulted Allah as no other human beings have.”

These people disparage the Creator, yet resent a created being being described as he deserves. They regard this as disparaging him, whereas it merely gives him his due and lowers him from the rank of divinity, which none but Allah deserves. Such is also the condition of those who resemble them in certain respects.

Another is his assumption that any act of devotion may be pursued by any means.

Another is his assumption that no scholar has held such travel to be forbidden; rather, that the respondent—if his report is accurate—has attributed this view only to someone who cannot be relied upon and whose dissent carries no weight. Yet this is Mālik’s explicit statement concerning the Messenger’s grave in particular, and it is the position of the majority of his followers and of the early generations and scholars.

Another is his claim that, apart from those whose views the respondent cited—al-Ghazālī, Ibn ‘Abdūs and Abū Muhammad al-Maqdisī—no one’s dissent carries any weight, and no one else should be consulted on this matter. Such a statement cannot be made even about any of the great imams. Rather, everyone’s statements may be accepted or rejected, except those of the bearer of the revealed Law. How, then, can such a statement be justified concerning people like these?

Another is that, when he sought to establish that the Prophet hears invocations from nearby and is informed of blessings and greetings of peace sent from afar, he did not mention the good hadiths on this subject found in the Sunan collections. Instead, he relied solely on a fabricated hadith:

“Whoever invokes blessings upon me at my grave, I hear it; and whoever invokes blessings upon me from afar, I am informed of it.”

This is narrated only by Muhammad ibn Marwān al-Suddī from al-A‘mash. He is unanimously regarded as a liar, and they unanimously agree that this hadith was fabricated in al-A‘mash’s name. Moreover, he has altered its wording. For the copy I saw had the following wording, marked as correct:

Another error is his appeal to the consensus of the early and later generations concerning visiting his grave. He assumed that the response prohibited something upon which there was consensus. Yet the response explicitly stated that travelling to his mosque is an act of obedience by consensus. The same applies to the recommended acts it discussed that fall under what is called visiting his grave: invoking blessings and peace upon him; praying that he be granted al-Wasīlah and other blessings; bearing witness in his favor; praising him for the distinctions Allah has bestowed upon him; loving him, maintaining allegiance to him, supporting him and honoring him; and other acts that may fall within the meaning of visiting. All of this is recommended, and the respondent explicitly affirms that it is recommended.

The scholars have differed over whether this is to be called a visit. He mentioned their disagreements concerning those matters over which they differed, and their consensus concerning those upon which they agreed. was disputed in this regard. This man assumed that travelling to visit our Prophet is like travelling to visit other prophets and righteous people. This is mistaken for several reasons.

First: His mosque is beside his grave, and travelling to it is prescribed by the revealed texts and consensus, unlike the case of others.

Second: It is not possible to visit him as others are visited. A person can only reach his mosque and perform there the acts prescribed for him.

Third: If our Prophet’s grave were to be visited as other graves are visited, the residents of his city would be the people most entitled to do so, just as the residents of every city are most entitled to visit the righteous people buried among them. Yet the early generations and the leading scholars of the religion agreed that the residents of his city do not visit his grave, nor even stand beside it to offer greetings of peace when entering or leaving the mosque—even if this is not called a visit. Rather, doing so outside the context of travel is disliked for them, as Mālik stated, explaining that it is among the innovations that the earliest generations of this community did not practise. It follows that whoever considers visiting his grave prescribed in the same manner as visiting another person’s grave has contradicted the consensus of the Muslims.

Fourth: He forbade making his grave a place of recurring gatherings, and commanded his community to invoke blessings and peace upon him wherever they might be, informing them that this reaches him. Thus, singling out that place for supplication on his behalf is not prescribed. Rather, supplication is made on his behalf in all places and at every

Allah has distinguished him with an excellence shared by no one else, so that his grave should not be treated like other graves. Rather, a distinction is drawn between them in several respects, making clear his superiority over others and the blessings Allah has bestowed upon his community.

Another point is his statement:

These words display ignorance of the Sharia and of what the Muslims have agreed upon, and equate worship of the Most Merciful—which the believers unanimously uphold—with worship of idols—which they unanimously prohibit. They also state that a journey constituting obedience to Allah and a means of drawing near to Him is one undertaken for the purpose of praying in the mosque; and that if someone vows to travel to Medina for a purpose other than praying in the mosque, he is forbidden to fulfil his vow, because it is a vow involving disobedience. Since this position of theirs is well known in works both short and lengthy, how can anyone suppose that the leading scholars unanimously agree on travelling solely to visit graves?

Another group of scholars call this visiting his grave. They say, “It is recommended to visit his grave,” or, “to travel to visit his grave.” By visiting, they mean what the first group means: travelling to his mosque and performing there the prescribed acts of invoking blessings and peace upon him, supplicating for him, and praising him. This is what they call visiting his grave, although all agree that no one visits his grave in the manner familiar with other graves. Those graves are in the open and can be approached, and one can sit or stand beside them. It is possible to perform beside them both prescribed acts, such as supplicating for the deceased and seeking forgiveness for him, and prohibited acts, such as calling upon him, associating him with Allah in worship, wailing at his grave, and uttering laments. This is what is understood by “visiting graves.”

The Messenger was buried in his house, in his chamber, and he prohibited people from entering there and gaining access to his grave. Thus, no one can visit his grave as one visits another person’s grave, whether in a manner prescribed by the Sharia or an innovated manner. Rather, everyone can reach only

his mosque, where they perform acts that are prescribed for them or disapproved. Travel to his mosque, being prescribed, is unanimously regarded as an act of obedience to Allah and a means of drawing near to Him. It is this on which the Muslims are unanimous. The respondent has stated in many places that this journey is recommended, and that its recommendation is established by scriptural evidence and consensus. He has also stated this in the present answer, explaining what is established by scriptural evidence and consensus concerning travel to his mosque and visiting him in the manner prescribed by the Sharia. He has also explained what is not prescribed concerning travel to visit the graves of others among the prophets and the righteous. For travelling to those places is not travelling to a mosque to which travel has been prescribed. Indeed, even if the mosques there are ones whose construction and use for prayer are prescribed—such as the Muslims’ congregational mosques in their cities—travelling to them is neither a means of drawing near to Allah nor an act of obedience, according to either the four imams or the Muslim imams generally.

All agree that travelling to them falls within his saying:

“No journey is to be undertaken except to three mosques.”

This is an exceptive construction in which the general term is left unstated. There are two possible ways of supplying it.

The first is to understand it as: “No journey is to be undertaken” to any mosque “except the three mosques.” Its explicit wording would thus prohibit journeys to other mosques, while its implication, its purport, and a fortiori reasoning would prohibit journeys to all other places believed to possess special merit. For, according to scriptural evidence and consensus, mosques and worship within them are dearer to Allah than worship in those places. Thus, a place may at one time be a frontier and at another not, just as it may at one time be a land of Islam and righteousness and at another a land of unbelief and wickedness. Mecca was once a land of unbelief and war, while Medina was a land of faith and emigration and a place of frontier duty. When Mecca was conquered, it became a land of Islam, and Medina was no longer a place of emigration and frontier duty as it had been before the conquest of Mecca. Indeed, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“There is no emigration after the conquest, but jihad and intention remain. When you are called to arms, go forth.”

The frontier regions then became the outer reaches of the Hijāz bordering the lands at war with the Muslims: Syria and Iraq. When the Muslims subsequently conquered Syria and Iraq, the frontier regions in Syria shifted to the seacoast, including Ashkelon, Acre, and the surrounding areas; in Iraq, they included Abbādān and similar places. This is why “Ashkelon” and “Abbādān” are frequently mentioned in the writings of earlier scholars: both were frontier towns. “Tartūsh” was also a frontier town when it belonged to the Muslims. When the unbelievers captured it, the frontier shifted to those parts of the Aleppo region bordering enemy territory.

Someone travelling to the frontier regions, to seek knowledge, to trade, or to visit a relative does not seek a particular place except incidentally, because he knows that what he seeks is there. Were it elsewhere, he would go there instead.

Scholars agree that travel of this kind is not covered by the hadith. Rather, it covers someone who travels to a particular place because of the virtue of that very place, such as someone travelling to mosques and sites associated with the prophets, including Mount Sinai, where Allah spoke to

Moses, the cave of Hirā’, where revelation first came to the Messenger, and the cave of Thawr, mentioned in the Quran in His words:

“When the two were in the cave”

—as well as caves and mountains of lesser standing, as in travelling to Mount Lebanon, the Cave of Blood, and the like. Many people travel to mountains and caves that they believe possess special merit. If travelling to Mount Sinai, where Allah spoke to Moses and which He called the blessed spot and the sacred valley, is not recommended, then there is all the more reason not to travel to other mountains.

When I say “by consensus,” I mean the consensus of the early generations and the imams. The Companions, including Ibn ‘Umar, Abū Sa‘īd, Abū Basrah, and others, understood the Prophet’s words, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Do not undertake a journey except to three mosques”

to include within the prohibition Mount Sinai, where Allah spoke to Moses and which He called the sacred valley and the blessed spot. They forbade people to travel there and did not restrict the prohibition to mosques. Accordingly, no one held that a vow makes such a journey obligatory. I know of no early disagreement concerning this, nor have I seen anyone explicitly state a contrary view except Ibn Hazm al-Zāhirī. Like the majority, he prohibits travelling to a mosque other than the three when one has vowed to do so. Yet if someone vows to travel to a site associated with the prophets, he considers fulfilling that vow obligatory, because he does not accept what an utterance implies or indicates beyond its literal wording. This is one of the two views reported from Dāwūd. Thus, he does not regard His words:

“Do not say to them even ‘ugh’”

If we consider the cave of Hirā’, the people of Mecca used to climb up to it to worship, and it is said that ‘Abd al-Muttalib instituted this practice among them. Before his prophethood, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to devote himself to worship there, and it was there that revelation first came to him. Yet once revelation had come to him, he never climbed up to it again or approached it—neither he nor his Companions. He remained in Mecca for ten-odd years after becoming a prophet without visiting it or climbing up to it, and the believers with him in Mecca did likewise. After the Hijrah, he came to Mecca several times: for the ‘umrah of al-Hudaybiyah; in the year of the conquest, when he stayed there for nearly twenty days; and for the ‘umrah of al-Ji‘rānah. Yet he neither went to the cave of Hirā’ nor visited it.

If, then, this cave is not to be travelled to or visited, there is all the more reason not to visit other caves, such as the Cave of Blood and the like. For, since the Messenger’s mission began, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, acts of worship such as prayer, remembrance of Allah, and supplication have been prescribed in every place: “The whole earth has been made a place of prayer and a means of purification for him and his community.”

The places possessing special merit are the mosques, which are the places most beloved to Allah, as authentically reported from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. It is in them that devotional retreat is observed.

so devotional retreat may be observed only in mosques, by scholarly agreement, as Allah Most High says:

“And do not have relations with them as long as you are staying for worship in the mosques.”

Devotional retreat, whether in seclusion or otherwise, is not to be observed in a cave, at a grave, or at any other place to which misguided people deliberately travel and where they remain in devotion, just as the polytheists remain devoted to their idols.

Abraham, Allah’s intimate friend, said:

“What are these statues to which you are devoted?”

And Allah Most High says:

“We took the Children of Israel across the sea, and they came upon a people devoted to their idols. They said, ‘O Moses, make for us a god just as they have gods.’ He said, ‘You are indeed an ignorant people.’”

“What these people are engaged in is doomed to destruction, and all that they have been doing is in vain.”

A fuller discussion of this belongs elsewhere.

It is authentically reported that Sa‘īd ibn al-Musayyib said:

“Whoever vows to observe devotional retreat in the mosque of Jerusalem, then observes it in the Prophet’s Mosque in Medina, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, has fulfilled his vow. Whoever vows to observe devotional retreat in the mosque of Medina, then observes it in the Sacred Mosque, has fulfilled his vow. Whoever vows to observe devotional retreat on mountaintops should not do so; rather, let him observe it in a congregational mosque.”

The general body of scholars agrees on the prohibition stated by Sa‘īd. Even supposing that a person does not call this devotional retreat, anyone who does outside a mosque what someone observing devotional retreat does inside one is observing devotional retreat outside a mosque, and this is prohibited by scholarly agreement. A fuller discussion of this belongs elsewhere.

This is because they have no argument for travelling to the graves of the other prophets except the journey to our Prophet. Since travelling to that place is prescribed in principle, they drew an analogy with it to justify travelling to other graves. Thus they went astray and led others astray, contradicting the Book of Allah, the Sunnah of His Messenger, and the consensus of the Muslims. They erred in many respects.

Among them is that the only prophet’s grave on earth known through mass transmission and consensus is the grave of our Prophet; all others are disputed.

Another is that those who recommended travelling to visit our Prophet’s grave meant travelling to his mosque, which is prescribed by consensus. Even if a traveller intends to visit the grave, he reaches only the mosque, and the mosque is the endpoint of his journey: he does not reach the grave itself. This differs from visiting another grave, where he does reach the grave.

The exception would be someone steeped in ignorance and misguidance who supposes that travelling to his mosque was prescribed only because of the grave; that this is why prayer there is equivalent to a thousand prayers; and that, were it not for the grave, the mosque would have no special merit over others. Or he might suppose that the mosque was built or designated as an adjunct to the grave, just as mosques are built over the graves of prophets and righteous people, and that praying in the mosque is secondary, while the grave is the real object of the visit. This is what those who travel to the graves of prophets and righteous people other than our Prophet suppose. It is like someone who goes to the Friday prayer and, upon entering, offers two units of prayer to greet the mosque: he came for the Friday prayer, not for those two units of prayer.

Islam, and the most ignorant of the lives of the Messenger and his Companions, and of his conduct, sayings, and deeds. Such a person needs to learn what he does not know of the religion of Islam, so that he may enter Islam rather than accept some of it and abandon the rest. His mosque was founded upon piety in the first year after the Hijrah, and it is the finest mosque on earth except for the Sacred Mosque. It has also been said that it is the finest without exception.

Would any rational person say that Muslim mosques—the congregational mosques in which Friday and other prayers are offered—derive their merit, and the recommendation to go there to pray, from a nearby grave? If this cannot be said of such mosques, how could it be said of one that is better and more excellent than them all?

According to the majority of scholars, the “Sacred Mosque” is the finest of all mosques without exception, and a prayer there is equivalent to a hundred thousand prayers, as reported in the Musnad and the Sunan collections. Would any rational person say that its merit is due to a grave there?

“Al-Aqsā Mosque” is the finest mosque after the Prophet’s Mosque, and Jerusalem contains so many graves of prophets that only Allah can count them. Would any rational person say that its merit is due to those graves? Indeed, this is what Christians believe: they believe that Jerusalem owes its merit to the “church” said to have been built over the grave of the crucified man, and they regard it as superior to Jerusalem’s sanctuary. These people are among the most misguided and ignorant of all.

And this resembles the practice of the polytheists at the Sacred Mosque when it contained idols and they would go there for the sake of those idols. They did not pray there; rather, as Allah Most High said:

“Their prayer at the House was nothing but whistling and clapping.”

Yet they revered the House itself and circumambulated it, just as they performed pilgrimage every year, despite the changes they had made to the religious law of Abraham. This continued until Allah sent Muhammad with guidance and the religion of truth, and commanded that the faith of Abraham be followed. Muhammad proclaimed it, called people to it, established the pilgrimage according to what Allah had prescribed for Abraham, and purged the House of polytheism. Allah Most High revealed:

“It is not for the polytheists to maintain the mosques of Allah while bearing witness against themselves to their disbelief. Their deeds have come to nothing, and they will abide in the Fire forever.

“Only those who believe in Allah and the Last Day, establish prayer, give zakah, and fear none but Allah maintain the mosques of Allah. It is they who may be among the rightly guided.”

He thus made clear that those who maintain the mosques are those who fear none but Allah. Whoever fears none but Allah places his hope and trust in Him alone, for hope and fear are inseparable. Those who make pilgrimages to graves call upon their occupants, implore them, worship them, fear others besides Allah, and place their hope in others besides Allah—like the polytheists who fear their gods and place their hope in them. Thus, when they said to Hūd, peace be upon him, “We say only that some of our gods have afflicted you with evil,” he said, “I call Allah to witness—and you too bear witness—that I am free of what

you worship besides Him. So plot against me, all of you, and give me no respite. I have put my trust in Allah, my Lord and your Lord. There is no living creature but He holds it by its forelock. Indeed, my Lord is on a straight path.”

When they disputed with Abraham, peace be upon him, he said to them:

“Do you dispute with me concerning Allah when He has guided me? I do not fear those you associate with Him, unless my Lord wills something. My Lord encompasses all things in knowledge. Will you not take heed? How could I fear those you associate with Him, while you do not fear associating with Allah that for which He has sent down no authority to you? Which of the two parties has more right to security, if you know? Those who believe and do not mix their faith with wrongdoing—it is they who will have security, and they are rightly guided.”

When they tried to frighten Muhammad—may Allah’s blessings and peace be upon him—with those besides Allah, Allah Most High said:

“Is Allah not sufficient for His servant? Yet they try to frighten you with those besides Him. Whoever Allah leaves astray has no guide, and whoever Allah guides, none can lead astray. Is Allah not Almighty, capable of retribution? If you ask them who created the heavens and the earth, they will surely say, ‘Allah.’ Say, ‘Have you considered those you call upon besides Allah? If Allah intends harm for me, could they remove the harm He inflicts? Or if He intends mercy for me, could they withhold His mercy?’ Say, ‘Allah is sufficient for me. In Him let those who trust put their trust.’”

And He Most High said:

“Say, ‘Call upon those you associate with Allah, then plot against me and give me no respite. Indeed, my Protector is Allah, who sent down the Book, and He protects the righteous.’”

As for the consensus some have claimed that a particular grave is superior to all mosques, this is a claim newly introduced into Islam. It is not known to have been held by any of the early generations. Rather, one of the later scholars mentioned it, and another took it from him and supposed it to be a consensus, on the grounds that the bodies of the prophets themselves are superior to mosques. Yet their argument applies to all believers: their bodies are superior to any earth in the world. The superiority of their bodies does not entail that their dwellings, whether in life or in death, are superior. Indeed, it is self-evident from their religion that their mosques are superior to their dwellings.

Some may appeal to the report:

“Every newborn is sprinkled with some earth from his burial pit.”

Thus, they argue, he was created from the earth of his grave. This argument is invalid for two reasons.

The first is that this is not established, and all the reports concerning it are weak. It is known with certainty that no earth has been sprinkled over the fetus in its mother’s womb. Rather, it was Adam himself who was created from earth; his descendants were then created from an extract of a lowly fluid. It is also known that no portion of that earth is distinguishable as belonging to one person, and another portion to someone else. For when it was transformed into a living body, as the spirit was breathed into Adam, it no longer remained earth. A fuller discussion of this belongs elsewhere.
